title: Gene Therapy: Advances in Delivery Systems, Genome Editing Technologies, and Applications in Human and Veterinary Medicine.
text: Gene therapy has emerged as a revolutionary therapeutic strategy for the treatment of inherited, acquired, and age-related diseases through the modification, replacement, or correction of defective genes. Advances in molecular biology, viral engineering, and genome-editing technologies have significantly enhanced the efficiency and safety of gene delivery systems. This review provides a comprehensive overview of gene therapy, including its classification, delivery methods, and therapeutic applications in both human and veterinary medicine. Viral vectors such as adenoviral, retroviral, lentiviral, adeno-associated viral, and poxviral vectors remain the most effective delivery platforms owing to their high transduction efficiency, whereas non-viral approaches including physical and chemical delivery systems offer improved biosafety and reduced immunogenicity. Recent developments in gene-editing technologies, particularly clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein systems, have expanded the therapeutic potential of gene therapy by enabling precise genome modifications. The review highlights the successful application of gene therapy in treating genetic disorders, cancer gene therapy, retinal diseases, neuromuscular disorders, hemophilia, and metabolic diseases in humans, as well as inherited and acquired diseases in companion and livestock animals. Despite remarkable progress, challenges related to delivery efficiency, immune responses, off-target effects, manufacturing scalability, regulatory approval, and long-term safety continue to limit widespread clinical implementation. Advances in vector design, genome-editing precision, artificial intelligence-assisted development, and regulatory frameworks are expected to address these limitations. Overall, gene therapy and CRISPRbased technologies represent promising platforms for the development of next-generation precision medicines that could transform disease management in both human and veterinary healthcare.

title: CRISPR opens the door to targeted therapy against glioblastoma (Review).
text: The progression in molecular understanding of glioblastoma (GBM) enables the identification of key therapeutic targets, allowing the advances of targeted therapy in GBM. However, to date, most clinical trial results have been disappointing. The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) system is a revolutionary genome‑editing tool that has the potential to improve basic research and therapy for GBM. In the present review, the current status and challenges of targeted therapy in GBM are examined. As a potential approach to address the challenges, the development process and application scope of CRISPR are investigated. Furthermore, the application of CRISPR in the study of GBM is explored, mainly by conducting CRISPR screens and employing CRISPR to target genes associated with the malignant phenotype of GBM. Finally, delivery of CRISPR/CRISPR‑associated protein 9 (Cas9) for the treatment of GBM is briefly reviewed.

title: AAV8-mediated CasRx delivery and expression in the cochlea and cochlear nucleus of mice.
text: CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing has made substantial progress in recent years and has enabled the treatment of a variety of genetic diseases, including hearing loss in congenitally deaf mice. However, successful gene editing for hereditary deafness may still induce off-target mutations in genomic DNA, which limits its clinical translation. CasRx, also known as RfxCas13d, is a compact RNA-targeting CRISPR effector that can be packaged into AAV vectors for in vivo delivery. CasRx, a recently identified member of the type VI CRISPR system, modulates target RNA expression without altering DNA sequences, thereby avoiding permanent off-target mutations and offering broad therapeutic potential. Here, we used adeno-associated virus serotype 8 (AAV8) to deliver CasRx into the cochlea and cochlear nucleus (CN) of C57BL/6J mice and evaluated its expression pattern and short-term safety. Two weeks after viral injection, the number and morphology of neurons and other cell types in the CN remained normal. Importantly, auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds were unchanged after viral delivery, indicating that AAV8-mediated CasRx expression did not detectably impair auditory function during the short observation period. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the feasibility and short-term safety of AAV8-mediated CasRx delivery and expression in the cochlea and cochlear nucleus, providing a delivery platform for future guide RNA-directed transcript-modulation studies in auditory disorders.

title: Unlocking genetic accessibility in Halomonas bluephagenesis: A high-efficiency transformation chassis enables linear DNA-mediated genome editing.
text: Halomonas bluephagenesis has emerged as a promising chassis for industrial biotechnology distinguished by its halophilic robustness and capacity for open and continuous fermentation. However, its poor transformability has substantially limited rapid, iterative, and automatable strain engineering. Here, we develop a "restriction release" strategy that increases transformation efficiency from approximately 102 to 107 cfu/μg DNA, rivaling the efficiency of standard laboratory Escherichia coli. A spontaneous IS30 insertion disrupting the type II restriction endonuclease gene notI increased plasmid transformation efficiency by about 2000-fold. Targeted deletion of notI reproduced this phenotype, confirming its role as a major barrier. Further deletion of the DNA phosphorothioation restriction locus dptFGH yielded an additional 10 to 37-fold improvement, generating the highly transformable ΔEPSΔFlgΔNotIΔPTRes chassis. Notably, the enhanced chassis further facilitated two linear-DNA-based editing strategies: direct RecET-mediated pyrF deletion using a linear donor coupled with phenotypic selection, achieving a recombination efficiency of 16.7%, and CRISPR/Cas9-assisted ribDHBA promoter replacement via co-delivery of a gRNA plasmid and a linear donor, achieving an efficiency of 11.1%. Together, these results identify endogenous restriction systems as primary barriers to genetic manipulation in H. bluephagenesis. Stepwise restriction release markedly improves plasmid transformation and enables linear DNA-mediated genome editing, providing an improved genetic platform for the iterative engineering of this industrial halophile. More broadly, this study suggests a practical strategy for overcoming the genetic inaccessibility of other non-model microorganisms and accelerating iterative strain engineering.

title: S100A4 facilitates influenza A virus replication by interacting with M2 in human alveolar epithelial cells.
text: Influenza A virus (IAV) replication depends on host cells and is regulated by numerous host factors. Therefore, investigating and understanding the role of these host factors is a significant topic. In this study, we found the IAV replication was attenuated after host factor S100 calcium-binding protein A4 (S100A4) was knocked down with RNAi or knockout with CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing technology. Conversely, IAV replication was enhanced upon the overexpression in A549 cells. The interaction between S100A4 and the IAV M2 protein was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation. Meanwhile, confocal microscopy experiment demonstrated that the viral M2 protein co-localized with endogenous S100A4 in IAV-infected A549 cells. Truncation analysis confirmed that amino acids 45-62 of the M2 protein constitute the main interaction region with S100A4. Further study showed that viral entry was reduced after S100A4 deletion. And the polymerase activity was significantly decreased in S100A4-knockout A549 cells compared to that in wild-type A549 cells. The S100A4 overexpression resulted in the downregulation of IFN-β, while the mRNA levels of the interferon-stimulated genes ISG15 and BST2 were also significantly reduced. Therefore, the host factor S100A4 was a positive modulator of IAV replication and was involved in the viral entry, polymerase activity maintenance and innate immune regulation. Collectively, our findings shed new light on the molecular mechanisms governing IAV infection and suggest a previously underexplored avenue for antiviral therapeutic intervention.

title: Application of AI-designed OpenCRISPR-1 for highly efficient gene editing in soybean (Glycine max L.) and Nicotiana benthamiana.
text: The widespread application of CRISPR/Cas genome editing for commercial crop improvement is currently hindered by a complex and restrictive intellectual property (IP) landscape. The recent development of OpenCRISPR-1, a fully AI-designed Cas9-like nuclease, provides a promising alternative with an accessible licensing framework; however, its efficacy in dicotyledonous plants remains largely uncharacterized. Here, we report the successful adaptation of the OpenCRISPR-1 system for targeted mutagenesis in soybean (Glycine max L.) and Nicotiana benthamiana. We constructed a plant-optimized binary vector (pBSE-OpenCRISPR-1) and validated its editing capability. In soybean (Glycine max), an Agrobacterium rhizogenes-mediated hairy root transformation assay targeting the GmFAD2-1B gene demonstrated that OpenCRISPR-1 actively induces site-specific mutations. In Nicotiana benthamiana, stable Agrobacterium-mediated transformation targeting the phytoene desaturase homologs (NbPDSa/b) achieved overall editing in 75% of T0 transgenic lines (27/36). Analysis of individual homologs revealed editing rates of 66.7% (24/36) at both the NbPDSa and NbPDSb loci. Complete editing of the target locus occurred in 13.9% of events for NbPDSb and 2.8% for NbPDSa, including one event (2.8%) displaying simultaneous complete editing across all alleles resulting in a visible albino phenotype. Deep amplicon and Sanger sequencing revealed a characteristic mutation profile dominated by small insertions and deletions occurring two to three nucleotides upstream of the PAM. These results demonstrate that the AI-designed OpenCRISPR-1 system is a highly active and versatile nuclease for dicot genome engineering. By providing expanded freedom-to-operate, this tool broadens access to crop trait improvement worldwide.

title: Microbiome-guided rhizosphere engineering for sustainable remediation of agricultural soil contaminants.
text: Agricultural soils increasingly carry mixtures of pesticide residues, heavy metals, petroleum hydrocarbons and microplastics, and conventional phytoremediation is too slow and too contaminant-specific to address them. Rhizosphere engineering, the deliberate manipulation of root-associated microbial communities, is widely proposed as the alternative, but the literature reports laboratory, pot and field results in a single register, so a reader cannot easily tell which approaches are deployable. This mini-review stratifies that evidence rather than surveying it. Every approach examined is assigned to one of three tiers: field-validated, emerging at pot or microcosm scale, or conceptual. Only two domains prove to be field-validated, namely metal immobilization and phytoextraction through bioaugmentation and bulk amendment, and hydrocarbon rhizoremediation by defined consortia; both rest on cultured isolates rather than engineered organisms. Microplastic rhizoremediation has not been demonstrated in soil, and we separate interception, adsorption, weathering, transformation and mineralization to show why reported removal is usually not degradation. Synthetic biology, CRISPR-based community editing and computational design remain conceptual, and we set out the horizontal gene transfer, containment, non-target and regulatory obstacles that stand between them and field use. We identify the measurements that would move an approach from one tier to the next, and argue that the principal deficit in this field is not technical capability but field-scale evidence reported to a common standard.

title: Subfunctionalization with Partially Overlapping Roles of AGAMOUS Paralogs RdAG1 and RdAG2 of Rhododendron delavayi in Floral Organ Development.
text: Rhododendron delavayi is an important ornamental plant in Southwest China that produces large showy flowers, yet the molecular basis of its complex floral morphology remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the functional divergence of two AGAMOUS (AG) paralogs, RdAG1 and RdAG2, to elucidate floral organ development. Our results support a subfunctionalization model with partially overlapping functions: RdAG1 likely acts as a C-class gene mainly for stamen and carpel identity, whereas RdAG2 likely acts as a D-class gene primarily for pistil and ovule development. Heterologous expression in Arabidopsis thaliana and Nicotiana benthamiana revealed both divergent and overlapping phenotypic effects: the two genes differed in their tendencies to induce stamen-like and pistil-like structures, yet both induced homeotic conversion of sepals into carpels and were associated with downregulation of class A genes. Since an efficient regeneration system has not yet been established for R. delavayi, the C/D-class functional assignment is based on heterologous expression and awaits validation in native floral tissues. Yeast two-hybrid assays confirmed the physical interaction between RdAG1 and RdAG2, while DAP-seq in floral buds identified RdGIK as a shared downstream target. Transcriptomic analysis of calli generated via Agrobacterium-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 editing revealed that the majority of downstream targets were classified as showing additive responses, while a smaller subset deviated from this additive expectation. Collectively, these findings define a subfunctionalization model for RdAG1 and RdAG2, providing a foundation for further investigation of their finely tuned functions in floral organ development in R. delavayi.

title: Virus-like particles enable highly efficient gene editing across porcine and avian in vitro, ex vivo, and in ovo models.
text: Pigs and chickens are not only the most important livestock species for global food production but also serve as key model organisms in various research disciplines. The pig is widely used in translational research due to its anatomical and physiological similarity to humans, providing valuable insights into immunology, metabolism, and disease mechanisms. In contrast, the chicken has become an essential model for studies related to poultry health, animal welfare, and developmental biology. Its externally developing embryo offers exceptional accessibility for experimental manipulation. Recent advances in genome editing technologies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9, have further expanded the potential of these species for functional genomic studies, although the efficient delivery of such tools remains a major challenge. Here, we overcome this delivery limitation by using virus-like particles (VLPs). We evaluated VLPs as delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools in porcine and avian cultures, two key livestock species at the human-animal interface. VLP-mediated delivery enabled efficient Cre recombination and high CRISPR/Cas9 editing rates in porcine cells, organoids, and oocytes, particularly when multiplexed. In chickens, VLPs supported robust Cre recombination and Cas9-mediated editing in cell culture, tracheal organ cultures, and in ovo. Reporter VLPs and dCas9 VLPs further demonstrated the versatility of this platform across porcine and avian systems. Together, these findings establish VLPs as an efficient and time-saving strategy for gene editing in livestock cultures across in vitro, ex vivo and in ovo systems, with potential future applications for animal health, agricultural productivity, and translational One Health research.

title: Tumor-Specific Gene Editing Enhances Cancer Immunogenicity through Succinate Metabolism-Mediated MHC-I Reprogramming.
text: Impaired expression of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) greatly compromises cytotoxic T-cell-mediated anticancer immunotherapy. Existing MHC-I activation strategies are greatly challenged by poor tumor specificity and off-target toxicity. Herein, we report a dual tumor-specific CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system that can precisely knock out succinate dehydrogenase subunit C (Sdhc) to activate the MHC-I pathway via epigenetic and transcriptional regulation. A tumor-specific gene editor is first engineered via reversible shielding of sgRNA using an apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1)-responsive, complementary ssDNA, yielding AP-sgRNA with blocked editing activity in normal cells yet completely restored activity in APE1-overexpressing tumor cells. Subsequently, tumor-targeted delivery of AP-sgRNA and Cas9 mRNA (mCas9) is achieved using dibenzocyclooctyne-decorated lipid nanoparticle (DLNP), which upon bioorthogonal click reaction can anchor cancer cells that are prelabeled with azido groups using the unnatural sugar DCL-AAM. Thus, AP-sgSdhc/mCas9@DLNP enables efficient and selective Sdhc editing in tumor cells, leading to epigenetic and transcriptional activation of MHC-antigen processing and presentation genes and thereby provoking robust antitumor efficacy in the B16-OVA melanoma model through enhanced, T cell-mediated immune responses. Moreover, it completely suppressed pulmonary metastasis after combination with aPD-L1 in the 4T1 lung metastasis model. This study provides an enlightened paradigm for precision gene editing and renders a promising mechanism for potentiating cancer immunotherapy.

title: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Palindromic Repeats-Cas Genome-Editing Systems in Filamentous Fungi: Current Tools, Optimization Strategies, and Future Perspectives.
text: Filamentous fungi are important microbial cell factories for producing antibiotics, organic acids, enzymes, and other valuable products, with broad applications in food, agriculture, and medicine. However, inefficient and imprecise genome editing remains a major bottleneck limiting rational strain engineering. This review summarizes major genome-editing tools in filamentous fungi, including Cre-loxP, TALENs, and CRISPR-Cas systems, with emphasis on their mechanisms, advantages, and limitations. We highlight CRISPR-Cas9 as the predominant platform and discuss optimization strategies involving sgRNA design, engineered Cas9 variants, promoter engineering, AMA1-based replicative plasmids, and ribonucleoprotein delivery. Emerging technologies, including base editing, prime editing, Cas12a, and Mad7, are also discussed for their potential to broaden editing capabilities. Finally, we outline future perspectives focusing on extending the application of existing genome-editing systems in filamentous fungi and discovering novel genome-editing tools from large-scale omics data sets. This review will accelerate the development of filamentous fungi as versatile platforms for biomanufacturing.

title: Mapping Osteosarcoma Biology With CRISPR/Cas: From Gene Function to Therapeutic Targets.
text: Osteosarcoma is a highly aggressive primary bone malignancy characterized by rapid proliferation, chemoresistance, and early metastasis. Recent advances in CRISPR/Cas (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/CRISPR-associated proteins) genome editing have enabled precise targeting of oncogenes, tumor suppressors, and regulators of epigenetic, metabolic, and signaling pathways, providing new insights into osteosarcoma biology. CRISPR-mediated knockout of cell-cycle regulators, including CDK11, impairs proliferation, while restoration of TP53 and suppression of TERT promoter activity inhibits tumor growth. Other line of studies has revealed that chemoresistance mechanisms mediated by ABCB1/MDR1, CD44, ATR, RAD18, and autophagy-related genes have been effectively reversed through CRISPR interventions, restoring sensitivity to cisplatin and doxorubicin. Furthermore, CRISPR applications in immune modulation, such as PD-L1 knockout, may enhance antitumor immunity. Importantly, high-throughput CRISPR screens also may identify essential genes, novel oncogenic drivers, and synthetic lethal targets, thus informing potential precision therapeutic strategies. This review aims to critically summarize CRISPR/Cas-mediated studies in osteosarcoma, focusing on targeting oncogenes and tumor suppressors, overcoming chemoresistance, modulating immune responses, regulating metabolism and autophagy, and identifying essential genes and vulnerabilities, providing a translational framework for precision therapy.

title: SmMYB44, a transcriptional repressor, negatively regulates anthocyanin biosynthesis in eggplant (Solanum melongena L.).
text: Anthocyanins are the main flavonoid secondary metabolites in plants. They not only protect plants against diverse biotic and abiotic stresses but also provide human health benefits. In this study, SmMYB44, an R2R3-MYB transcription factor, was identified from the photosensitive eggplant cultivar 'Lanshan Hexian'. SmMYB44 was localized in the nucleus, induced by light, and expressed specifically in peel, petals and roots. Overexpression of SmMYB44 in transgenic eggplant significantly inhibited anthocyanin accumulation, whereas virus-induced gene silencing of SmMYB44 in fruit peels markedly increased anthocyanin content and upregulated the transcription levels of key biosynthetic genes SmCHS and SmF3H. Furthermore, Agrobacterium-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 editing of NtMYB44 in tobacco cultivar K326, with an editing efficiency of 84.62%, markedly suppressed NtMYB44 transcription and strongly upregulated anthocyanin biosynthetic genes in tobacco petals, resulting in a 2.5- to 4.2-fold increase in anthocyanin content and significantly darker petal color. Yeast one-hybrid and dual-luciferase assays confirmed that SmMYB44 could directly bind to the promoters of SmCHS and SmF3H and repress their transcriptional activity. In addition, SmMYB44 physically interacts with the co-repressor SmTPL to form a transcriptional repressive complex. Although SmTPL alone has no capacity to activate SmCHS and SmF3H transcription, it cooperates with SmMYB44 to strengthen the repression of target gene promoters. Collectively, SmMYB44 negatively regulates light-induced anthocyanin biosynthesis in eggplant through direct transcriptional repression of key structural genes and synergistic inhibition through physical association with the co-repressor SmTPL.

title: Comprehensive characterization of the cellular and molecular consequences of LCN2 loss in MDA-MB-231 triple-negative breast cancer cells.
text: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype characterized by high metastatic potential and limited targeted therapeutic options. Lipocalin-2 (LCN2) has been implicated in tumor progression and metastatic dissemination, but its functional role in TNBC remains incompletely understood. This study investigated the role of LCN2 in the human TNBC cell line MDA-MB-231. Stable LCN2-deficient (LCN2KO) cells were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, followed by isolation of single-cell-derived clones. RNA sequencing was performed to characterize transcriptomic changes, with selected findings validated by reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Western blotting was used to assess protein-level changes. Transwell migration and invasion assays and adhesion assays were performed to evaluate functional effects. LCN2KO cells largely retained the mesenchymal phenotype of parental cells. RNA sequencing revealed changes associated with inflammatory signaling, iron homeostasis, oxidative stress, ferroptosis-related processes, and cellular metabolism. Functional assays demonstrated reduced migration, invasion, and adhesion, accompanied by altered adhesion to extracellular matrix components. LCN2 deficiency is associated with transcriptional and functional changes in MDA-MB-231 cells, particularly affecting migratory and invasive behavior and cell-matrix interactions, while largely preserving the mesenchymal phenotype. These findings provide further insight into the role of LCN2 in cellular processes relevant to TNBC progression and metastatic behavior.

title: Therapeutic and Prophylactic Agents for Viral Diseases: Current Status, Challenges, and Future Prospects.
text: Viral diseases remain a major global health challenge despite substantial advances in vaccination, antiviral therapeutics, and public-health interventions. However, current antiviral strategies are still constrained by important gaps, including rapid viral evolution, limited broad-spectrum efficacy, immune escape, antiviral resistance, incomplete durability of protection, and inequitable global access to prevention and treatment. This review provides a comprehensive and integrated overview of contemporary antiviral prevention and therapeutic strategies, spanning vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, direct-acting antivirals, host-targeted therapies, immunomodulators, RNA-based therapeutics, gene-editing technologies, and cellular immunotherapies. We discuss the mechanistic foundations, clinical applications, pharmacologic considerations, and translational challenges associated with each modality across major human viral pathogens, including HIV, HBV, HCV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSV, Ebola virus, arboviruses, and herpesviruses. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging innovations such as long-acting prophylaxis, Fc-engineered monoclonal antibodies, nanoparticle and mucosal vaccine platforms, CRISPR-based antiviral systems, and broadly protective host-directed approaches designed to overcome resistance and enhance pandemic preparedness. In addition, we highlight the growing importance of real-time genomic surveillance and equitable global deployment strategies in shaping future antiviral responses, collectively underscoring that the next generation of antiviral medicine will depend on the convergence of universal immunization strategies, durable therapeutics, precision immune modulation, and rapidly deployable platform technologies capable of addressing both endemic and emerging viral threats.

title: ASAOT: an accentuated structure-differentiated asymmetric optimal transport model for cell type and single-cell spatial mapping.
text: Spatial transcriptomics (STs) characterizes spatiotemporal gene expression and facilitates analysis of cellular architecture and cell-cell crosstalk within tissue microenvironments. However, existing spatial deconvolution methods employ globally fixed smoothing without local sharpening, which blurs cellular boundaries and impedes reconstruction of layered, heterogeneous cellular patterns in brain tissue. Here, we present Accentuated Structure-differentiated Asymmetric Optimal Transport (ASAOT), a deconvolution framework built on structure-enhanced asymmetric optimal transport. Coupled with spatial neighborhood constraints, ASAOT introduces a differentiated accentuated sharpening term to maintain global spatial continuity, enhance boundary detection, and preserve spot-level expression heterogeneity. Using asymmetric optimal transport, the framework jointly estimates spot-wise cell-type proportions and performs spatial assignment of reference single-cell coordinates. Benchmarks on diverse simulated datasets demonstrate that ASAOT achieves competitive overall accuracy and robustness across moderate spatial resolutions, with the best average comprehensive rank among tested methods. Applications to mouse olfactory bulb and cerebral cortex datasets demonstrate that ASAOT reduces signal diffusion and boundary distortion, effectively recovering layered brain anatomy and stratified cell distributions to build interpretable spatial maps of reference single-cell profiles. Collectively, ASAOT addresses critical drawbacks of conventional methods via a sharpening regularization term, serving as a reliable tool for STs analysis and mechanism exploration of tissue spatial organization.

title: Multi-omics insights into stem cell-mediated regeneration after traumatic spinal cord injury: cell fate, niche remodeling, and functional integration.
text: Stem-cell grafts may replace neural cells, protect host tissue, or change local signaling after spinal cord injury. Their effects depend on the starting cell product, how donor cells respond to the lesion, and whether they contribute to useful function. This narrative review examines neural stem/progenitor cells and neural products derived from pluripotent stem cells. Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) provide a comparison for repair driven mainly by secreted factors. Transplantation studies show that regional identity and developmental stage affect graft behavior, that the lesion can redirect donor-cell fate, and that neural and stromal products can alter host responses. In selected models, neural grafts also form active connections with host circuits. Molecular profiling identifies product heterogeneity, early donor-cell states, and secreted factors associated with host responses. Injury atlases describe changes in cell populations, tissue locations, and metabolites, helping researchers choose questions for graft studies. These findings come from separate studies; no study has yet tested the full multi-omics sequence from product features to recovery. Future work should connect product measurements before transplantation to donor, host, and functional changes over time. It should test whether proposed mechanisms affect function and whether findings hold across products and recipients. Clinical translation will also require potency tests tied to intended function, long-term safety monitoring, and measures of motor, sensory, autonomic, and daily function.

title: Spatial Multi-Omics Integration with Mass Spectrometry Imaging: Decoding Metabolic Landscapes and Disease Mechanisms.
text: Spatial multi-omics links molecular measurements to tissue architecture, but integrating spatial transcriptomics with mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) remains challenging because the modalities differ in sampling unit, spatial resolution, data structure, and molecular-identification certainty. This review synthesizes the enabling technologies and presents an evidence-calibrated workflow spanning tissue acquisition, spatial registration, modality-specific preprocessing, cross-modal annotation, mechanistic modeling, and orthogonal validation. We examine how MSI can complement single-cell and spatial transcriptomic or proteomic measurements in studies of tumor-host interfaces, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, adipose-tissue organization, and decidualization at the maternal-fetal interface. Across these applications, spatial colocalization is most informative when annotation confidence is reported and key chemical identities are validated, registration error is quantified, and candidate cell-metabolite relationships are tested by isotope tracing or perturbation. We further discuss molecular ambiguity, resolution-sensitivity-throughput trade-offs, 3-dimensional reconstruction, interlaboratory reproducibility, and requirements for clinical translation. The central conclusion is that spatial multi-omics is best used to formulate anatomically explicit, falsifiable hypotheses rather than to infer causality from aligned maps alone.

title: Liver immune tolerance and regulated cell death in transplantation and hepatocellular carcinoma: shared mechanisms, divergent outcomes.
text: The liver constantly encounters gut-derived antigens, microbial molecules, and food antigens. This environment has shaped a tissue-specific tolerance network centered on tolerogenic antigen presentation, immune-checkpoint activation, regulatory cell expansion, and metabolic suppression. This feature protects the liver during prolonged inflammation and gives it an immunological identity that most solid organs lack. Regulated cell death (RCD) and dead-cell clearance form a critical mechanistic layer within this network. Efficient efferocytosis of apoptotic cells reinforces resolution and tolerance, whereas necroptosis, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis disrupt cell membranes and release danger signals that reshape myeloid activation, T-cell function, and the tumor microenvironment. In liver transplantation, this tolerogenic tendency produces donor-specific hyporesponsiveness, allowing a selected subset of stable recipients to stop immunosuppression while maintaining graft function-a state called operational tolerance. In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), tumors exploit the same immunosuppressive axes to block anti-tumor T-cell infiltration and effector function. Anti-PD-L1 therapy combined with anti-angiogenic treatment improves survival, demonstrating that partial disruption of tumor immunosuppression is therapeutically effective. Spatial transcriptomics and single-cell sequencing reveal that SPP1-positive macrophages and cancer-associated fibroblasts form a tumor immune barrier that excludes lymphocytes, showing that hepatic tolerance is organized in space. This duality becomes most dangerous in HCC recurrence after liver transplantation, where immune checkpoint inhibitors boost anti-tumor immunity but also raise the risk of acute rejection, graft failure, and death. Unlike reviews focused on hepatic immune tolerance, regulated cell death, or HCC immunobiology in isolation, this review integrates these processes across the physiological liver, transplantation, HCC, and post-transplant recurrence. We define this coordinated hyporesponsive state as the liver immune tolerance program (ITP), generated by cellular, molecular, spatial, metabolic, and cell-death-related networks. Rather than treating these processes separately, we position RCD and dead-cell clearance as a "death-to-immunity axis," systematically compare ITP remodeling in the physiological liver, transplantation, and HCC, and use post-transplant HCC recurrence as a clinical crossover setting in which graft protection and antitumor immune surveillance become therapeutic considerations. On this basis, we propose precision immune homeostasis: rather than choosing between immunosuppression and immune activation, immune status should be adjusted to an individualized range that protects the graft while preserving anti-tumor immune surveillance.

title: Cell-Cell Communication Network Analysis of Tertiary Lymphoid Structures in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer.
text: Tertiary Lymphoid Structures (TLS) are associated with a favorable prognosis in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC). However, the mechanisms governing their formation, particularly the existence of breast cancer subtype-specific critical cell communication networks, remain unclear. This study aims to systematically decipher the specific cellular interaction networks associated with TLS in TNBC and Estrogen Receptor-positive Breast Cancer (ER+ BC). Public spatial transcriptomics (TNBC: GSE210616; ER+ BC: 10x Genomics public Visium dataset) and single-cell transcriptomics (GSE176078) data were integrated to attribute TLS-associated genes to their cell-type origins and infer intercellular communication. TLS regions were independently identified by two pathologists based on H&E images (TNBC: 7 TLS; ER+ BC: 12 TLS), followed by differential expression analysis. Using single-cell data, a dual-criterion (expression rate ≥20% and average expression level ≥ upper quartile) was employed for cell-type expression attribution, with sensitivity analysis across thresholds. Cell-cell communication network inference and quantitative analysis were performed based on an expanded ligand-receptor database (CellTalkDB, 3,398 pairs), and the core findings were cross-validated using CellChat. TLS in TNBC exhibited a far more active transcriptional state compared to ER+ Breast Cancer (ER+ BC), with 198 vs 29 differentially expressed genes. Interaction network analysis revealed that in TNBC TLS, fibroblasts (cancer-associated fibroblasts, CAFs) constituted the dominant core signaling hub (net signal output strength: +458.7), whereas endothelial cells were the predominant net signal receiver (net output: -808.6). In contrast, TLS in ER+ BC were characterized by interactions predominantly involving fibroblasts (dominant output, +261.1) and plasma cells (dominant reception, -127.0). Cell-type expression attribution further confirmed that TLS-associated signals in TNBC predominantly originated from fibroblasts (70.3% of core TLS genes). Our intercellular communication analysis reveals a stark subtype-specific landscape: TLSs in TNBC are predominantly characterized by a fibroblast (CAF)-centered signaling hub, whereas TLS in ER+ BC features a fibroblast-plasma cell axis. The association between the TLS-related transcriptional signature and immune cytolytic activity was further supported in the independent The Cancer Genome Atlas breast cancer cohort (r = 0.747, P < 0.001). However, as these inferences are drawn from transcriptional correlations in public datasets, further mechanistic studies-such as ligand-receptor functional assays or in vivo perturbation models-are essential to determine whether this TNBC-specific hub actively contributes to TLS formation or merely reflects the local immune microenvironment. This study identifies a TNBC-specific fibroblast (CAF)-centered communication hub as a prominent feature of TLS-associated intercellular networks, offering prioritized candidate axes warranting further functional validation for potential immunotherapy development.

title: Neutrophil Extracellular Traps Contribute to Peri-Implant Bone Loss: Insights Into Pro-Inflammatory Macrophage-Neutrophil Crosstalk.
text: To investigate the contribution of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) to peri-implant bone loss and explore upstream cellular mechanisms associated with aberrant NETosis. Clinical specimens were analysed for NET formation and inflammatory markers. A rat peri-implantitis (PI) model with local DNase I treatment was used to evaluate the contribution of NETs to peri-implant bone loss. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, cell-cell communication analyses and functional experiments were integrated to investigate macrophage-neutrophil interactions. NET-associated markers were increased in PI specimens and correlated with inflammatory cytokines. DNase I attenuated peri-implant bone resorption and inflammation in rats. Integrated transcriptomic analyses identified a NETosis-associated neutrophil subpopulation (NNeu) with a prominent NET-forming phenotype. Spatial proximity and cell-cell communication analyses identified pro-inflammatory macrophages (PMac) as a candidate upstream population. Mechanistically, PMac-derived macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) promoted NETosis through CD74-p38 MAPK signalling in vitro, while experimental modulation of MIF-CD74 signalling in vivo was accompanied by corresponding changes in NET formation, inflammation and peri-implant bone loss. NETs contribute to inflammatory bone loss in an experimental PI model. in vitro findings further suggest that pro-inflammatory macrophage-neutrophil crosstalk regulates NET formation through MIF-CD74-p38 MAPK signalling, highlighting a potential immunomodulatory target.

title: Spatial Niches Shape Function in the Intratumoral Microbiome: From Multiscale Mapping to Niche-Informed Therapy.
text: Most studies of the intratumoral microbiome describe microbial composition and abundance but do not reveal where bacteria are located within the tumor microenvironment. Evidence that microbial signals vary across tumor regions and host-cell compartments makes spatial context essential to biological interpretation. In this review, we organize evidence at three levels: tissue niches reflect oxygenation, perfusion, pH, necrosis, and anatomy, cellular niches involve malignant, immune, and stromal cells, and physical interfaces include intracellular residence, extracellular association, biofilms, and diffusible products. We examine how contamination-aware sequencing, single-cell host-microbe profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and imaging distinguish detection from localization and relate microbial geography to host-cell states. Spatial organization may affect oncogenic signaling, cytoskeletal remodeling, DNA damage, immune regulation, metastatic fitness, and treatment response. The same bacterial strain may exert opposing immune effects inside and outside host cells. This framework clarifies therapeutic implications. Engineered bacteria can deliver payloads to hypoxic, poorly perfused regions, whereas intracellular nanocarriers, species-selective phages, and biofilm-disrupting platforms address different microbial reservoirs. Major limitations include low-biomass contamination, uncertain viability, incomplete localization, limited causal evidence, and poorly resolved temporal dynamics. Integrating microbial identity with location and physical state should yield more mechanistic models of the intratumoral microbiome and better-defined therapeutic strategies.

title: PIANO enables generative modeling of gene expression and scales multi-omics integration to 100 million cells.
text: Single-cell RNA technologies enable the routine acquisition of transcriptomic atlases. However, these molecular profiles are influenced by overlapping sources of variation. Since these covariates confound comparisons, data integration is the first step in most analyses. Three challenges remain: correcting strong batch effects, scaling to millions of cells, and modeling how covariates influence gene expression. To address these challenges, we developed PIANO, probabilistic inference autoencoder networks for multi-omics, a deep learning framework whose central feature is a generative model of gene expression data. Additionally, PIANO achieves robust integrations and trains 10× faster than previous methods. PIANO accurately integrates single-cell data across species and across single-cell and spatial transcriptomics modalities. As practical applications, PIANO models spatially resolved gene expression during Alzheimer's disease progression in human brains and integrates over 100 million cancer cells to model drug perturbations. In summary, PIANO's integration and generative modeling capabilities will empower novel insights for a wide range of future studies.

title: Human neocortical glutamatergic neurons revealed through multimodal profiling.
text: The human neocortex underlies higher cognition, yet our understanding of its neuronal diversity is limited by sparse access to viable tissue, inconsistent cell-type definitions, and limited multimodal data. Although single-cell transcriptomics has transformed our understanding of cell type diversity, transcriptomic data alone cannot explain neuronal function. Here, we introduce a multimodal patch sequencing (patch-seq) resource of human neocortical glutamatergic neurons spanning cortical layers 2-6. Combining morphoelectric features with spatial transcriptomic data to provide laminar context, we sampled 39 of 42 transcriptomically defined glutamatergic neuron types. This systematic approach enabled the identification of unique phenotypes for understudied populations in the human neocortex including L4 intratelencephalic, L5/6 near-projecting, and diverse L6 neurons. Human, macaque, and mouse comparisons of transcriptomically homologous L5 neurons reveal that morphoelectric differences across species were subclass specific. This dataset provides a unified multimodal reference for studying human cortical circuitry and neuronal diversity.

title: Population-scale integration of spatial omics networks for clinical prediction and biological discovery by SPIN.
text: Spatial omics enables the integration of high-dimensional molecular organization with clinical outcomes, yet incorporating spatial single-cell information into predictive models at the population scale remains challenging. We introduce SPIN (spatial predictive integration network), which integrates subject-specific, cell-type level, spatially informed co-expression or co-abundance networks for population-scale clinical prediction. Current implementation of SPIN includes three key modules: network construction, molecular-to-clinical prediction by Bayesian scalar-on-network regression with manifold learning (BSNMani), and visualization & interpretation module. In the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas (SEA-AD) multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) transcriptomics cohort, SPIN achieved an accuracy of 0.81 for dementia-status prediction and revealed co-expression subnetworks with clear biological relevance. SPIN also achieved robust survival prediction in a breast cancer single-cell proteomics cohort (C-index = 0.78), identifying two survival-associated spatial proteomic subnetworks. In summary, SPIN is an interpretable tool for spatial-omics-based clinical outcome prediction at the population scale.

title: Amyloid and tau display distinct patterns across Alzheimer's in anterior caudate.
text: The anterior caudate shows a pattern of Alzheimer's disease pathology that differs from the more extensively studied cortex. Across 41 donors, we found mostly diffuse amyloid beta plaques in gray matter and phosphorylated tau threads associated with white matter. Combining digital pathology with single-nucleus and spatial gene expression data, we detected no significant loss or gain in neuronal cell-type abundance with increasing pathology. However, we did observe increases in an FLT1+/IL1B+ microglial population with tau burden. Fast-spiking PTHLH-PVALB interneurons showed changes in genes related to ion channels, cellular trafficking, and phosphorylation. These findings offer a cellular-resolution reference for investigating how Alzheimer's disease affects subcortical brain regions.

title: A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia.
text: Human basal ganglia (BG) neurons and inhibitory interneurons originate in the ganglionic eminences (GEs), transient structures in the ventral prenatal brain. This study delineates the specification and maturation of GEs and GE-derived neurons using single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq), spatial transcriptomics, and single-molecule chromatin + RNA imaging, and we found heterogeneous temporal progression across GE subregions. Spiny projection neurons (SPNs), the principal cells of the BG, acquire distinct subtypes through synchronized 3D-epigenomic remodeling, in contrast to the asynchronous maturation of other neuron types. Oligodendrocyte differentiation involves a transient short-range chromatin state during infancy, showing that the short-range and long-range chromatin conformations previously linked to terminal glial and neuronal fates can also be transient. The temporal cortex matured epigenomically faster than other cortical regions during this period. Lastly, SPNs were enriched in genetic risk for neuropsychiatric disease. Our study extends findings on unique 3D-epigenomic dynamics during human brain development.

title: Spatial and regulatory organization of cell identity across the primate subcortex.
text: Mammalian brain cell identity is shaped by intrinsic factors and external context. We present a spatially resolved transcriptomic and gene regulatory atlas of cell types across all subcortical regions in a primate, the common marmoset. Dense sampling and cross-species integration revealed spatially precise neuronal assemblies, including ones in complex midbrain and diencephalic structures. Chromatin accessibility and transcriptional identity are spatially tuned within and across subcortical structures; spatial gradients within hippocampal subfields are orchestrated by graded transcription factors acting through graded enhancers. The primate-expanded thalamic γ-aminobutyric acid (GABAergic) population shares transcriptional and regulatory syntax with conserved midbrain populations, reflecting an evolutionary adaptation compared with rodents. Similar regional expression across cell types can arise by distinct regulatory architectures, as observed in telencephalic astrocytes and neurons. Conversely, distant cell types can share regulatory programs despite divergent identities: striatal GABAergic spiny projection neurons and telencephalic glutamatergic neurons share a postsynaptic regulatory program despite divergent lineages, regions, and neurotransmitter identities.

title: Single-cell multimodal atlas reveals regulatory programs in the human brain.
text: Direct measurement of chromatin states together with transcription is essential for understanding how cell-type-specific regulatory programs are established and maintained in the adult human brain. Here, we present a large-scale single-cell multimodal atlas by jointly profiling the transcriptome with active (H3K27ac) or repressive (H3K27me3) histone modifications across 18 adult brain regions. We targeted over 750,000 nuclei spanning 160 cell types and integrated these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, 3D genome architecture, and spatial transcriptomes. This framework resolved chromatin states for over 500,000 candidate regulatory elements, identified enhancer-gene links and regulatory programs, revealed Polycomb-associated ultra-long-range contacts, and uncovered brainwide epigenomic heterogeneity. We further developed a sequence-to-function model to predict cell-type-specific effects of candidate neurological disease variants. Finally, comparative analyses across species reveal conservation in active regulatory programs but divergence in repressive programs. Together, this study provides a comprehensive epigenomic reference for interpreting regulatory principles and epigenetic memory underlying human brain organization and disease.

title: Multiscale spatial atlas of human basal ganglia cell types and communities.
text: The human basal ganglia comprise functionally varied nuclei, but their cell-type composition and spatial organization have not been comprehensively resolved. We generated a multi-region, subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomic atlas by integrating multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH)+ and spatiotemporal enhanced-resolution omics sequencing (Stereo-seq) across four neurotypical donors. The datasets profiled ∼7.9 million cells across the caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, and globus pallidus, resolving 60 transcriptionally distinct cell types. We identify region-selective molecular and spatial diversification of spiny projection neurons and non-neuronal populations. Subcellular RNA localization captures somatic size and projection-inferred signatures, reflecting direct- and indirect-pathway topology. Cellular community analyses reveal astrocyte and oligodendrocyte subclusters enriched at striosome-matrix borders, while primate-expanded interneurons are confined to matrix territories. Cross-species comparisons reveal conserved and species-specialized organization, including orthologous striosome-matrix architecture and conserved dorsolateral-to-ventromedial transcriptional gradients. Together, this multi-centimeter-scale human basal ganglia atlas links cell types, spatial architecture, and subcellular transcript topography across scales.

title: Design and Evaluation of Next-Gen Inhibitors Targeting SARS-CoV-2 3CL Protease Clinical Variants.
text: The 3C-like protease (3CLpro), also known as main protease (Mpro), is currently the target of the commercially available drugs nirmatrelvir and simnotrelvir which are used to treat SARS-CoV-2 infections. Global sequencing efforts of clinical isolates of SARS-CoV-2 from infected patients treated with nirmatrelvir have identified several 3CLpro clinical variants that are potentially drug resistant. Two variants, E166 and S144, have been widely studied and confirmed to have drug resistance in vitro. Using the Coronavirus 3D database, we identified and characterized ten additional SARS-CoV-2 3CLpro clinical variants deemed likely to render drug resistance. Of these, we identified a new variant, V186G, as being highly drug resistant, i.e., 116-times, 44-times, and 25-times more resistant to nirmatrelvir, simnotrelvir, and the inhibitor GRL-051-22, respectively, than the wild type. The V186G variant also displayed a 23-fold decrease in dimerization affinity. Surprisingly, no changes in drug resistance or dimerization affinity were observed for the V186F or V186I variants. X-ray structures of WT, V186G, V186F, M165I, M49I, and T190I in complex with the inhibitor GRL-051-22 were determined at resolutions between 1.3 Å and 1.9 Å revealing only small structural changes associated with any of the variants, e.g., <1.5 Å in the S2 loop of the V186G variant. Structure-based design was then used to overcome SARS-CoV-2 V186G 3CLpro drug resistance, producing the compound GRL-157-23 which is 6.5-times more potent against the V186G variant compared with the wild type. Structure-activity data for six designed compounds and their interactions with the ten variants revealed an important crosstalk between the SARS-CoV-2 3CLpro S2 and S4 subsites that plays a key role in the kinetic activity and inhibition of these variants. These results demonstrate that it is possible to design and optimize drug scaffolds that target 3CLpro variants to overcome potential drug resistance.

title: From Enzyme to Parasite: Enzymatic and Phenotypic-Guided Evaluation of Repurposed Inhibitors against Schistosoma mansoni cathepsin D1 (SmCD1).
text: Schistosomiasis remains a major public health concern in endemic regions, with treatment relying almost exclusively on praziquantel (PZQ). Although vital, PZQ shows limited activity against immature parasites and raises potential resistance concerns. In this context, Schistosoma mansoni cathepsin D1 (SmCD1), an essential enzyme for hemoglobin digestion and parasite development, has emerged as a promising target for the development of new antischistosomal drugs. In this work, we evaluated SmCD1 inhibition by a series of 76 acylguanidine compounds, obtained through a drug repositioning approach. Effects on adult and juvenile worms' motility and morphology were evaluated by an image-based ex vivo assay, while selected compounds were also tested for cytotoxicity and cell permeability. Upon screening at 10 μM, 11 compounds inhibited at least 90% of SmCD1 activity and/or reduced parasite motility by more than 60% (72h). Three compounds, M3336, M2110, and M8214, potently inhibited SmCD1 (IC50 30-90 nM) with up to 12-fold selectivity for SmCD1 over the human orthologue. Computational analyses identified structural features likely related to potency and selectivity.

title: Therapeutic Peptides for Breast Cancer - Advances in Design, Development and Applications.
text: Breast cancer is a malignant disease that commonly affects women worldwide. Chemotherapy is often indicated for the treatment of breast cancer, particularly when surgery alone is insufficient to achieve a cure. However, chemotherapy can cause serious adverse effects, which impede its effective use. Anticancer peptides (ACPs) may serve as safer alternatives or adjunctive agents to conventional chemotherapeutic agents for breast cancer treatment, owing to their unique properties, including charge-based targeting and lysis of cancer cell membranes and selective binding to intracellular components to cause signaling interference and induce apoptosis. Herein, we review the development, classification, and common characteristics of ACPs, as well as their applications and efficacy in the treatment of breast cancer as single agents and as components of synergistic combination regimens. In addition, strategies for optimizing the anticancer efficacy of peptides based on key physicochemical properties, including hydrophobicity, amphipathicity, molecular charge, peptide length, amino acid composition, and structural modifications, are presented and discussed to facilitate the rational design of next-generation anticancer peptides. Particular emphasis is placed on recent advances in computational and AI-driven strategies for ACP discovery and design, including molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, QSAR modeling, machine learning, transformer-based protein language models, and generative AI approaches for rational peptide engineering and de novo peptide design. These emerging computational techniques have substantially accelerated ACP screening while reducing the time and cost associated with experimental discovery. In the concluding remarks, we highlight the challenges, limitations, and prospects of anticancer peptides as an emerging therapy for breast cancer.

title: Discovery of 7-Aminofuro[2,3-c]pyridine-Based Irreversible Inhibitors of TGFβ-Activated Kinase 1 (TAK1) with In Vivo Antitumor Activity.
text: TGFβ-activated kinase 1 (TAK1) plays essential roles in proinflammatory and prosurvival signaling pathways, and has been implicated in various human diseases, including cancer and inflammation. Although several TAK1 inhibitors have been reported, an effective tool compound with a combination of favorable potency, selectivity, and in vivo efficacy is still lacking. Herein, we present a 7-aminofuro[2,3-c]pyridine-based α,β-unsaturated aldehyde (compound 26) as a potent TAK1 irreversible covalent inhibitor. This compound exhibited excellent inhibitory activity for TAK1-dependent signaling in cells and demonstrated a sustained TAK1 inhibition effect in vivo. Furthermore, it significantly prevented tumor growth in a lymphoma (DoHH2) xenograft mouse model. Although a contribution from the inhibition of other kinases to the observed effects cannot be ruled out, compound 26 provides a promising starting point for further optimization of TAK1 selectivity and pharmacokinetic properties toward the development of TAK1-targeted agents.

title: Discovery of INCB161734: A Selective Inhibitor of the KRAS G12D Mutant.
text: The discovery of the clinical KRAS G12D inhibitor INCB161734 is described. Starting from a previously disclosed orally bioavailable tool compound 1, a concerted effort to improve the predicted human dose via modulation of potency and pharmacokinetics was undertaken. Careful consideration of the metabolic profile was key to designing low clearance compounds. In addition, the molecular size and fraction sp3 character were carefully controlled to improve permeability and crystalline solubility. From this effort, INCB161734 was identified as a balanced compound with excellent oral exposure, potent antiproliferative activity in xenograft tumor models, and excellent selectivity against wild-type K/H/NRAS. INCB161734 is currently undergoing clinical trials in patients with KRAS G12D mutations.

title: Democratizing Drug Discovery: A Scalable Open-Source Pipeline for Massive Specific Protein Target QSAR Modeling Using ChEMBL.
text: The proprietary nature of AI/ML tools in drug discovery limits access to advanced virtual screening methodologies. To address this, we present an open-source, automated pipeline for large-scale Quantitative Structure-Activity Relationship (QSAR) modeling utilizing ChEMBL. Our batch processing system constructed 2263 predictive models across multiple protein targets, applying both regression and classification strategies with strict quality control thresholds. The pipeline integrates ErG and RDKit descriptor families, employs Random Forest and XGBoost algorithms with Optuna-based hyperparameter optimization, and handles class imbalances using SMOTE. Models are saved only when achieving R2 ≥ 0.7 for regression or MCC ≥ 0.55 for classification. Data is stratified by assay and measurement types to maintain biological relevance. Additionally, we feature an interactive EDA visualization tool with ErG heatmaps and external validation via the DELTA database. This work democratizes industrial-grade QSAR infrastructure, empowering the research community to reproduce and extend computational workflows.

title: Discovery of a Novel Pyrido[2,1-h]pteridin-6-one Derivative as a Potent and Orally Bioavailable HPK1 Inhibitor.
text: Hematopoietic progenitor kinase 1 (HPK1), a key negative regulator of T-cell activation, represents a highly promising yet challenging target for cancer immunotherapy. To date, no HPK1 inhibitor has received marketing approval, underscoring the need for innovative scaffolds. Here, we report the structure-based drug discovery of a potent HPK1 inhibitor featuring a unique pyrido[2,1-h]pteridin-6-one core. Through a series of chemical modifications, including scaffold hopping and ring-system optimization, starting from a known diaminopyrimidine carboxamide structure, we successfully constructed this key tricyclic core. The lead compound 29 exhibited remarkable potency against HPK1, along with outstanding selectivity. It effectively suppressed HPK1-mediated SLP-76 phosphorylation, thereby enhancing T-cell activation in both Jurkat cells and human PBMCs. Moreover, 29 displayed excellent oral bioavailability and markedly enhanced antitumor efficacy in combination with anti-PD-1 in a CT26.WT syngeneic mouse model. Collectively, these findings identify a novel, potent, and selective HPK1 inhibitor, offering a promising candidate for advancing cancer immunotherapy.

title: Rational Design of Potent and Highly Selective FGFR1 Irreversible Inhibitors Guided by Molecular Dynamics Simulations.
text: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed distinct P-loop conformational differences in the ATP-binding domain between FGFR1 and other FGFR subtypes. A conformation-restricted linker optimization strategy was applied to identify a potent and selective irreversible FGFR1 inhibitor (compound 24). MD models demonstrated that the covalent warhead of compound 24 retained an optimal distance and orientation toward the P-loop cysteine of FGFR1, facilitating efficient Michael addition. After covalent conjugation, compound 24 interacted with the hinge region and precisely matched the unique FGFR1 conformation. Its robust antitumor activity was validated in cellular, CDX, and PDX models by suppressing FGFR1-dependent tumor growth, providing a novel strategy for subtype-selective FGFR1 inhibitor development.

title: Design and Biological Evaluation of a Potent Dual PARP and BRD4 Inhibitor for Tumor Therapy via Disrupting HRR and BRD4-cJUN-CCL2 Axis.
text: Inducing homologous recombination repair (HRR) deficiency is an attractive strategy to expand the therapeutic scope of PARP inhibitors. Since BRD4 inhibition impairs HRR function and sensitizes cancer cells to PARP inhibition, we designed and synthesized a series of dual PARP/BRD4 inhibitors. Structure-activity relationship studies identified D6 as a potent dual inhibitor with low nanomolar inhibitory activities against PARP1 and BRD4. D6 exhibited potent antiproliferative activity in MDA-MB-231 and KP4 cells and induced cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and inhibition of colony formation and metastasis-associated phenotypes. Mechanistically, D6 suppressed the BRD4-cJUN-CCL2 signaling axis, reducing macrophage recruitment and macrophage-mediated cancer cell invasion. In an MDA-MB-231 xenograft model, D6 inhibited tumor growth without obvious toxicity. These findings support D6 as a promising dual PARP/BRD4 inhibitor for cancer therapy.

title: Discovery of Novel Pyridine-Dihydropyrrolo[3,4-b]Pyrrolidone Derivatives as Orally Active PIM Kinase Inhibitors for the Treatment of Acute Myeloid Leukemia.
text: PIM kinases are promising therapeutic targets for acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Merging PIM447 with C28 via molecular hybridization, we successfully designed and synthesized a series of novel pyridine-dihydropyrrolo [3,4-b]pyrrolidone derivatives. Among them, compound 50 exhibited potent inhibitory activity against PIM-1/2/3 (IC50 = 6.71/15.14/10.10 nM, respectively) and significant antiproliferative activity against MV4-11 cells (IC50 = 0.21 μM). Mechanistic studies demonstrated that 50 dose-dependently inhibited substrate phosphorylation (e.g., BAD), thereby inducing PARP cleavage, apoptosis, and G2/M arrest. It possesses favorable drug-like properties and high oral bioavailability. Kinase profiling against 217 kinases showed good PIM selectivity. In an MV4-11 xenograft model, oral administration of 50 at 50 mg/kg once daily achieved 84.7% tumor growth inhibition without significant toxicity, and platelet toxicity was lower than C28. Overall, compound 50 is a potent, orally bioavailable PIM kinase inhibitor with a favorable safety profile that warrants further systematic evaluation in AML models with diverse genetic backgrounds.

title: Discovery of Novel Orally Bioavailable STING Inhibitors with 4,5,6,7-Tetrahydropyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrazine Moiety for STING-Mediated Inflammatory Disorders.
text: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling pathway plays a pivotal role in host defense against pathogenic microbes and tumors. However, aberrant activation of this pathway is tightly associated with a wide spectrum of inflammatory and autoimmune disorders, positioning STING inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy. In this study, we designed and synthesized a series of novel 4,5,6,7-tetrahydropyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrazine derivatives as STING inhibitors. Compound 37 displayed potent STING inhibitory activity and favorable in vivo pharmacokinetic properties and safety. Further studies revealed that 37 blocks STING palmitoylation, thereby suppressing downstream signaling pathway activation. Oral administration of 37 exhibited significant anti-inflammatory effects in 10-carboxymethyl-9-acridanone (CMA)-challenged mice, Trex1-/- mice and cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury (AKI) mice. Collectively, compound 37 represents a novel orally bioavailable STING inhibitor with therapeutic potential against STING-driven inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.

title: Structure-Based Design of 2-(Pyridone)Indoles as Antagonists of the Toll-Like Receptors TLR7 and TLR8 for the Treatment of Autoimmune Disorders.
text: Toll-like receptors 7 and 8 (TLR7/8) are innate immune sensors whose activation by endogenous RNA ligands is a hallmark of chronic autoimmune disorders, notably cutaneous and systemic lupus. We present the structure-based design and optimization of 2-(pyridin-2(1H)-one)indoles as potent dual TLR7/8 antagonists with properties improved over our prior series, including increased permeability, reduced ion channel activity, and reduced volume of distribution at steady state (Vss). Initial pyridone leads displayed unexpected anti-proliferative activity in a panel of immune cell lines; optimization against an identified off-target BRD4 liability, hypothesized to drive this effect, delivered potent antagonists devoid of BRD4 binding and of anti-proliferative activity. These compounds potently inhibited TLR7/8-mediated IL-6 production in human whole blood, with 9a giving IC50 values of 9.4 and 1.3 nM against TLR7 and TLR8, respectively. This orally bioavailable lead dose-dependently suppressed TLR7-mediated IL-6 and IFNα release in a mouse pharmacodynamic model.

title: Design, Synthesis, and Biological Evaluation of Novel Benzimidazole Derivatives as Dual PI3K/HDAC8 Inhibitors with Potent Anti-Cervical Cancer Activity InVivo.
text: The dual inhibition of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and histone deacetylase 8 (HDAC8) has emerged as a promising strategy for cervical cancer (CC) therapy. We synthesized 34 novel benzimidazole derivatives and evaluated their anti-CC cell line proliferation. The compound 50 exhibited equivalent antiproliferative effect to cisplatin (Pt) in CC cell lines SiHa, Ca Ski, and HeLa, especially in HeLa cells with an IC50 value at 1.42 ± 0.50 μM (Pt 1.70 ± 0.28 μM). Further assessment in the HeLa cell xenograft mouse model, the intraperitoneal medium- (30 mg/kg) and high-dose group (60 mg/kg) and and intragastric high-dose group (100 mg/kg) exhibited antitumor efficacy no less than that of Pt (i.p. 5 mg/kg) but much more safe during the experiment period. Mechanism studies demonstrated that 50 could inhibit the PI3K/Akt pathway and HDAC8 expression and function. These findings prove that the PI3K/HDAC8 dual inhibition may be an efficient way in cervical cancer treatment and compound 50 deserved for further development.

title: Discovery of Threonine Tyrosine Kinase (TTK) Degraders Utilizing an Electrophilic Monomethyl Fumarate Handle.
text: Threonine tyrosine kinase (TTK), a core component of the spindle assembly checkpoint, plays an essential role in mitosis, and its inhibition has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy for human cancers. We previously reported multiple approaches to target TTK, including reversible inhibitors, covalent inhibitors, and PROTAC degraders. In this study, we advance these efforts by developing a novel monovalent degrader of TTK. The representative compound, 26, generated by appending an electrophilic monomethyl fumarate handle to a TTK inhibitor, effectively induced TTK degradation and demonstrated superior antiproliferative activity across diverse cancer cell lines. Mechanistic investigations suggested that compound 26 primarily engages RNF126 and stabilizes its association with TTK, thereby inducing TTK ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Collectively, this work provides the first example of a TTK molecular glue-like degrader and introduces a new electrophilic handle for the rational design of degraders with reduced nonspecific cytotoxicity.

title: Discovery of Pyrazolo[1,5-a]-1,3,5-Triazine Derivatives as Potent, Highly Selective and Orally Available Macrocyclic CDK7 Inhibitors.
text: Cyclin-dependent kinase 7 (CDK7) is a promising cancer therapeutic target due to its dual role in cell cycle progression and gene transcription. However, current CDK7 inhibitors generally exhibit poor kinase selectivity. Herein, we performed in-depth structural optimization on a 17-membered macrocyclic scaffold, and identified compound I-23, which potently inhibits CDK7 with an IC50 value of 3 nM and exhibits exceptional CDK7 selectivity with no significant off-target activity across 416 kinases. I-23 also potently inhibits cell proliferation across a panel of tumor cell lines, induces cell cycle arrest and transcriptional suppression, and downregulates oncoprotein c-Myc, particularly in triple-negative breast cancer cells. Importantly, I-23 shows favorable oral bioavailability (up to 28%) with linear pharmacokinetics. Collectively, this work provides a highly selective and orally bioavailable macrocyclic CDK7 inhibitor, which can serve as a valuable chemical tool for dissecting CDK7 biological functions and a promising lead compound for CDK7-based anticancer drug discovery.

title: Passive rotational substrate handling in three-axis gantry robots.
text: Simple three-axis gantry-based robots are widely used in laboratory automation due to their low cost, ease of implementation and flexibility. However, solid sample manipulation tasks that are intuitive for human operators, such as positioning and reorientation, often require motion capabilities beyond those of standard gantry systems, limiting the implementation of more advanced, uninterrupted automated experiments. Dexterous movements can be achieved using robotic arms or advanced motor systems, but with substantially increased system integration complexity and cost. This work presents a low-cost substrate handling and rotation module that enables passive degree-of-freedom augmentation in existing three-axis gantry-based automated workflows, addressing a key manual handling bottleneck. The modular pick-and-place hardware leverages the existing linear motion of an Opentrons OT-2 gantry to drive a rack-and-pinion mechanism, thereby enabling repeatable 180° rotational motion about a horizontal axis without the need for additional motors, electronics, or an external robotic system. We demonstrate this module in the automated manipulation of contact lens hydrogels for wettability characterization assays, though this platform can be used in broader laboratory automation applications including sample repositioning for microscopy or coating formation.

title: Autane: An autonomous crane for sustained port operations.
text: Fully automated cranes are revolutionizing modern port operations by addressing labor shortages, improving precision, and enhancing safety. Toward this goal, we present the Autane (autonomous crane) system specifically developed for rubber tire gantry (RTG) cranes handling standardized containers in port yards, enabling autonomous safety-critical container grabbing, transport, and placement with high accuracy, adaptability, and efficiency. Autane overcomes the challenges of safe motion of large-scale cranes with centimeter-level precision requirements, providing long-distance high-precision perception. It uses multisensor fusion, real-time obstacle detection, and simultaneous localization and mapping to perceive the environment, identify container features, and dynamically adjust trajectories. By tightly coupling perception, planning, control, and operation and maintenance, Autane achieves safe and precise alignment, seamless interaction with transport vehicles, and robust execution of long-distance handling tasks. Deployed in multiple ports, Autane shows full-day operation and has autonomously handled more than 2 million 20-foot equivalent units. This work highlights the potential of fully autonomous RTG cranes to enable sustained, resilient, and low-intervention port automation.

title: Picoinjection of Microfluidic Chip Enables Controllable Concentration of Magnetic Particle inside Droplet Microrobots.
text: Although magnetically controlled microrobots hold great promise for application in next-generation interventional medical procedures, the insufficient magnetic particle concentration and limited drug-loading capacity of these robots remain significant challenges to their practical implementation. Herein, a droplet microfluidic platform integrated with picoinjection technology was developed to enable controlled adjustment of the magnetic particle concentration and drug load in droplet microrobots. The flow-focusing microfluidic chip, integrated with a liquid metal electrode, was fabricated to inject nanoliter-scale volumes of the alginate (ALG)-Fe3O4 precursor solution into preformed calcium chloride (CaCl2) droplets. The effects of gas pressure on droplet size and generation frequency were investigated, and the influence of injection rate on droplet diameter and injected volume was characterized. Furthermore, the effects of voltage, frequency, and duty cycle on injection success rates were analyzed through experiments and numerical simulations. By adjusting the injection rate, three types of microrobots with different magnetic particle concentrations were successfully fabricated. Characterization results indicate that these microrobots exhibit superparamagnetic behavior and distinct magnetic responsiveness. The motion performance of the microrobots was also verified. Finally, dual picoinjection was employed to incorporate DOX into the microrobots, demonstrating the feasibility of the platform for therapeutic-agent loading. Overall, this work provides a microfluidic strategy for quantitatively tuning the magnetic particle concentration and magnetic responsiveness of droplet microrobots, while demonstrating its potential for drug-delivery applications.

title: Automated Perovskite Film Fabrication with High-Resolution Data Acquisition and Machine Learning Analysis.
text: Lead halide perovskite solar cells have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation photovoltaics; nevertheless, fabrication of the perovskite photoactive layer remains highly intricate with film formation strongly modulated by various processing and environmental factors. Here, we report an environment-controlled, robot-assisted platform for automated thin-film fabrication designed to quantify and visualize perovskite crystallization in situ. Beyond precise control of each processing step, the system captures dynamic phenomena spanning subsecond color evolution and millisecond antisolvent droplet behavior while simultaneously recording slower environmental parameters (temperature, humidity/moisture, and concentrations of oxygen and volatile organic compounds). For optoelectronic assessment, we implemented time-resolved microwave conductivity (TRMC) measurements together with photoluminescence intensity quantification by using a complementary automated evaluation system. By combining machine-learning regression with SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) analysis, we identify the environmental parameters that most impact film properties and propose a feedback strategy to refine data and extract precise effects of process factors. A comparative study of a two-cation perovskite, (FAPbI3)0.87(MAPbBr3)0.13, and a three-cation perovskite, FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3, further reveals markedly different sensitivities to environmental factors (FA, formamidinium; MA, methylammonium), in particular, temperature and resultant phase transition kinetics during thermal annealing. Based on the ML analysis and feedback, we tuned the antisolvent droplet velocity and obtained the maximized power conversion efficiency of 24.4%. Notably, this manual device fabrication was consistent with the results obtained by the automated system. This work establishes a practical route to stable, quantitative, and mechanistically informed investigation of solution-processed photovoltaic films.

title: Associations between digital and automated work and psychosocial outcomes: Cross-sectional results from the Gutenberg Health Study.
text: As technology increasingly shapes workplaces, evidence associated psychosocial effects remains limited. This study explored demographic correlates of digital and automated work, and examined associations between digital and automated work and psychosocial outcomes. A cross-sectional study was conducted within the Gutenberg Health Study (Mainz/Mainz-Bingen, Germany; 2019-2022). Digital and automated work were assessed using the GAP (Gesunde Arbeit in Pionierbranchen) module. Digital work refers to the use of digital information, digital communication tools and digital networking in work processes, whereas automated work refers to the support of work from machines and robots. Psychosocial outcomes were examined using the Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire (COPSOQ). Unadjusted ordinal logistic regression models estimated odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals for primary analyses. Linear regression models adjusted for age, sex, socioeconomic status, and data collection timing estimated β coefficients and 95% confidence intervals for secondary analyses. Among 5,730 participants, frequent digital work was common (≈ 80%), whereas frequent automated work was rare (≈ 6%). Digital work was associated with higher job satisfaction and lower presenteeism, but also with greater intention to leave the profession and lower work engagement. Automated work was linked to higher burnout and lower job satisfaction. Technical and skill-related demands of digital and automated work were related to burnout, presenteeism, intention to leave, and reduced job satisfaction and general health. Positive experiences of digital and automated work were consistently associated with better psychosocial outcomes, including higher job satisfaction, work engagement, and general health.
