title: Building Capacity for the Engineering of Biology and Biomanufacturing in Finland.
text: Finland's efforts on engineering biology (synthetic biology) originate from the investments in genetic engineering at the beginning of 1980s. The efforts were linked early on with industry, such as dairy companies, vaccine production and production of ethanol and industrial enzymes, and development of commercial scale bioprocesses. Timely support for activities in metabolic engineering, systems biology and genome wide technologies (omics) and incorporating bioinformatics and cell level modelling evolved the field naturally towards synthetic biology and biofoundry activities. This foundation has created a strong basis in industrial biotechnology in particular, its insights and capabilities being increasingly relevant today within the green transition and bioeconomy contexts. In Finland, more than 830 companies are categorised to operate in biotechnology, collectively producing a turnover of 7.1 billion euros and providing jobs for around 19,400 people. Technology and business opportunities are developing fastest in the field of modern biotechnology rooted in molecular biology. Consequently, in the past 15 years, Finland has evidenced the founding of many new biotechnology firms. In relation to bioeconomy, Finland has also a significant research tradition in plant biotechnology and breeding and in pilot scale cultivation of plant cells. Furthermore, engineering biology activities within medical biotechnology and diagnostics are strong. According to a recent report, 88.5% of the revenue of Finnish biotechnology companies comes from activities classified as industrial biotechnology. This article focuses on engineering/synthetic biology developments for industrial biotechnology, including microbial production of food components and pharma products.

title: CLEAN Database: providing enzyme function coverage for over 55 million sequences.
text: Enzyme function annotation is critical for decoding biological systems and enabling rational enzyme design. However, experimentally characterized enzyme functions remain available for only a small fraction of known protein sequences, resulting in a widening gap between rapidly expanding sequence space and reliable functional assignments. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have accelerated enzyme function annotation by facilitating accurate and high-throughput prediction from protein sequences. Here, we present CLEAN Database (CLEAN DB), a comprehensive resource encompassing >55 million enzyme function annotations across 1 098 305 strains, predicted by the CLEAN AI model. The database features an intuitive web interface that enables users to efficiently search, explore, and download enzyme function data through flexible query options. Additionally, powered by a protein language model, CLEAN DB supports mutation effect prediction through interactive heatmaps, structural overlays, and tabular data visualizations. We anticipate that CLEAN DB will serve as a valuable platform for advancing enzyme discovery and applications in synthetic biology, metabolic engineering, enzyme engineering, retrosynthesis, and drug discovery. The database is freely available at https://cleandb.platform.moleculemaker.org/.

title: Discovery, identification of tricyclic sesquiterpene avermitilol synthase, and its heterologous production in plasmid-free Corynebacterium glutamicum.
text: Tricyclic sesquiterpenes are bioactive natural products with broad applications in pharmaceuticals, fragrances, and sustainable aviation biofuels. However, the repertoire of characterized tricyclic sesquiterpene synthases (tSTSs) remains limited. To systematically expand this enzyme class, we developed a multi-step bioinformatics workflow to identify genes encoding for cyclic sesquiterpene synthase integrating BLAST-based homology filtering, conserved motif validation, AlphaFold2-based structural modeling, and molecular docking. This workflow progressively refined an initial set of 1063 tSTS candidates to six putative enzymes that satisfied a C1-C10 distance criterion. Heterologous expression of all six candidates in Corynebacterium glutamicum JP-2 overexpressing a methylerythritol 4-phosphate pathway gene module confirmed biosynthetic activity, yielding five known cyclic sesquiterpenes and tricyclic avermitilol produced by a tSTS (AtTPS) identified from Actinokineospora terrae by NMR spectroscopy and high-resolution electrospray ionization mass spectrometry. To improve industrial feasibility, the chemical-inducible promoter was replaced with constitutive leaderless synthetic σB promoters, and fusion of avermitilol synthase with farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase via a GGGGS linker enhanced the local concentration of intermediates between enzymes. In addition, a plasmid-free, antibiotic selection-free strain was constructed via the CRISPR-associated transposons, enabling dual chromosomal integrations of the avermitilol synthase expression cassette and achieving 81.52 mg/L avermitilol production. The chromosomally integrated strain maintained stable production over serial passages, whereas the plasmid-based strain exhibited greater than 90% loss of productivity. Fed-batch fermentation of AVM-int02cp in a 2-L bioreactor achieved a final avermitilol titer of 100.99 mg/L. This work demonstrates a sequence- and 3D structure-assisted gene discovery-to-production workflow for a tricyclic sesquiterpene through the identification of an uncharacterized synthase gene in a microbial host.

title: Converging quality by design, artificial intelligence, and biofoundry automation: A new paradigm for scalable circular biomanufacturing.
text: Synthetic biology applies engineering principles to the rational design of biological systems with the aim of producing predictable and tunable behaviour. Although the field's conceptual foundations and core technologies are well established, the recent simultaneous maturation of Quality by Design (QbD), artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted biological design, and automated biofoundry workflows is beginning to outline a more replicable pathway from laboratory innovation to industrial-scale circular biomanufacturing. This review argues that the convergence of these three elements, rather than any one alone, characterises the current phase of the field. We examine how the Design-Build-Test-Learn (DBTL) cycle is being transformed from a research heuristic into a systematic industrial development framework; show how shared toolsets now transfer across microbial, plant, and animal systems to enable a holistic bioeconomy; benchmark synthetic biology-derived products against conventional alternatives where techno-economic and life-cycle data permit; and examine scale-up, regulatory, and societal bottlenecks through recent market-scale case studies in which these bottlenecks have been navigated in practice. We also contrast EU and US regulatory frameworks to show how policy divergence shapes technology adoption. We conclude by identifying what the coming decade of convergent synthetic biology must deliver to support a circular bioeconomy at the scale the 2030 Agenda demands.

title: Pan-Canadian health workforce data sources: Bridging the divides to better inform research, policy and planning.
text: High-quality data on the health workforce are needed for effective health workforce research, policy and planning in support of care delivery and system strengthening. Standardized data in uniquely decentralized health systems makes it possible to understand overall supply, distribution and mobility trends across jurisdictions and to inform international benchmarking. To describe two key pan-Canadian health workforce data sources, identifying key challenges and opportunities for optimizing data for research, policy and planning. We conducted a multi-phase environmental scan: (1) mapping CIHI and Statistics Canada data holdings and collection methods; (2) reviewing 2015-2025 literature to assess their use, strengths, and gaps; and (3) comparing sources to identify discrepancies and implications for pan-Canadian workforce analysis and planning. Two data pan-Canadian custodians - the Canadian Institute for Health Information and Statistics Canada - collate health workforce data from health administrative sources and undertake population census, labour force, education and health-focused surveys respectively. Both custodians maintain datasets that reflect the breadth and depth of health workforce information. Neither source is designed primarily to inform health workforce planning, resulting in variability in the coverage of professions and policy-relevant topics. Despite the policy priority of interprofessional collaboration, when data are used for health workforce analysis it remains focused on a single sector or profession reflective of data silos and divergent standardization. Targeted investments into data development, standardization and interoperability are key areas for enhancing interprofessional and cross-jurisdictional health workforce policy and planning.

title: When Systems Talk-Measuring Neurology Care in the Digital Era: Emerging Issues in Neurology.
text: Neurology is entering a decade in which rapid growth in diagnostic technologies, data streams, and care delivery models collides with persistent fragmentation of neurologic information across electronic health records, imaging systems, and remote monitoring platforms. As these data sources proliferate, interoperability has emerged as a foundational requirement for high-quality neurologic care. The current landscape limits longitudinal understanding of disease trajectories, impedes care transitions, burdens quality measurement, and constrains research. This article articulates the current and future challenges of interoperability for neurology by characterizing the current state of interoperability; surveying relevant national standards and platforms; identifying key technical, semantic, and organizational barriers; and proposing future goals for improving interoperable neurologic care. Part and parcel of these challenges and goals are the evolving regulatory and policy frameworks, including the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement, provisions of the 21st Century Cures Act, and federal interoperability rules that mandate standardized, Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)-based application programming interfaces (APIs), and a common data foundation such as the United States Core Data for Interoperability Version-3 (USCDI v3). In parallel, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) initiatives have accelerated the transition to digital quality measures (dQMs), increasing the need for automated, multisource, standards-based data exchange aligned with real-time quality improvement. Using hypothetical use cases in vascular and behavioral neurology, we demonstrate how FHIR-based implementation guides could replace manual stroke quality reporting and enable the migration of cognitive assessment measures from legacy electronic clinical quality measures (eCQMs) to interoperable FHIR eCQMs, laying the groundwork for future dQMs. These examples highlight the potential of shared terminologies, structured neurologic observations, and API-enabled exchange, while underscoring persistent challenges, including limited availability of discrete neurologic data elements and the substantial effort required for mapping and governance. As the neurology ecosystem prepares for USCDI-aligned interoperability mandates taking effect in 2026, the neurology community plays a critical leadership role. Priorities include expanding neurologic data models and terminologies, ensuring that dQMs reflect clinical realities, strengthening governance across registries and networks, and enabling interoperable workflows that support remote monitoring and AI-enabled analytics. Together, these strategies position interoperability as a strategic imperative for the future of neurologic care, quality measurement, and research.

title: From Static Records to Virtual Digital Patients: An Artificial Intelligence-Driven Framework for Medical Data Assetization and Governance.
text: Healthcare data remain difficult to use because of fragmentation, sensitivity, and overlapping rights and responsibilities. A virtual digital patient links a longitudinal representation of an individual patient with modeling capabilities for specified clinical or research questions. This article proposes a conceptual socio-technical framework for governing how virtual digital patients are created, accessed, used, and updated. A narrative synthesis of selected policy, modeling, interoperability, and health artificial intelligence literature informs four interdependent layers: data and representation; artificial intelligence modeling and simulation; governance and control; and clinical and external use. The framework connects standardized longitudinal representations, knowledge-supported reasoning, disease-specific simulation, authorization, output review, lifecycle management, and accountability. It distinguishes data resources, model services, operational capabilities, and potentially recognizable assets; technical functionality alone does not establish asset status. An illustrative oncology trial-design scenario shows how purpose-limited requests could produce bounded, reviewed outputs without transferring raw patient records. A staged validation agenda addresses data quality, model performance, workflow safety, clinical utility, and governance controls. The article reports neither a new algorithm nor a deployed or clinically validated system. Its contribution is an integrated reference architecture for evaluating how patient-specific modeling, institutional stewardship, and value return may be aligned. Disease-specific implementation and empirical evaluation are required before clinical or commercial claims can be established.

title: An interoperable and reusable research environment for digital medicine.
text: Clinical research infrastructures remain fragmented and project-specific, with semantic inconsistency accumulating across studies and constantly increasing "interoperability debt". Repeated transformations between heterogeneous standards cause semantic drift and information loss. Prospective studies require duplicate data entry across clinical and research systems, increasing workload and introducing inconsistencies. Project-driven data models accumulate technical debt that undermines the sustainability and maintainability of research infrastructure across studies and funding cycles. Here, we explore how a reusable research environment can be built, and whether governing data semantics at the persistence layer provides a foundation that outlasts individual projects. We present an environment addressing these deficiencies at the architectural level. An openEHR-based clinical data repository with governed archetypes serves as the canonical persistence layer, integrating retrospective EHR data, prospective study data, patient-reported outcomes, and wearable sensor streams under a shared semantic model. Prospective data is captured directly through openEHR-based forms, which removes the separate capture system for study variables, while duplicate documentation with a hospital information system that does not run on openEHR remains. Reusable transformation pipelines support bidirectional FHIR interoperability and OMOP-based analytics. Federation nodes at three institutions were tested with cohort count queries across sites and are not yet in routine use. Deployed at Charité university medical center across five studies covering approximately 16,000 patients and 7.9 million data points, the environment shows that one governed repository can be reused across successive studies from different clinical domains within an existing healthcare IT landscape. Of its 125 archetypes, 57 are shared between at least two studies. Sustainability beyond these five studies and scaling beyond one institution remain to be shown. All tooling is publicly available and provided as a deployable configuration for institutional adoption.

title: The Chemical Probes Portal-2026: expanding and enhancing this expert review-based public resource to sustain chemical probe selection and application in bioscience.
text: The Chemical Probes Portal (https://www.chemicalprobes.org) is an open, international, resource empowering scientific robustness by supporting responsible research using chemical probes. The Portal informs best-practice in the selection and application of small-molecule chemical probes through expert review, manual curation, and community engagement. Used correctly, high-quality chemical probes are powerful, versatile research tools enabling the fundamental study of protein function, target validation, and development of new therapeutics. Conversely, the inappropriate selection and use of these chemical tools can compromise experimental interpretation, reliability, and translational impact, highlighting the need for trusted advisory resources. The Portal addresses this challenge, providing a unique collection of curated data, expert reviews, and related guidance. We describe significant developments to the Portal's content and infrastructure. We have substantially expanded the content, with curated probes increasing by 26% since our last update. We have significantly enhanced website functionality through implementation of new, more informative probe pages, improved search tools and enhancements in data accessibility, machine readability, and interoperability. Together, these developments strengthen the Portal as a trustworthy, user-friendly provider of expert-reviewed chemical probe information and an increasingly valuable source of gold-standard FAIR, accessible data in the era of AI-assisted information discovery, underpinning reliable bioscience research.

title: Integrating Patient-Reported Outcome Measures Through the Health Outcomes Observatory (H2O) Digital Infrastructure: Multicenter Mixed Methods Feasibility Study.
text: The integration of patient-reported outcomes (PROs) into routine clinical practice remains limited despite their well-documented benefits in facilitating clinical communication and research. Systematic digital PRO collection can enable real-time symptom monitoring, timely clinical interventions, and greater patient empowerment. The Health Outcomes Observatory (H2O) initiative was developed to enable systematic digital patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) collection and integration with clinical data to support value-based, patient-centered care across health care systems. This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility, usability, acceptability, clinical utility, and implementation of the H2O digital infrastructure from patient and health care professional perspectives across multiple health care settings and medical conditions. A noninterventional, multicenter, convergent mixed methods feasibility study was conducted in Spain, Austria, the Netherlands, and Germany across multiple medical conditions. Locally implemented smartphone, tablet, and web-based solutions captured and displayed PROs. Surveys and interviews assessed usability, acceptability, perceived clinical utility, and implementation conditions among patients and health care professionals. Of 241 participants assessed initially, 115 (47.7%) contributed follow-up data. Although 83% (44/53) of the respondents indicated willingness to recommend H2O, the mean System Usability Scale (SUS) score was 44.65/100 (SD 9.78), indicating poor usability. Among 50 participants with paired Patient Satisfaction Questionnaire Short Form assessments, satisfaction with technical quality declined (t49=2.20; P=.03). Interviews identified perceived value alongside login difficulties, technical instability, weak integration with clinical systems, and inconsistent use of PRO data during consultations. The H2O infrastructure could be deployed across heterogeneous settings, and participants perceived value in digital PRO collection; however, poor usability, substantial attrition, technical friction, and limited workflow integration qualify conclusions about feasibility and acceptability. More reliable technology, stronger interoperability, and evaluation in larger and more complete samples are needed before broader implementation.

title: "Bureaucratic Blockage" in Healthcare Resource Management: A Qualitative Study of Nurse Managers' Operational Decisions.
text: Reliable access to materials, pharmaceutical products, and functional equipment is essential for operational readiness and quality management in healthcare. However, nurse managers often make resource-management decisions within fragmented information systems and governance arrangements that limit timely local action. This study examined how information and governance constraints shape nurse managers' operational decisions in healthcare resource management and developed, inductively, from the qualitative findings, the concept of "bureaucratic blockage" to describe a mechanism that may constrain timely local action. A qualitative descriptive study was conducted with 16 nurse managers (8 from hospital and 8 from primary care/community settings) in Portugal. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews conducted between January and August 2025. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim in Portuguese, pseudonymized, and analyzed using Bardin's inductive content analysis. ATLAS.ti was used for data management. Reporting was guided by the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research. Sixty-two resource-related meaning units were identified and organized into 2 thematic domains: management of material and pharmaceutical resources (reported across both settings) and management of equipment (reported by hospital managers only). Material and pharmaceutical decisions were constrained by limited order traceability, weak stock and lifecycle monitoring, restricted access to consumption and cost data, fragmented platforms, material shortages, and repeated ordering work. Equipment-related decisions, reported only by hospital managers, were shaped by unclear failure-response pathways, the absence of fault-management systems, limited autonomy in acquisition decisions, and administrative overload. In participants' accounts, information opacity, nonintegrated systems, and escalation-dependent processes co-occurred across domains, and restricted decision rights were described in hospital equipment management; their accumulation was synthesized inductively as a mechanism termed "bureaucratic blockage." Resource-management decisions are constrained by system-level factors that limit managerial capacity for timely, locally actionable responses. Quality-management interventions should strengthen resource traceability, system interoperability, and lifecycle monitoring and, in hospital equipment management, fault-management circuits and the alignment between managerial accountability and decision rights. Addressing "bureaucratic blockage" may reduce administrative escalation and support operational readiness; these consequences were inferred from participants' accounts, were not measured, and require empirical testing.

title: Digital twin technology in cardiovascular care: future perspectives for nursing practice, patient management, and clinical decision-making.
text: Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of mortality globally and continue to impose substantial clinical, economic, and organisational burdens on healthcare systems due to increasing disease complexity, recurrent hospitalisations, and the need for long-term monitoring and personalised care. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence, computational modelling, wearable biosensors, telehealth, and digital health technologies have accelerated the emergence of Digital Twin Technology (DTT) as a promising innovation in precision cardiovascular healthcare. Although DTT has gained growing attention in medicine and engineering, its implications for cardiovascular nursing practice, patient management, and clinical decision-making remain insufficiently synthesised. This scoping review aimed to explore the current applications of DTT in cardiovascular healthcare and examine its implications for cardiovascular nursing practice, patient management, clinical decision-making, and future healthcare delivery. Review was conducted using the Arksey and O'Malley methodological framework and reported according to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A comprehensive search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, Embase, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar was performed for studies published between 2020 and 2026. Eligible studies included literature related to digital twins, computational cardiovascular modelling, artificial intelligence-assisted cardiovascular care, wearable technologies, remote monitoring systems, and nursing implications in cardiovascular healthcare. Data were charted and synthesised narratively according to predefined research questions and thematic areas. Thirty studies met the inclusion criteria. The findings demonstrated that DTT is increasingly applied in heart failure monitoring, arrhythmia prediction, telecardiology, smart ICU systems, virtual cardiac modelling, personalised rehabilitation, and population-level cardiovascular risk prediction. Artificial intelligence, machine learning, wearable biosensors, cloud computing, electronic health records, and predictive analytics were the most commonly reported technological components. The review further identified important implications for cardiovascular nursing, including transition from reactive to predictive care, expansion of telehealth nursing, enhanced data-driven clinical decision-making, and the growing need for digital competency. However, ethical concerns, cybersecurity risks, interoperability challenges,infrastructure costs, workforce preparedness, and limited nursing-focused evidence remain significant barriers. DTT has the potential to transform cardiovascular healthcare through predictive, personalised, and continuously adaptive models of care. Strengthening nursing leadership, digital competency and interdisciplinary collaboration is essential for integration of DTT into future cardiovascular practice.

title: Pathology AI clinical integration: From promise to practice.
text: Despite substantial advances in digital and computational pathology over the past decade, pragmatic and systematic guidance for translating AI models from research into clinical practice remains limited. Most existing frameworks offer only high-level recommendations on validation, regulatory compliance, and implementation, often lacking pathology-specific roadmaps aligned with laboratory standards. This review first summarizes current progress in digitalization and AI in pathology, with emphasis on key applications in biomarker quantification, molecular status prediction, and multimodality integration. We then outline nine major components essential for pathology AI clinical integration, from defining clinical needs through analytical and clinical validation, workflow interoperability, to health economics, and further summarize and compare eight available frameworks. Next, we introduce the AI Development and Optimization in Pathology for Translation (ADOPT) framework, a practical, phased deployment roadmap specifically designed to align with College of American Pathologists and Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CAP/CLIA) guidelines, to facilitate safe and effective clinical integration of pathology AI tools. We conclude by discussing future perspectives of digital and computational pathology in cancer care, emphasizing widespread clinical adoption of digitized pathology, effective multidisciplinary collaboration, and optimized pathologist-AI synergy to fully realize the promise of pathology AI.

title: Standardising ocular surface photography for artificial intelligence: current limitations and a proposed roadmap.
text: Slit-lamp colour photography remains a cornerstone of anterior segment documentation and longitudinal monitoring. However, conventional slit-lamp photography has seen relatively limited technological advancement compared with the rapid development of quantitative anterior-segment modalities such as AS-OCT, Scheimpflug tomography and confocal microscopy. Despite the wide diffusion of digital cameras, smartphones, and high-end slit-lamp systems, ocular surface photography (OSP) remains hampered by the absence of standardised acquisition and processing protocols. The convex, aspheric geometry of the ocular surface, off-axis illumination, peripheral defocus, automatic colour correction, and pupil-driven exposure variation in retroillumination limit reproducibility, inter-device comparability, and clinical utility. In this review we critically appraise current OSP applications across major ocular surface conditions (dry eye disease, conjunctival hyperaemia, infectious keratitis, ocular surface burns, and ocular surface neoplasia), mapping the hardware, software, and reproducibility limitations that constrain clinical practice. We then examine how these limitations propagate into artificial intelligence (AI) development, where the absence of large, well-annotated, demographically diverse OSP datasets, together with the lack of reproducible quantitative phenotypes and reliable labels, is now the principal bottleneck to clinically deployable models; we discuss patient-level data partitioning and external validation, and outline how deep learning, federated learning and foundation models can both utilise and improve OSP. Finally, we propose a minimum acquisition and dataset specification, tiered by clinical setting from research to community screening, and a staged roadmap that combines hardware standardisation (focus-stacked, illumination-controlled, colour-calibrated acquisition), interoperable metadata-rich storage (DICOM where infrastructure permits), quantitative phenotype definition, and diverse international dataset collaborations, so that the ocular surface can benefit from quantitative imaging and AI as other areas of ophthalmology have begun to.

title: The GA4GH Workflow Execution Service: A Standard API for Workflow Execution and Management in Genomics.
text: Rapid growth in life science data generation has led to large and increasingly distributed collections of sensitive genomic data. To analyse this data, researchers increasingly rely on computational workflows to enable scalable, portable and reproducible analysis. However, these workflows are executed by specialized workflow engines across heterogeneous compute environments, each with its own requirements. As a result, users often need engine- and compute-environment-specific knowledge to submit, monitor and manage workflow execution, increasing the barriers to interoperability. These challenges are compounded in large-scale projects, where workflow runs must be dispatched to local clusters, cloud platforms or data hosting infrastructures with different underlying technologies. We describe the Global Alliance for Genomics and Health (GA4GH) Workflow Execution Service (WES) API, an approved GA4GH standard first released in 2018, together with its data model and the endpoints that define a unified interface for workflow execution. By standardizing workflow invocation, the WES API allows a single client to submit, monitor and cancel workflow runs across diverse workflow engines and compute backends, such as scheduling clusters or cloud platforms. We surveyed thirteen adoptions of the standard, covering standalone services and platforms in four programming languages. In a two-site demonstration, a WES implementation from Germany and one from Japan executed the same federated allele-frequency analysis with site-specific adjustments and only aggregated results leaving either site, demonstrating that it is possible to run the same analysis across independently built and operated WES services in different countries. From the gaps identified, we propose extensions for community discussion. The latest version of the WES API repository can be found at https://github.com/ga4gh/workflow-execution-service-schemas (DOI: https://doi.org/10.59756/m382x-ww ). The full Reference Documentation can be viewed at: https://ga4gh.github.io/workflow-execution-service-schemas/docs/. valentin.schneider-lunitz@bih-charite.de.

title: [Not Available].
text: The AIFA (Agenzia Italiana del Farmaco) monitoring registries represent one of the most distinctive regulatory tools within the Italian pharmaceutical governance framework. Initially introduced to support the appropriate use of reimbursed medicines and pharmaceutical expenditure control, they have progressively evolved into an infrastructure linking access to medicines, reimbursement governance, managed entry agreements (MEAs), and real-world data collection. This article examines the evolution and the policy relevance of AIFA monitoring registries within the Italian Health Technology Assessment framework. Firstly, it outlines the main legislative and regulatory milestones shaping the system, from the establishment of AIFA in 2003 to the publication of the 2024 guideline, which formally defined the criteria for registry activation. Secondly, it describes the main registry types, the criteria guiding their establishment, and the role of MEAs within the monitoring process. Thirdly, it provides an updated overview of the current registry landscape based on recent AIFA lists, identifying 340 closed registries (March 2026) and 366 active registries (April 2026), with “registri propriamente detti” (comprehensive registries) representing the predominant tool. Among those registries, MEAs were applied in nearly half of cases, with payment by result being the commonest scheme. The article also reviews the use of registry-derived data in peer-reviewed studies across hematology, oncology, cardiovascular diseases, and infectious diseases. Finally, it discusses key challenges, including duplication of information, limited interoperability with healthcare databases, administrative burden and residual discretion in registry activation despite recent transparency reforms. Overall, AIFA monitoring registries emerge as a strategic interface between pharmaceutical regulation, reimbursement governance, and evidence generation.

title: Veterinary drug residues in animal-derived foods: From analytical detection to intelligent and sustainable surveillance.
text: Veterinary drug residues in animal-derived foods remain a major challenge for food safety, public health, and international trade. This review examines residue control through the complementary roles of analytical technologies, digital tools and green analytical chemistry. Rapid screening can support local decisions, while liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry provides laboratory confirmation. Digital tools offer opportunities to connect analytical results with treatment records and product traceability, but their value depends on data quality, interoperability and validation. Solvent reduction and miniaturization should be assessed alongside energy use and material life cycles. The proposed farm-to-fork roadmap links these approaches with regulatory requirements and One Health priorities, emphasizing reliable measurements, coordinated data use and feasibility in resource-constrained settings.

title: Mapping early childhood development data systems in Kenya and sub-Saharan Africa: a scoping review.
text: Holistic child development requires a nurturing environment, yet aggregated data on how children fare across the five Nurturing Care Framework (NCF) domains; health, nutrition, early learning, responsive caregiving, and safety and security, remain scarce, especially where vulnerabilities cluster. In sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), the absence of comprehensive, real-time, actionable data impedes timely, evidence-based action to promote healthy development and prevent developmental delays. This scoping review mapped early childhood development (ECD) and ECD-related data systems in SSA, focusing on Kenya and profiling three counties (Nairobi City, Isiolo and Homa Bay). Following Arksey and O'Malley's framework with Levac et al.'s refinements, we searched PubMed, ScienceDirect, African Journals Online (AJOL), Scopus, APA PsycINFO and PsycNet (August 2010-August 2025), plus grey literature from Google Scholar, OpenGrey and national and subnational reports and websites. Of 2,773 records, 2,703 were screened after deduplication and 222 full texts assessed, yielding 49 records describing 44 ECD and ECD-related data systems, sources and platforms. Two reviewers extracted system type, indicators and sources, linkages, stakeholders, and reported challenges and lessons. Five ECD dashboards were identified: UNICEF's ECD Dashboard; the National Evaluation Platform (Malawi, Mali, Mozambique, Tanzania); the Tanzanian ECD Dashboard; and two South African platforms, Ecdinfohub.org and HearScreen. Overall, 44 systems were identified across nine countries, as well as regional and LMIC-wide sources; More than half (23/44; 52.3%) were based in Kenya, including five county-specific platforms. Coverage of the Nurturing Care Framework (NCF) domains was uneven: Health indicators were the most commonly represented (30 systems, 68.2%), followed by nutrition (18, 40.9%). In contrast, early learning (13, 29.5%), safety and security (7, 15.9%), and responsive caregiving (6, 13.6%) were substantially less represented. Only eight systems (18.2%) included cross-cutting financing indicators. Most Kenyan platforms were not specifically designed for ECD, and several suffered from irregular updates or limited public accessibility. Common challenges across systems included technical limitations, poor data quality, insufficient capacity, fragmented data ecosystems, and weak links between data and policy processes. Notably, only three platforms and one multi-country survey instrument, the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) covered all five domains, none of them subnationally at child level. ECD data in Kenya and SSA remain fragmented along sectoral lines, and no single system generates the information on indicators across the five components of NCF. Closing this gap requires an interoperable, standards-based platform that federates rather than replaces sectoral systems, built on an agreed minimum ECD indicator package and explicit metadata governance. https://osf.io/ht24x/overview.

title: Population-wide implementation of comprehensive cancer registration in Germany-overview article on current status quo and future perspectives.
text: The landscape of the existing population-based cancer registries (CRs) has evolved significantly in Germany since 2008. This overview article presents the general framework of cancer registration in Germany, with a particular focus on harmonization and standardization of data collection and registration processes. Moreover, it outlines key challenges and limitations and illustrates both current status and future scope of utilization of comprehensive CR data with clinical and epidemiological relevance. Federal and state legislation, resources such as the nationally standardized oncological core dataset for cancer reporting and its technical specifications, jointly developed and maintained by consortia of the CRs and stakeholders, as well as registration recommendations of national and international organizations, have contributed to harmonization, standardization, and validation of data collection and registration processes. The current scope of utilization of CR data is illustrated through a variety of topical examples, including consecutive monitoring of cancer burden on a population level, evaluation of the effectiveness of early detection and screening programs, monitoring of the provision of cancer care and implementation of clinical practice guidelines, and identification of gaps between evidence-based recommendations and real-world practice. Linkage with external real-world data and usage of CR data for novel study designs and research methods are gaining importance. This overview concludes with current developments and perspectives on future directions regarding both the national developments and integration of CRs into the European Health Data Space.

title: Why Computational Predictions Fall Short in Subclass B1 Metallo-β-Lactamase Inhibitor Discovery: Progress, Pitfalls, and Translational Opportunities.
text: The global dissemination of subclass B1 metallo-β-lactamases (MBLs), especially New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-1 (NDM-1), Verona integron-encoded metallo-β-lactamase-2 (VIM-2), and imipenemase-1 (IMP-1), threatens the clinical utility of carbapenems and other β-lactam antibiotics. This challenge is compounded by the absence of any commercially available MBL inhibitors for clinical use, underscoring the urgent need for novel inhibitor development. Computational approaches now guide much of MBL inhibitor discovery, yet many compounds predicted to bind B1 MBLs, or even shown to inhibit purified enzymes, fail to become biologically useful β-lactam rescue agents. This Perspective argues that this prediction-to-translation gap arises less from the absence of computational tools than from their fragmented use across metal coordination chemistry, enzyme dynamics, bacterial permeability, efflux, zinc availability, and β-lactam potentiation. Drawing on recent advances from 2018 to 2026 and selected foundational studies, we examine why predictions fail and how the field can improve translation. Major failure points include inaccurate treatment of the dizinc active site, uncertain protonation states, poor modeling of catalytic and structural water molecules, insufficient sampling of L3 and L10 loop dynamics, incomplete treatment of conformational, solvation, and other entropic contributions, overinterpretation of docking scores, and extrapolation from NDM-1-biased datasets to broader NDM, VIM, and IMP inhibition. We propose that standardized multiscale workflows integrating metal-aware docking, validated zinc models, replicate molecular dynamics simulations, mechanistic quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics refinement, permeability-aware prioritization, and multi-enzyme validation can reduce avoidable prediction failures and improve the likelihood that computational hits progress toward biologically relevant MBL inhibition and β-lactam potentiation.

title: Causal Machine Learning for Treatment Effect Heterogeneity: Interpretation, Benchmarking, Validation.
text: Causal machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising approach for predicting individualized treatment effects and advancing precision medicine, moving beyond the limitations of conventional one-variable-at-a-time subgroup analyses of randomized trials. A recent benchmarking study by Chen and colleagues evaluated several causal ML learners across two large trials and concluded that current methods do not yet demonstrate reliable performance for clinical application. While such applied methodological investigations are valuable, this conclusion warrants a more nuanced examination. Multiple independent research groups have successfully applied causal ML across respiratory medicine and critical care, identifying clinically meaningful treatment effect heterogeneity that prior subgroup analyses had not resolved, although these applications have methodological limitations and do not yet establish that the detected heterogeneity is robust across internal and external validation. We outline four sequential and iterative dimensions central to credible causal ML analyses: choice of learner, model training with cross-fitting, internal validation using calibration-for-benefit and rank-weighted metrics, and external validation aligned with the original causal question. With careful methodological execution, causal ML holds considerable promise for personalized treatment decisions and warrants continued development; dismissing the field prematurely risks overlooking a powerful tool for personalized treatment decisions.

title: Machine Learning Algorithms for Predicting Psychostimulant Intoxication in Emergency Department Patients: A Multicenter Study.
text: Psychostimulant detection rates among emergency department (ED) patients presenting with suspected substance intoxication are low and are influenced by limited access to confirmatory testing, insufficient clinical information, and variability in physician experience. These challenges often result in high false-positive rates and unnecessary resource use. We hypothesized that machine learning (ML) algorithms could maintain reliable diagnostic performance across a temporal validation cohort and perform comparably to physicians with varying experience levels. This multicenter study prospectively enrolled ED patients with suspected substance intoxication between March 2019 and January 2020. We chronologically partitioned data into a training set (March-October 2019) and a temporal validation cohort (November 2019-January 2020) to assess model generalizability. After determining psychostimulant intoxication via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry from urine samples, we trained the ML algorithms using the confirmed positive cases. The primary outcome was the diagnostic discrimination of the models, measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) in the temporal validation cohort. Secondary outcomes included model accuracy, the Youden index, and a comparative assessment of sensitivity and specificity relative to five physicians of varying experience levels. Among 1,382 patients (mean age 43.8 [standard deviation 19.2] years; 55.3% male), 302 patients (21.9%) had confirmed psychostimulant intoxication, primarily involving (meth)amphetamines (134 [44.4%]), cathinones (107 [35.4%]), and ketamine (97 [32.1%]). In the temporal validation cohort (n = 382), the ML models demonstrated consistent performance, with AUCs ranging from 0.786 to 0.836. The primary outcome was met by the top-performing extreme gradient boosting (XGB) model (AUC, 0.836, 95% CI, 0.785-0.882; accuracy, 0.866 (95% CI, 0.838-0.895); and Youden index, 0.590 (95% CI, 0.480-0.694). To evaluate secondary outcomes, the XGB model's predictive accuracy was evaluated against 5 emergency physicians. The model surpassed the junior emergency physicians in both specificity (0.910 vs 0.633-0.867) and sensitivity (0.681 vs 0.500-0.633); its specificity was comparable to that of the senior emergency physicians (0.900-0.933). Machine learning models provide reliable diagnostic utility for identifying psychostimulant intoxication, achieving performance comparable to senior emergency physicians. While moderate sensitivity (0.389-0.708) limits their role as standalone rule-out tools, their high specificity provides a standardized tool to assist clinical decision-making and reduce diagnostic uncertainty in the fast-paced ED setting.

title: Modeling distinct pathogenesis of early- and late-onset preeclampsia via hierarchical representation learning of interactome.
text: We developed and validated the pathogenesis models by hierarchical representation learning of interactomes connecting endometrial maturation, placentation, chorioamnionitis, and hemolysis, elevated liver enzyme, and low platelet (HELLP) syndrome. We utilized 19 gene sets from our previous work to infer interactomes to develop (n = 177) and validate (n = 352) explainable artificial intelligence models for each preeclampsia subtype using deep-insight visible neural network, gradient-weighted class activation mapping, and large language model. The hierarchically learned representations identified novel genes for late-onset preeclampsia (LOPE), similar to chorioamnionitis (ANKRD13A, SLA), and HELLP syndrome (PDE5A). We also identified novel genes for early-onset preeclampsia (EOPE), similar to HELLP syndrome (SWAP70, GREM2, GPR146, PIP5K1B, EZR). Our pathogenesis models connected HELLP syndrome with both LOPE and EOPE. However, chorioamnionitis was only connected with LOPE.

title: Cortical Network Alterations and Treatment-Induced Reorganization in Panic Disorder: A Longitudinal High-Density EEG Study.
text: Although neuroimaging has identified network abnormalities in panic disorder (PD), the rapid and transient nature of panic symptoms highlights the need for methods with high temporal resolution. This study used high-density electroencephalography (EEG) to investigate cortical network alterations in PD and explore their potential as translational biomarkers. This longitudinal study enrolled 52 drug-naïve PD patients and 43 healthy controls. High-density (128-channel) resting-state EEG was collected from both groups at baseline, with repeat assessments performed in PD patients after 6 weeks of venlafaxine treatment. Source-level functional connectivity and network topology were analyzed to characterize cortical network features. Support vector machine (SVM) was used to evaluate the discriminative potential of baseline network features. At baseline, PD patients showed frequency-specific network disruptions, with enhanced connectivity within and between the default mode network, frontoparietal network, and dorsal attention network in the α band, but reduced connectivity across multiple networks in the θ and δ bands. Graph theory analysis revealed decreased global efficiency and increased characteristic path length in the α and δ bands. The SVM classifier achieved 86.32% accuracy in distinguishing PD patients from controls. Following treatment, clinical improvement was accompanied by network reorganization, including increased global efficiency and small-worldness in the α band, and enhanced fronto-temporal connectivity in the δ band. Exploratory brain-behavior associations did not survive FDR correction. PD is characterized by frequency-specific cortical network disruptions that show dynamic reorganization following treatment. These findings highlight the potential of EEG-derived network features as candidate markers for PD identification and treatment monitoring.

title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence with Stimuli-responsive Smart Polymers in Gastroretentive Drug Delivery Systems: A Systematic Review and Optimization Framework.
text: To systematically assess the existing literature on the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with stimuli-responsive smart polymers in gastroretentive drug delivery systems (GRDDS) and evaluate their potential to improve formulation optimization, gastric retention, and controlled drug release. The literature review aimed to identify potential advances relative to standard systems and areas where data are incomplete and to present a conceptual framework guided by scientific evidence for the future perspectives of AI-integrated smart polymer-based GRDDS. A structured literature review was carried out following the PRISMA checklist using Scopus, PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science databases. Articles from 2008 to 2025 were identified using predetermined search terms relevant to GRDDS, smart polymers, stimuliresponsive systems, and AI-enabled pharmaceutical formulations. Studies fulfilling the predefined inclusion criteria and not meeting any exclusion criteria were included for data analysis. A total of 131 papers met the inclusion criteria. Floating systems were the most frequently investigated gastroretentive drug delivery approach, while pH- and temperatureresponsive smart polymers enabled prolonged gastric retention and controlled drug release. AI approaches, including artificial neural networks (ANNs) and genetic algorithms (GAs), improved formulation optimization by increasing prediction accuracy and reducing the number of experimental trials. Overall, the included studies indicate that formulation optimization and GRDDS performance may be enhanced by combining smart polymers with AI-based models. The available evidence suggests significant potential for smart polymers and AIassisted formulation development in gastroretentive drug delivery systems. However, the currently available scientific literature consists mainly of preclinical studies and is highly heterogeneous. This review draws on a systematic review of existing evidence to offer an evidence-informed conceptual framework for how smart and sensitive (stimuli-responsive) polymers and AI-predicted trends are used in GRDDS applications. It is vital to remember that this framework has neither been empirically nor clinically validated. This study fills the research void by suggesting an optimal methodology for developing GRDDS using AI-based integration of smart polymers with prediction models. Further experimental validation and welldesigned clinical trials are required to establish its clinical applicability. The integration of stimuli-responsive smart polymers with AI-assisted strategies shows promise for advancing GRDDS formulation development and optimization. However, current evidence is predominantly preclinical and computational, with methodological heterogeneity and limited clinical validation. The proposed AI-assisted framework provides an evidence-informed conceptual basis for integrating predictive and optimization strategies into GRDDS development. Further experimental studies and clinical trials are needed to validate the framework and establish its translational applicability.

title: Data-Driven Virtual Reality Environment Recommendation for Long-Term Care Residents With Major Neurocognitive Conditions: Feasibility and Proof-of-Concept Study.
text: Virtual reality (VR) comfort sessions are increasingly used in residential dementia care, but environment selection remains ad hoc-staff have no systematic way to identify which virtual experience best suits a given resident. This feasibility and proof-of-concept study aimed to determine whether a pipeline integrating wearable physiological signals (heart rate variability and electrodermal activity), behavioral observations, and semantic environment characteristics can detect a person-specific, environment-level signal usable for between-session VR environment recommendation in long-term care and whether the resulting recommendations can be communicated to care staff and families through plain-language reports. Twenty-one residents with major neurocognitive conditions received 420 immersive VR sessions (5 environments, 2 sessions per week, 10 weeks) in a long-term care facility. We defined an operational hybrid calm target requiring behavioral calm (Pittsburgh Agitation Scale vocal intensity score of 0) and root mean square of successive differences at or above the participant's personal median to address the ceiling effect of behavioral measures alone (sessions already rated calm: 234/358, 65%). A compact 23-feature model (10 physiological, 3 behavioral, and 10 environment) was selected from more than 2100 configurations on the basis of cross-validation error and interpretability; the environment-level signal was tested with an environment permutation test on held-out sessions (weeks 8-10) and in sensitivity analyses. Environment features carried a statistically significant but borderline signal for predicting hybrid calm (environment permutation test, P=.045 with 200 permutations; P=.04 with 2000 permutations; Cohen d=1.75); 4 alternative models using 344 to 368 features ignored environment entirely (all P>.79). Person-level effects dominated prediction variance (partial η²=0.42; P<.001); environment-level discrimination was modest (pairwise ranking accuracy 57.9% vs 50% chance; top-1 hit rate 27.8%, 95% CI 19.8%-35.7%, including chance). Water presence was the most influential environment characteristic. In sensitivity analyses, the calm label was robust to the threshold (κ=0.79-0.89), but the environment permutation significance was not: under alternative thresholds and a continuous target, the effect kept its direction (d=0.65-1.60) without reaching significance (P=.06-.57), and a selection criterion computed on training period data only did not select the compact model. The pipeline generated 60 evidence-traced plain-language reports (30 family and 30 staff); all passed automated safety checks, with staff reports showing higher data fidelity and family reports showing better nonmedical framing. An end-to-end pipeline from wearable sensor to plain-language report is technically feasible in residential dementia care. The environment-level signal is suggestive-consistent in direction across target definitions and seeds-but its significance was specific to one labeling of one configuration whose selection was partly informed by the test set; it is exploratory evidence requiring independent replication, not a demonstration that the recommendations improve resident outcomes. Prospective validation against resident outcomes is required before any use in care decisions.

title: AI-Enhanced finite element analysis for optimal material selection in total knee replacement.
text: The increasing prevalence of total knee replacement (TKR) surgery and its association with aseptic loosening present a significant research challenge. This issue can be mitigated by selecting optimal materials for TKR components. This paper presents a hybrid approach combining Finite Element Method (FEM) with Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques for optimal material selection in TKR. Simulations of four normal movements-compression, distraction, medial bending, and lateral bending-were performed on a 3D model of the artificial knee. Four materials were evaluated: Cobalt-Chromium (Co-Cr), Zirconium (Zr), Stainless Steel, and Titanium (Ti). To simulate ligamentous constraints during distraction loading, a model of a nonlinear spring element was included, furnishing more physiologically realistic boundary conditions. An Artificial Neural Network (ANN) was trained on FEM simulation data to predict material performance with 98.7% accuracy for stress prediction (R2 = 0.987), while displacement prediction achieved R2 = 0.985. Multi-criteria decision-making using TOPSIS ranked Co-Cr as the optimal material under stress-prioritized weighting (0.6/0.4); though, sensitivity analysis revealed that Stainless Steel converts optimal when displacement/compliance is prioritized (0.4/0.6). Under axial compression of 1300 N, maximum stress for Co-Cr and Zr was 4.207 × 108N/m2 and 3.921 × 108N/m2, respectively. Under distraction: 4.321 × 108N/m2 and 4.142 × 108N/m2. Under medial bending: 1.101 × 108N/m2 and 1.088 × 108N/m2. Under lateral bending: 1.119 × 108N/m2 and 1.102 × 108N/m2. The AI-based approach reduced computational time by 73% compared to full FEM simulations while maintaining high prediction accuracy. This time-saving shows the promise of the surrogate model for large scale materials screening and patient specific implant optimization, but further biocompatibility and tribological validation will be required for clinical translation of these findings.

title: Artificial intelligence-driven precision management of Helicobacter pylori: an integrated framework from endoscopy and multi-omics to vaccine design and digital care.
text: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection, affecting half of the world's population, is the principal cause of peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer, yet its clinical management is increasingly undermined by the rapidly escalating global burden of antibiotic resistance, the suboptimal accuracy of conventional diagnostic methods, and the declining efficacy of empirical therapeutic regimens. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping this landscape, but existing research remains fragmented across single modalities. We propose a conceptual five-module framework that integrates AI approaches across the H. pylori care continuum: (1) global disease burden and the evolutionary dynamics of H. pylori drug resistance; (2) the application of multimodal AI, from convolutional neural networks to vision-language foundation models, for endoscopic early screening, pathological identification, and functional assessment; (3) the harnessing of machine learning (ML) on genomic and electronic health record data to decipher resistance mechanisms and generate personalized eradication regimens; (4) AI-driven vaccine target discovery and generative design, spanning reverse vaccinology to de novo immunogen creation; and (5) a digital closed-loop patient management platform that leverages new media and reinforcement learning to enhance adherence and eradication rates. We further delineate the core challenges of data bias, cross-scenario generalization, and the critical absence of prospective randomized evidence, and propose a future direction anchored in multimodal foundation models, federated learning, and continuous AI quality improvement. Rather than an established clinical pathway, this framework is proposed as a conceptual blueprint that, once prospectively validated, could upgrade AI-enabled H. pylori care from isolated image recognition toward an end-to-end "perception-reasoning-intervention" system, offering a blueprint for precision prevention and control.

title: An interpretable machine learning model for predicting response to anti-GD2 combined with umbilical cord blood-derived natural killer cell immunotherapy in neuroblastoma.
text: Neuroblastoma remains a major therapeutic challenge for children with high-risk or relapsed/refractory disease. Anti-GD2 therapy combined with umbilical cord blood-derived natural killer (UCB-NK) cell therapy represents an emerging strategy, but responses vary substantially. Imaging and bone marrow assessments require specialized resources, creating a need for complementary tools based on routinely available data. However, whether serial routine peripheral blood measurements can support response prediction in this treatment setting remains unclear. Serial peripheral blood measurements from 42 patients were used to derive dynamic coupling features that reflected longitudinal trends and coordinated changes between biomarkers. These features were integrated with static variables to develop machine learning models for response prediction. Seven machine learning models were compared using the same repeated stratified cross-validation framework. Model selection considered discrimination, probability-estimation quality, and interpretability. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was used to interpret the final model. Considering cross-validated performance, the quality of probability estimates, and clinical interpretability, L2-regularized logistic regression was selected as the final model for response prediction. The model leveraged dynamic peripheral blood features to predict response to anti-GD2 combined with UCB-NK cell immunotherapy, achieving a cross-validated AUC of 0.873 (95% bootstrap CI, 0.735-0.976) and a Brier score of 0.131 (95% bootstrap CI, 0.087-0.182). SHAP analysis characterized the direction and magnitude of feature contributions to model predictions. This study developed an interpretable response-prediction model using serial routine peripheral blood tests obtained in clinical practice. The model may complement treatment-response assessment using routinely available data. However, validation in larger, independent cohorts is required before clinical use.

title: Tongue image analysis for early warning of neonatal necrotizing enterocolitis: a translational perspective integrating tongue phenotyping and microbiome dynamics.
text: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) remains a life-threatening challenge in neonatology, primarily due to the lack of sensitive early biomarkers that precede overt clinical and radiological signs. This Perspective proposes a hypothesis-generating, non-invasive early-warning framework by integrating quantitative tongue image analysis with modern pathophysiological insights. We hypothesize a dynamic association between tongue phenotypic changes (e.g., a transition from pale to purplish color) and the progression of dysbiosis and intestinal microcirculatory disturbance, which correspond to two distinct but potentially complementary pathways. The proposed biological link rests on evidence for the candidate oral-gut microbial relationship, with such evidence derived primarily from adult and non-neonatal studies; gut dysbiosis-known to precede NEC-may be associated with changes in the tongue-coating microbiome, offering a potential remote yet accessible window into intestinal health. We outline a three-phase translational research roadmap: (I) prospective discovery of tongue-image biomarkers and establishment of dynamic baselines for each infant, (II) development of an exploratory machine-learning-based risk prediction model, and (III) mechanistic exploration using multi-omics approaches and animal models. Critically, we propose three testable hypotheses regarding temporal changes in tongue colorimetric and microbial parameters before NEC onset. If prospectively validated, this approach may eventually contribute to a dynamic bedside monitoring tool for NEC risk stratification.

title: Temporal stability of an electronic health record-driven machine learning model predicting type 2 diabetes among patients with mental illness.
text: We previously trained and tested a machine learning model to predict incident type 2 diabetes (T2D) in patients with mental illness using electronic health record (EHR) data from routine clinical practice. This hyperparameter-tuned XGBoost model - based on information on sex, age and mean HbA1c within the past two years - predicts whether a patient will meet criteria for T2D in the two years following each contact to psychiatric services. The performance of such a model may drift over time due to changes in standards of care, baseline risk, registration procedures, etc. Therefore, we set out to examine its temporal stability. In the present study, we fitted the model described above on EHR data from January 1, 2013 to December 31, 2017, and examined its stability in predicting T2D two years into the future for patients with contacts in 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023, respectively. Performance was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). The model showed good discriminative performance across all years (AUROC for 2018 = 0.84, 2019 = 0.83, 2020 = 0.87, 2021 = 0.80, 2022 = 0.84, 2023 = 0.80), with a linear model estimating a decrease in AUROC for T2D prediction of only 0.004 per year (95%CI: -0.024; 0.016). Secondary analyses suggested that models trained on recent data (past year) may achieve similar or better discrimination than models trained on longer historical periods. The temporal stability of the T2D prediction model supports its potential for clinical implementation, facilitating early detection and tailored interventions, while highlighting the importance of continued evaluation.

title: Can radiomics outperform radiologists in predicting Ewing sarcoma response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy from longitudinal MRI?
text: This retrospective, multicenter study evaluated whether MRI-based radiomics can predict the histological response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in Ewing sarcoma patients and compared their performance to that of radiological findings. Definitive histological assessment is only possible during surgery, potentially delaying therapy changes and increasing metastatic risk; therefore, a positive outcome would enable early adaptations. Radiomics features were extracted from pre- and post-neoadjuvant (after first chemotherapy cycle) chemotherapy scans of patients treated from 2004 to 2020. Four machine learning models were trained using nested cross-validation to predict histological response, and their performance was compared to models trained on semantic features derived from expert radiological readings. Diagnostic performance was measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). 96 patients (mean age, 19.9 ± 11.7 years; 41 women) with Ewing sarcoma were evaluated. Radiomics features related to low gray level intensity changes in T1 fat-saturated contrast-enhanced sequences showed the highest responder identification performance (AUROC, 0.62; 95% CI: 0.59, 0.65), surpassing the best radiological model, which relied on the relative change in maximum diameter of extratumoral soft tissue components (AUROC, 0.58; 95% CI: 0.56, 0.60). Radiomics models relying on pre-treatment T2-weighted data performed similarly (AUROC, 0.61; 95% CI: 0.58, 0.64), outperforming the clinical baseline (AUROC, 0.53; 95% CI: 0.51, 0.55). MRI-based radiomics moderately identified responders to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, suggesting a role for earlier, tailored therapeutic strategies in Ewing sarcoma. Larger studies to validate these findings within a multimodal framework are warranted. Radiomics extracted from MRI scans may aid with non-size tissue signals in early prediction of neoadjuvant chemotherapy response in Ewing sarcoma patients, potentially guiding personalized treatment adaptations, reducing delays for non-responders, and improving patient outcomes. These exploratory findings are complementary to standard size-based assessment from clinical routine, and warrant larger, prospective trials to be established.

title: MicroRNAs in aflatoxin B1-associated hepatocellular carcinogenesis: a scoping review of molecular networks, multiomics evidence, machine learning and translational potentials.
text: Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) is a foodborne hepatocarcinogen, but it remains unclear whether microRNA dysregulation reflects AFB1-associated hepatocarcinogenesis or general hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) biology. This scoping review mapped evidence linking AFB1 exposure, microRNA regulation, molecular mechanisms, multiomics, computational modelling, and machine learning approaches to HCC diagnostics, prognostics, and therapeutics. Peer-reviewed studies published from 2016 to 2026 were identified through Scopus, Embase, PubMed, and Web of Science, supplemented by citation searching, and screened using PRISMA ScR-aligned criteria. The final corpus comprised 104 unique studies classified by AFB1 attribution strength and evidence type across five strata spanning direct human AFB1 HCC microRNA evidence to general HCC contextual evidence. Experimental mechanistic studies predominated, whereas only one study directly combined measured AFB1 exposure, HCC, and microRNA assessment in humans. The study enrolled 366 HCC cases and 662 controls; circulating miR-4651 provided the strongest exposure-anchored clinical signal, discriminating AFB1-positive HCC with an area under the curve of 0.85, 78.1% sensitivity, and 92.1% specificity. Other studies evaluated exposure-responsive hepatotoxicity, experimental malignant transformation, or rat hepatocarcinogenesis, which cannot be considered interchangeable endpoints. Functionally investigated injury candidates included miR-1679 and miR-124a-3p. Multiomics findings implicated DNA damage, methylation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation, although pathway overlap was heterogeneous and independent functional confirmation was limited. Computational and machine learning studies have expanded network and feature prioritisation, but they have often relied on inferred exposure and limited external validation. Direct human evidence remains scarce, and candidate microRNAs occupy different validation stages. Biological plausibility does not establish clinical readiness; multicentre exposure-anchored validation, harmonised assays and prospective evaluation are required.

title: A practical guide to self-organising maps in psychological research.
text: Identifying shared and distinct profiles, whether of symptoms, personality traits, or cognitive abilities, is essential for understanding psychological phenomena, yet doing so requires navigating interrelated theoretical, conceptual, and technical complexities. First, most psychological phenomena typically exist along continuous spectra rather than discrete categories, complicating the characterisation of inherently heterogeneous constructs. Second, studying individual differences requires balancing population-level generalisation with person-level interpretability, which is critical for applied science and clinical practice. Third, psychological data often contain missing values, non-linear relationships, and high-dimensional patterns that violate standard statistical assumptions. Commonly used approaches for profile detection often fall short of these demands, producing oversimplified or difficult-to-interpret results that are hard to map back to the individual. In contrast, self-organising maps (SOMs) offer a powerful, visual, and intuitive solution that addresses these challenges. Despite growing interest, SOMs remain underutilised in psychology, likely due to a lack of accessible tutorials and clear guidelines tailored to the field. This tutorial introduces SOMs to psychologists without technical backgrounds, emphasising practical implementation. We provide evidence-based recommendations for key methodological decisions, accompanied by annotated R code. Using a dataset of depressive symptoms as an illustrative case, we present a complete workflow covering data preprocessing, map initialisation, parameter optimisation, and interpretation. We further discuss advanced SOM extensions relevant to psychological research and highlight key limitations of the method. By making SOMs accessible, this tutorial supports nuanced, person-centred analyses that preserve the complexity of psychological phenomena.

title: Global, Regional, and National Burden of Heart Failure, 1990-2023: A Systematic Analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023.
text: Heart failure (HF) is a common condition with substantial geographical variation in its prevalence and underlying etiologies. Consistent and comparable data on the burden of HF within populations are needed to inform health system priorities. To estimate the global burden of HF. This cross-sectional study estimates disease burden using Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) methodologies to integrate multiple information sources. Data come from 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023 representing the global population with prevalent HF. HF and underlying etiologies. Estimates with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs) for the prevalence and years lived with disability (YLDs) for HF by age, sex, location, year, and underlying etiology. Globally, there were 56.0 million (95% UI, 49.9-62.2 million) estimated cases of HF in 2023. The estimated prevalence of HF generally increased with age for all locations. While ischemic heart disease and hypertensive heart disease were the 2 most common etiologies globally among older adults, there was substantial variation in etiological pattern by location and age. Congenital heart anomalies and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) were common etiologies in children and young adults, while the proportion of HF due to alcohol use peaked in middle adulthood. Location-specific estimates highlighted regions with higher burden of HF due to specific etiologies, including RHD (south Asia, east Asia, Oceania, southeast Asia, central sub-Saharan Africa, eastern sub-Saharan Africa, southern sub-Saharan Africa, and western sub-Saharan Africa), alcohol use (eastern Europe, Australasia, the Caribbean, and central Europe), and Chagas disease (southern, Andean, tropical, and central Latin America). Heart failure is a significant global public health burden, and the impact is likely to increase as populations age. However, most HF etiologies can be prevented by interventions that reduce exposure to modifiable risk factors, such as elevated blood pressure, excessive alcohol consumption, and tobacco use. Etiology- and location-specific estimates can provide necessary information for public health officials to determine how best to prioritize interventions to reduce HF disease burden.

title: Artificial intelligence in odontology education.
text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored in dental education as a tool to support teaching, learning, assessment, and clinical decision-making. This systematic review synthesized current evidence on the implementation and educational impact of AI technologies in undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing dental education. A PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted using Scopus, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Studies published between 2020 and 2025 evaluating AI applications in dental education were identified using predefined PICO criteria. Educational outcomes included knowledge acquisition, diagnostic accuracy, clinical reasoning, procedural skills, learner engagement, and perceptions of AI-assisted learning. The included literature reflects an expansion from machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision systems primarily evaluated for diagnostic support toward generative AI platforms, including large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems. Across the included studies, AI applications were frequently associated with favorable diagnostic and examination performance and, in selected educational contexts, with supportive findings related to clinical reasoning, technical competency, feedback, and self-directed learning. However, the evidence was predominantly based on technical performance assessments and observational or cross-sectional designs. AI is increasingly being explored as a potential complementary educational resource, with applications including interactive tutoring, adaptive learning, and support for clinical reasoning. Nevertheless, heterogeneous methodologies and limited longitudinal evidence indicate the need for standardized educational evaluation and responsible curricular integration. AI shows potential as a complementary resource in dental education. Its integration should remain pedagogically guided and ethically supervised while future research establishes its educational effectiveness through standardized and longitudinal evaluation.

title: Diabetic retinopathy feature utilisation in 54 convolutional neural networks: a heatmap analysis
text: PurposeTo investigate how artificial intelligence (AI) systems detect referable diabetic retinopathy (DR) from retinal photographs by analysing heatmap patterns and determining their overlap with DR features. MethodsFifty-four AI systems were developed using 27 backbone architectures, with each implemented as both binary-referable and multi-class grading models based on the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy (ICDR) grading scale. Models were trained on DDR, BRSET and Kaggle datasets. After training, each model analysed 749 images with DR feature annotations, with Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients, LIME and SHAP heatmaps generated and compared to pixel-level annotations of microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots, venous beading, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities and neovascularisation. ResultsAll models achieved acceptable predictive performance (AUROC >0.8 for most architectures). Heatmap analysis revealed consistent attention to the central and temporal macular region. Exudates and cotton wool spots were highlighted most frequently by the heatmaps, with venous beading and neovascularisation at the disc showing poor overall coverage for binary referable classifiers.
