title: Quantum Metrology and Quantum Battery in a Hyperfine-Coupled Spin System
text: We investigate multiparameter quantum metrology and the energetic properties of an effective electron--proton spin system inspired by the hyperfine structure of the hydrogen atom. Considering the external magnetic field $\mathcal B$ and the hyperfine coupling strength $Λ$ as unknown parameters, we derive the quantum Fisher information matrix and establish the corresponding quantum Cramér--Rao bounds for their simultaneous estimation. We analyze the estimation precision and the correlations between the two parameters, showing that the weak-commutativity condition is satisfied despite the noncommutativity of the associated symmetric logarithmic derivatives. Independently, we explore the energetic properties of the system under a unitary charging protocol, characterizing its ergotropy, anti-ergotropy, storage capacity, and energy-basis coherence. We investigate the dependence of these quantities on the magnetic field, hyperfine coupling, temperature, and charging time. Our results provide a comprehensive characterization of the metrological properties and energetic performance of a hyperfine spin-based quantum system, highlighting its potential as a platform for quantum sensing and energy storage.

title: Observation of Genuine Multi-Time Quantum Memory
text: Memory effects in open quantum systems do not by themselves imply quantum memory, since non-Markovian dynamics can often be reproduced by classical-memory models. Known criteria certify the presence of quantum memory in the environment by comparing the evolution of the system at two different times. We show that quantum memory can remain hidden from all such pairwise tests and become detectable only when three or more times are considered jointly. We derive an analytical three-time witness and use it to certify quantum memory in a minimal qubit example in which every pair of times has a classical-memory explanation, thus establishing a strict hierarchy of quantum memory effects. Genuine multi-time quantum memory does not rely on fine-tuned time-dependent Hamiltonians or gate-based evolution. We experimentally demonstrate the hierarchy of quantum memory in a time-continuous realization on a superconducting-qubit platform with time-independent couplings.

title: LiveGeo: Benchmarking Geographic Agents in Continuously Evolving Worlds
text: We introduce GeoWorld, a controllable and continuously evolving geographic environment platform for LLM agents, and LiveGeo, a benchmark for evaluating reliable decision-making in real-world geographic environments using GeoWorld. Unlike existing evaluations that largely reason and plan over fixed geographic states, GeoWorld is grounded in real-world geographic structure and allows external world states to evolve along their own temporal processes while preserving verifiable state histories. LiveGeo places geographic tasks within this evolving environment, requiring agents to actively acquire task-relevant information, verify whether the evidence supporting prior decisions remains valid, and revise their plans when necessary. Our results reveal that even frontier LLMs struggle with static tasks, with no model consistently excelling across tasks, while strong static performance does not ensure dynamic reliability. Further analysis identifies a key bottleneck: agents struggle to acquire and translate relevant evidence into valid decisions and maintain their correctness as the world evolves. By releasing LiveGeo together with its GeoWorld platform, we aim to provide the community with a flexible and extensible infrastructure for studying the next generation of agents capable of reliable action in evolving geographic worlds.

title: Non-interferometric tests of gravitational decoherence models with mechanical oscillators
text: Phenomenological models of quantum-gravity-induced decoherence can leave observable effects even in experiments that do not rely on interferometric measurements. We study three such models, based respectively on deformed relativistic symmetries, stochastic metric fluctuations, and a stochastic generalized uncertainty principle, all of which induce decoherence in the momentum basis. For a free particle, the models preserve momentum distribution and mean energy but produce position diffusion and momentum-space decoherence with model-specific momentum dependences. For a harmonic oscillator, the noncommutativity of the collapse operators with the oscillator Hamiltonian results in anomalous heating, with the three models leading to qualitatively different energy dynamics. The first gives heating at a constant rate, the second at a rate proportional to the kinetic energy, which can lead to exponential growth, and the third at a rate growing cubically with excitation. We further derive the stationary position power spectral density and show that all three models produce the same leading-order excess lineshape in the weak-noise regime, distinct from that of force noise. Comparing with existing mechanical platforms, we find that displacement-noise measurements can already constrain the fluctuation time of the first model below the Planck time, while occupation measurements could improve the bounds on the second model by up to fourteen orders of magnitude over those from ground-state heating of levitated particles. Summing the heating over all phonon modes of a solid, the residual heat release of low-temperature experiments constrains the first model far below the Planck time and the second at the Planck time. Our results establish heating and continuous measurements as complementary non-interferometric probes of gravity-related decoherence.

title: Characterising a population of fast-declining SNe Ia in galaxy cluster cores
text: Galaxy cluster cores, characterised by old stellar population and suppressed star-formation are ideal for studying the environmental dependence of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia). It is unclear whether the diversity of SNe Ia, parametrised by light curve stretch, stems from distinct explosion mechanisms or varying initial conditions, both closely tied to progenitor age. We analyse the light curve stretch and colour distribution of photometrically identified SNe Ia within the galaxy clusters cores, utilising the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) archival data. Using the AMPEL platform, we filter 89,025 ZTF transients spatially coincident with our galaxy cluster catalogues to identify 4,969 likely SN Ia candidates. We split this sample into three populations: core cluster SNe Ia $r \le 0.5R_{500}$, outer-core cluster SNe Ia $0.5R_{500}< r\le 2R_{500}$, and a reference population of non-cluster SN Ia. We present the largest sample of photometrically identified cluster SNe Ia to date, notably isolating a population of 242 SNe Ia within innermost cluster cores $r \le 0.5R_{500}$. This fast-declining SN Ia population is statistically different from the outer-core cluster and field SN Ia population at $\sim4σ$ level. A marginal statistical preference for a bimodal distribution over a unimodal one $ΔAIC$ of 1.53 and 2.3 for each catalogue, indicate cluster cores almost entirely host fast-declining SNe Ia. Conversely, the colour distribution show no significant environmental variation. By filtering out the prompt SN Ia population, cluster cores provide an environment to directly probe the delayed SN Ia progenitor channel. Our observations support a two-population model where progenitor age drives the light curve stretch diversity. The low-stretch values observed in core cluster SNe Ia suggest sub-Chandrasekhar mass double degenerate systems as their likely progenitors.

title: SpotDiff: A Plug-and-Play Framework for Zero-Shot Change Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery
text: Remote sensing change detection usually relies on large collections of temporally aligned, pixel-level annotations, which limits its scalability across regions, imaging platforms and application domains. Recent zero-shot approaches reduce the need for supervision, but they often localize fine-grained changes poorly because their features are coarse or inconsistent across time. We present SpotDiff, a training-free, plug-and-play framework for zero-shot change detection built by composing complementary vision foundation models. SpotDiff uses DINOv3 for semantically robust features, AnyUp to reconstruct them at pixel resolution, and SAM 3 for text-guided region-of-interest proposals, which an inference-time multi-scale strategy (SWIMS) makes reliable on small objects. Change is then measured by comparing the reconstructed features of the two dates inside the proposed regions, with no learnable components, fine-tuning or change labels. To our knowledge, SpotDiff is the first change detection method to use a universal feature upsampler, which alone adds 13.8 F1 over bilinear upsampling of the same features. On LEVIR-CD, SpotDiff reaches 82.46 F1, 2.06 points above the strongest prior training-free method, and on the multi-class SECOND benchmark it improves building change detection by 10.3 IoU and the six-class average by 2.2 IoU. Qualitative results on PlanetScope (3 m) and Sentinel-2 (10 m) imagery show that the same pipeline transfers across resolutions without modification. Our results indicate that composing modern foundation models is an effective route to scalable, label-free change detection.

title: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes
text: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game. Within this new framework players' strategies are represented as positions within a trait space. Players then receive a share of a portion of a resource based on their relative influence at that resource's points traits. For the influencer's game, we show that there is a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium that exists under strict log-concavity of the influence kernel. Using the unique equilibrium we show that the stability of the system depends on the influence kernel's parameters, number of players, and the resource distribution shape. For any dimension we demonstrate a stability threshold that depends on both the scatter and curvature of the players. When this threshold is crossed, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes and gives way to a variety of bifurcation types; including, specialist clusters, limit cycles, and sub-games that reproduce the larger game's structure. We ground these results using real-world data for resources as a demonstration of the game's application. Finally we extend the game dynamics to use multi-agent reinforcement learning and further show that the predicted bifurcation structure persists under partial observability and discretized strategy spaces. In all, the influencer's game provides a novel framework for predicting when competitive pressure drives convergence versus fragmentation with possible applications across domains.

title: Acoustically driven motion of single molecules at hBN surfaces
text: Developments in single-molecule imaging and sensing techniques have enabled direct observation of biomolecular dynamics at interfaces, which has important implications for the fields of membrane biophysics, nanofluidic sensing and transport. However, integrating active surface transport, localization and control over molecule motion remains challenging, limiting further progress in the realization of single-molecule devices. Here, we introduce an integrated surface acoustic wave (SAW)-hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) platform as a contactless actuation platform for directional transport of biomolecules over hBN surfaces. hBN provides an atomically flat surface on which DNA can be confined and still retain in-plane mobility, whereas SAW actuation enables active and guided transport without requiring specific electrical, dielectric or magnetic properties of the biomolecules. Trajectory- and jump-based analyses show that increasing the SAW power leads to higher displacement bias in the streaming direction, resulting in transport velocities along increasingly more linearized trajectories. We thus demonstrate that SAWs can induce tunable directional transport of DNA molecules confined on hBN surfaces, providing a new approach for the on-chip manipulation of biomolecules in nanofluidic systems. Our findings have important implications for the development of advanced single-molecule sequencing platforms and other technologies for biomolecular manipulation and analysis.

title: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help
text: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

title: The full Gaia colour-magnitude diagram with white dwarfs reveals a declining Milky Way star formation history
text: White dwarfs (WDs) provide a fossil record of the Milky Way star formation history (SFH) through the combined effects of stellar evolution and cooling. They have, however, generally been modelled in isolation from the non-degenerate population, so that no single self-consistent set of Galactic assumptions has been required to reproduce both. We present CALOMERA, a semi-analytic chemo-dynamical population synthesis framework in which the vertical density profiles of mono-age subpopulations are computed self-consistently with the Galactic potential and coupled to modern WD cooling sequences, metallicity-dependent progenitor lifetimes and synthetic photometry. We calibrate 18 parameters describing the initial mass function, SFH, initial-final mass relation and WD population against a Gaia DR3 sample of $7.98\times10^{6}$ stars within 1 kpc, including $1.1\times10^{5}$ WDs. The calibrated model reproduces the star counts in each colour-magnitude diagram region to within 3% and the total number count to within 0.5%, compared with the 81% excess in the predicted WD count obtained with the previous main-sequence-only calibration. The recovered SFH peaks early, declines exponentially thereafter, and includes two recent bursts, located at $τ\approx2.4$ and $0.5$ Gyr. Three cooling libraries (Montréal, BaSTI and LPCODE) yield comparably good fits, with differences confined to ${\rm M_G}\gtrsim15$ mag. The predicted luminosity function is in reasonable agreement with the 100 pc Gaia WD sample. We further predict the Galactic WD distribution and differential number counts for surveys of varying depth. Extending the framework to the substellar regime using ATMO models, we predict the Galactic L, T, and Y dwarf populations and their contribution to the deep JWST fields.

title: Interactions from memory footprints: Cage-hopping, mnemotaxis & nonreciprocity
text: Cellular motility is integral to biological processes ranging from foraging to immune responses and cancer metastasis. While cells often navigate by sensing pre-existing environmental cues, many actively steer their future trajectories by remodeling their surroundings via shared, long-lived physicochemical trails called memory footprints. These stigmergic responses to shared footprints also influence large-scale self-organization, such as the early stages of microcolony formation. Despite recent progress, a unified framework connecting single-cell dynamics and collective organization through effective pairwise interactions remains elusive. To bridge this gap, we perform extensive agent-based simulations of an interacting random walk model that explicitly accounts for footprint deposition and decay. Our approach reveals distinct cage-hopping dynamics in solitary cells, as well as complex mnemotactic responses to externally imposed memory gradients. Furthermore, we demonstrate that shared spatial memory fields generate nontrivial effective pairwise interactions, both reciprocal and nonreciprocal, that shape the collective organization of cell populations. Beyond multiscale cellular dynamics, our findings have broader implications for the collective behavior of synthetic active matter, such as swarm robots.

title: Circular phonons generate negligible magnetization in insulators
text: The optical excitation of circular phonons has opened up non-equilibrium phenomena with no equilibrium counterparts, ranging from the generation of synthetic magnetic fields to the control of topological order or the manipulation of ferroaxial states. In this area, significant controversy has arisen on whether sizeable "true" magnetizations accompany circular phonons. Several confounding factors cloud the interpretation of the experiments, which are based on probing polarization rotation in the driven material. These range from the interpretation of the Faraday effect in non-equilibrium conditions to spurious nonlinear optical contributions in pump probe experiments. Here we resolve these ambiguities by measuring both polarization rotation inside the driven material and the stray magnetic field generated outside it with a proximate Faraday detector. For a 5 MV/cm mid-infrared drive, we observe a colossal polarization rotation inside a driven SiC crystal, similar to what was reported in previous work. Depending on the assumptions made, this could correspond to magnetizations as high as $μ_0 M = 0.3 T$ or as low as 4 $μT$. However, when measuring the magnetic stray field outside the driven sample we unambiguously determine that the magnetization in SiC is negligibly small ($μ_0 M \lt 0.001 T$).

title: Structure-Preserving Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Dynamics on Arbitrary Time Scales
text: The leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron combines a passive membrane law with threshold-triggered firing and reset. We formulate this hybrid neuron model, under constant input, on an arbitrary Hilger time scale $\mathbb{T}$. Our central result is that, after the first spike, the firing times satisfy $t_{n+1}=Π_{\mathbb{T}}^{+}(t_n+T_c)$, where $T_c$ is the classical reset-to-threshold travel time. This recursion requires no periodicity, homogeneity, or translation invariance of $\mathbb{T}$; it holds for every time scale that is unbounded above. To preserve the passive membrane physics, we use the inverse cylinder transformation to construct a positively regressive coefficient $p_m$. The resulting delta-dynamic equation is exactly the restriction to $\mathbb{T}$ of the classical continuous-time LIF trajectory. By contrast, the direct transcription $V^Δ=-(V-V_\infty)/τ_m$ exhibits graininess-dependent sign reversal and amplification at coarse right-scattered points. The first firing time is the forward projection of the classical continuous threshold-crossing time onto $\mathbb{T}$, and, when the graininess is bounded by $μ^\ast$, the per-event forward-projection delay -- from each reset to the next realized firing time, relative to the continuous crossing time computed from that same reset -- is bounded above by $μ^\ast$. On $\mathbb{T}=h\mathbb{Z}$ we obtain the explicit lattice-quantized law $T_{\mathrm{ISI}}^{(h)}=h\lceil T_c/h\rceil$, which converges to the classical continuous-time inter-spike interval as $h\to0^+$. The framework therefore separates preserved membrane physics from the temporal opportunity structure imposed by the time domain. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic Hilger-calculus treatment of a threshold-and-reset LIF spiking neuron on an arbitrary time scale.

title: Omakase: Execution Congestion Control through Conflict-Graph Integration in Multi-Proposer Blockchain
text: As multi-proposer protocols push consensus throughput, transaction execution has become the dominant bottleneck in blockchains. Layer-1 blockchains parallelize execution either pessimistically (Solana, Sui), requiring upfront state-access declarations and serializing contended transactions, or optimistically (Aptos, Sei, Monad), resolving dependencies at run time but suffering cascading aborts under contention. Both treat blocks in isolation, leaving inter-block parallelism unexploited and most cores idle. We introduce Omakase, a parallel execution framework that combines pre-execution, inter-block conflict-graph integration, and graph-aware Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC). Replicas use idle cores to pre-execute only the blocks they propose, spreading prediction work across concurrent proposers. After building per-block conflict graphs and identifying their hot resources, a greedy scheduler integrates graphs across the blocks committed in a round, keeping an integration only when a lightweight balance heuristic predicts a parallelism gain. A graph-aware OCC executor then runs the integrated graph, admitting transactions in dependency order, which eliminates aborts when the predicted graph is exact and reduces re-executions when it is not. On 15,000 Ethereum mainnet blocks (~2.4M transactions) and synthetic workloads with configurable contention, Omakase reaches a 2.47x speedup over sequential execution, well above single-block OCC and graph-aware baselines. Against the strongest alternative, which runs the whole round as one optimistic window, Omakase matches mean throughput but is markedly more stable under high contention, because integration bounds how much optimistic work is in flight: this is the congestion control of our title. Integration is not free, but overlapping it with execution across rounds hides 94% of its measured cost in the validator pipeline.

title: Using an energy pixels approach to estimate the size a 2nd Generation DEL must be to train a high-resolution binding model
text: DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) are commonly used to find small-molecule binders to a target protein. But the hard part is no longer finding a hit. It is building a machine-learning model good enough to guide the medicinal chemistry that follows, one that can resolve the shift in affinity when a chemist changes a single atom. Such a model needs two things from its training data: dense sampling of the small patch of chemical space around the hit, and an adequate number of genuinely tight binders within it. A diverse naive DEL gives neither. It samples an enormous space, so any one neighborhood is covered far too thinly, and the tightest binders are rare. A model trained on that naive DEL data must extrapolate to binders tighter than any it has seen, and that is where models can fail. One way to get training data with both properties is a second-generation DEL built around the hit. We ask how complex that library must be. We treat binding as a sum of small, independent interactions, called pixels on the target and antipixels on the ligand. From the spread of affinities measured in the naive library, with no structural information and nothing yet synthesized, we estimate the complexity such a library must have to supply that dense sampling and those tight binders. The method does two useful things. It turns the number of tight binders a model needs into the number of compounds a library must contain. And it estimates the expected yield of a randomly designed second-generation DEL, so the gain from designing the library with machine learning or active learning can be measured against a baseline, without the expense of a control library as large as the experiment itself.

title: Disentangling Spurious Correlations: How IRM Handles Diverse Shortcuts in Text Classification
text: In NLP, models trained via Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) often exploit spurious correlations, such as dialectal markers, at the expense of robust linguistic features, thereby degrading their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) aims to suppress such shortcuts by identifying predictive relationships that remain stable across environments, but its practical utility for NLP remains debated. We use a causality-driven framework to evaluate IRM under three shortcut-generating mechanisms: label-generated features, confounding, and selection bias. Our results show that IRM successfully rejects shortcuts across the evaluated causal and anti-causal structures, including under limited environmental variation and increasing label noise. We then extend our analysis beyond controlled synthetic artifacts to two less constrained settings: gender-profession associations in Bias in Bios and semantically loaded actor-name shortcuts in ActorCorr. These experiments show that invariant learning can mitigate more realistic textual shortcuts, while semantically meaningful features require careful calibration of the invariance penalty.

title: FlinkEval: A Synthetic Corpus for Evaluating Natural Language Interfaces to Streaming SQL
text: Existing natural-language-to-SQL benchmarks primarily evaluate queries over bounded relational data, leaving streaming semantics underexplored. We introduce FlinkEval, an execution-grounded synthetic benchmark comprising 3,903 question--SQL pairs across 45 industry domains and 45 semantic labels. We create diverse schemas and domain-plausible, temporally consistent data through iterative generation and validation. SQL patterns collected from the human-written NL2SQL pairs and vendor documentation drive quota-balanced generation, and execution with a repair loop on Confluent Cloud Apache Flink produces reference queries covering windowing, temporal joins, pattern matching, nested types, and data manipulation. The corpus includes paired schema-explicit and business-language requests, with annotations for analysis by query pattern, complexity, and execution mode. A seven-level Question Specification Ladder examines semantics-preserving reformulation and underspecified requests augmented with oracle-derived clues. Baseline evaluations combine execution outcomes with adjudicated LLM judgments, revealing challenges in pattern composition and request specification.

title: On-the-Fly Gaussian Process Reconstruction of the Galaxy Redshift Distribution for 3$\times$2pt Cosmology
text: The joint analysis of weak gravitational lensing, photometric galaxy clustering, and their cross-correlation, the so-called 3$\times$2pt analysis, is one of the primary probes Stage-IV surveys will use to constrain the dark-energy equation of state. Its accuracy depends critically on the calibration of the underlying photometric redshift distributions, $n(z)$, whose residual uncertainties can bias cosmological inference. However, conventional parametric nuisance models may not adequately capture the full range of plausible $n(z)$ uncertainties. We therefore present a cosmological inference framework that instead reconstructs $n(z)$ on the fly using Gaussian Processes (GPs), replacing per-bin shift-and-width parameterisations by a non-parametric, data-driven model. We validate the method on synthetic Euclid-like 3$\times$2pt data vectors representative of Euclid Data Release 1, sampling GP hyperparameters jointly with cosmological and nuisance parameters to reliably propagate $n(z)$ uncertainties into the posterior distributions. We find that the dependence of the inferred parameters on the adopted $n(z)$ model is markedly stronger in $w_0w_a$CDM than in $Λ$CDM. Opening the dark-energy sector both amplifies the biases induced by a given $n(z)$ treatment and changes which $n(z)$ reconstruction the data prefer, so that a model validated in $Λ$CDM does not automatically remain adequate once $w_0$ and $w_a$ are free. Our results thus indicate that Stage-IV surveys should define $n(z)$ uncertainty marginalisation requirements separately in cosmologies beyond $Λ$CDM to ensure unbiased dark-energy constraints.

title: Adaptive Constraint Sampling for Stochastic Gradient Methods in Constrained Optimization
text: This paper proposes an adaptive constraint-sampling technique for stochastic gradient-based methods to efficiently solve constrained optimization problems with a large number of inequality constraints. The proposed constraint-sampling technique maintains a set of recently violated constraints and draws the constraint used in each iteration uniformly either from this set or from the set of all constraints. This keeps its per-iteration arithmetic overhead independent of the number of constraints. In simulations on synthetic convex optimization problems and in the synthesis of a control barrier function for the Dubins Car, the constraint-sampling technique is shown to significantly outperform uniform constraint sampling.

title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
text: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.

title: ArchSpace: Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing LLM Architecture Research
text: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.

title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
text: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.

title: BrickFlow: Connectivity-Guided Brick Reconstruction
text: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies. We then finetune this model to inject image conditioning, using 1% as much data. However, while the learned flow captures global structure, it does not enforce connectivity. To address this, we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time. Through this, we demonstrate improved build quality with model size, pretraining, and guidance. We make our models and data available for research purposes at https://kulits.github.io/BrickFlow/

title: The Cauchy problem for skew-torsion-parallel spinors with applications to supergravity
text: We solve the Cauchy problem for an irreducible real spinor parallel with respect to a metric connection with skew-symmetric torsion on a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian four-manifold, proving that it is well-posed modulo an obstruction that we identify explicitly, and obtaining an initial-data characterization of such spinors. Our proof relies on the theory of spinorial forms, which we use to explicitly integrate the coupled flow for the spinor and underlying metric via a rotated pull-back action of the flow generated by a vector field on the Cauchy hypersurface $Σ$. We characterize the corresponding constraint equations as an explicit exterior differential system and describe all its solutions in terms of contact structures and flat foliations, obtaining a complete classification in the compact case. In particular, we conclude that every oriented compact three-manifold arises as the Cauchy hypersurface of a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian four-manifold equipped with a skew-torsion parallel spinor. Building on these results, we study the interaction between the four-dimensional Neveu-Schwarz supergravity evolution flow on an abelian bundle gerbe and the spinorial evolution flow determined by its supersymmetric conditions, which we prove to be well-posed and compatible. This establishes the well-posedness of the supersymmetric Neveu-Schwarz system in four dimensions and provides an initial-data characterization of supersymmetry. Furthermore, we obtain a strong rigidity result stating that every globally hyperbolic supersymmetric Neveu-Schwarz solution with a compact Cauchy hypersurface is flat and has vanishing bundle-gerbe curvature.

title: Spatial Foundry: A Multimodal Dataset for Spatial Intelligence
text: Spatial intelligence requires connecting visual observations to the geometry, objects, and persistent state of an environment. Images alone leave these relationships implicit, while disconnected annotations make it difficult to study appearance, camera motion, and scene changes under a common reference. We introduce Spatial Foundry, a collection of 5,280 furnished residential 3D scene configurations with editable assets and aligned visual, geometric, and temporal data. Its modalities include floor plans, perspective and panoramic RGB, metric depth, point clouds, meshes, instance-level 3D bounding boxes, and camera trajectories paired with video. Shared scene coordinates link observations across views and time; editable source scenes enable additional camera paths and controlled object changes. We describe the data representation and construction workflow, and discuss applications in floor-plan-conditioned 3D generation, geometric reconstruction, instance-level perception, camera-conditioned video generation, shared world modeling, and scene editing. Controlled camera and scene variations support spatial perception and world-model research. The public project page provides videos and an interactive colored point-cloud preview.

title: Sketching Language Models for Context Attribution
text: Context attribution asks how removing parts of a prompt changes a language model's output. We study leave-one-out (LOO) attribution for a prompt of $n$ tokens and a fixed measurement function. Computing all LOO values directly requires $n$ model evaluations. Under a stability assumption, our algorithm estimates all LOO values to error proportional to $\varepsilon$ with constant probability using $O(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ evaluation calls. To complement our upper bound, we prove a matching $Ω(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ lower bound on the number of evaluation calls in an oracle model. Empirically, we verify coefficient decay consistent with stability and evaluate the performance of our sketching algorithm on a small language-model retrieval task. Technically, our result is based on a sketching algorithm for arithmetic circuits whose Taylor coefficients satisfy the stability condition recently introduced by Gunn [Gun26]. A direct adaptation of their forward differentiation sketches would require $\widetilde{O}(\log(n)/\varepsilon^2)$ evaluation calls. Our key observation is that we can apply forward differentiation to the backpropagation circuit, with only constant overhead over a forward sketch of the same Taylor degree. This reduces the variance of the sketches and is key to our improved evaluation bound. Our lower bound builds on the techniques of Amsel, Chen, Duman Keles, Halikias, Musco, and Musco [ACDH+26, SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications] for lower bounding the number of matrix-vector queries to estimate the diagonal elements of random matrices.

title: Integer Programming with Polyhedral Constraints on the Image
text: We generalize integer programming to the setting in which the image $A \mathbf{x}$ is restricted to an explicitly given rational polyhedron $P$. That is, we solve $\min\{\mathbf{c}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}:A\mathbf{x}\in P, \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^n\}$, where $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{d\times n}$ and $P$ is an explicitly given rational polyhedron. We present a randomized algorithm running in time $(dΔ)^{O(d)}\operatorname{poly}(L)$ in this regime, where $Δ:= \|A\|_\infty$ and $L$ is the binary input length. This running time matches that of the best-known parameterized algorithms for integer programming, due to Eisenbrand and Weismantel and to Jansen and Rohwedder, and improves on the $O(d^2)$ exponent achieved by Dadush, Léonard, Rohwedder, and Verschae in a more general setting. This result enables several applications, including exact algorithms for integer programming and unbounded knapsack in which the consumed resources $A\mathbf{x}$ must satisfy arbitrary additional linear constraints. We also obtain a randomized fixed-parameter algorithm for Unbounded Subset Sum parameterized by the doubling constant, resolving an open problem of Randolph and Węgrzycki. For integer programs with $m$ constraints and bounded row doubling, we obtain an $f(C,m)n^{O(m)}\operatorname{poly}(L)$-time algorithm and show that the dependence on $m$ in the exponent of $n$ is necessary under $\mathsf{W[1]}\ne\mathsf{FPT}$.

title: Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000x Faster than Looped Models
text: Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can be unstable, slow to train, and use many parameters and FLOPs to solve simple puzzles. Descent on an energy not only mitigates these issues but also offers advantages: built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, fast training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the constraints of the puzzle. Here we demonstrate this with a learned version of Hopfield & Tank's energy from the 80s, which we term CRAM, solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000x faster than looped models on these tasks. CRAM also matches baseline looped models at their highest accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using at least 282x fewer inference FLOPs. Our work suggests two things. First, that energies are an extremely promising direction for training reasoning from data. Second, a caution against using trivially solvable benchmarks like Sudoku and Maze to test the scalability of looped reasoning techniques.

title: Quantifying structural stability of transparent models for general insurance pricing
text: The short duration of general insurance contracts leads to rapid distributional shifts in the data, warranting regular model updates. This process may yield a post-update model that differs considerably from the pre-update model in both predictions and structure. Structural stability is upstream of predictive stability, yet existing structural stability metrics are mostly restricted to simple decision trees. Thus, we first introduce the notion of functional transparency, characterising models with a prediction function that can be expressed as a sum of univariate functions for main effects and bivariate functions for pairwise interactions. Then, we propose the Mean Squared Shape function distance, a metric to quantify the structural stability of functionally transparent models, which are particularly relevant in actuarial science. Using three public auto insurance datasets, we present a benchmark study to demonstrate the usefulness of our metric in identifying a stable and accurate transparent model. Generalised linear models with centred numerical covariates are stable, and explainable boosting machines (EBMs) offer a compromise between stability and performance. We also find that stabilisation strategies, such as sequential modelling and fixed hyperparameters, can substantially improve stability for both EBM and XGBoost models, with negligible impact on performance.

title: TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models
text: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality. The second key addresses a modality misalignment between context prefilling and novel-view rendering: we disentangle context tokens into camera-only context rendering tokens to serve as TTB input, and context ground-truth tokens with image content to serve as the TTB mapping target, ensuring the baked MLPs are relieved of the modality generalization challenge between context and novel-view processing. Our method achieves up to **23x** rendering speedup with quality on par with the state-of-the-art across several benchmarks. Project page: https://test-time-baking.github.io

text: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. title: Internalizing Investment Mandates: A Neurosymbolic RL Approach to Portfolio Allocation
text: Institutional portfolios operate under investment policy statements that specify asset allocation constraints, often conditioned on market regime information. Deep reinforcement learning has been shown to optimize financial performance but typically does not enforce rule compliance, making it unsuitable for real-world deployment. Existing neurosymbolic methods such as Probabilistic Logic Policy Gradient (PLPG) offer constraint-satisfying reinforcement learning (RL) via differentiable symbolic supervision but assume a finite, discrete action space. We present a PLPG-inspired continuous allocation method that estimates the probability that the policy's own executed action satisfies the investment mandate, using reparameterized Monte Carlo sampling, and adds it to the training objective. No post-hoc enforcement mechanism intercepts actions at inference time and compliance is learned by the agent. Audited directly on deterministic mean actions with no correction, the policy reduces violations of a six-rule regime-conditional mandate from 96-98% for unconstrained RL and 33.4% for a reward-penalty baseline to 4.8%, showing that a continuous-action neurosymbolic policy can substantially internalize a symbolic mandate.

title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
text: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.

title: BrickFlow: Connectivity-Guided Brick Reconstruction
text: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies. We then finetune this model to inject image conditioning, using 1% as much data. However, while the learned flow captures global structure, it does not enforce connectivity. To address this, we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time. Through this, we demonstrate improved build quality with model size, pretraining, and guidance. We make our models and data available for research purposes at https://kulits.github.io/BrickFlow/

title: Learning When Diffusion Language Models Should Regenerate
text: Remasking allows diffusion language models to revisit generated text, but effective correction requires knowing when and what to revise. Our diagnosis on Sudoku reveals two gaps. Hidden states contain error information that token confidence does not reliably expose, and remasking an isolated error usually reproduces it when the surrounding context remains fixed. These findings motivate DiVR , a verifier that predicts whether a partially generated sequence will reach a correct answer. Trained on the final correctness of the model's own trajectories, DiVR decides when to regenerate a block and which alternative to retain, while the generator itself stays unchanged. On five reasoning benchmarks with LLaDA-8B-Base, DiVR raises the average accuracy of the fine-tuned generator from 35.3\% to 43.4\% at $1.9$-$3.5\times$ the cost of greedy decoding, above search baselines that use $3.8$-$7.4\times$. It also complements post-training such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and generalizes to other generators, including Dream.

title: Spatial Foundry: A Multimodal Dataset for Spatial Intelligence
text: Spatial intelligence requires connecting visual observations to the geometry, objects, and persistent state of an environment. Images alone leave these relationships implicit, while disconnected annotations make it difficult to study appearance, camera motion, and scene changes under a common reference. We introduce Spatial Foundry, a collection of 5,280 furnished residential 3D scene configurations with editable assets and aligned visual, geometric, and temporal data. Its modalities include floor plans, perspective and panoramic RGB, metric depth, point clouds, meshes, instance-level 3D bounding boxes, and camera trajectories paired with video. Shared scene coordinates link observations across views and time; editable source scenes enable additional camera paths and controlled object changes. We describe the data representation and construction workflow, and discuss applications in floor-plan-conditioned 3D generation, geometric reconstruction, instance-level perception, camera-conditioned video generation, shared world modeling, and scene editing. Controlled camera and scene variations support spatial perception and world-model research. The public project page provides videos and an interactive colored point-cloud preview.

title: Linking Rapid Learning to Compositional Structure in Neural Networks: Evidence from Additive Analogies in Meta-Learned Parameter Spaces
text: Humans can learn rapidly from limited experience, while neural networks typically require extensive training. In this work, we investigate what properties of a neural network can enable it to learn rapidly. We study neural networks that have been optimized via meta-learning, a technique that exposes a network to many related functions to facilitate its subsequent learning of similar functions. Prior work has shown that these meta-learned networks can learn new functions rapidly, but how they do so remains unclear. To investigate their internal structure, we take inspiration from classic work demonstrating additive relationships among the learned vectors that neural networks use to represent words (e.g., "king" minus "man" plus "woman" approximates "queen"). Analogously, we look for additive relationships among a meta-learned network's "representations" of different functions; when a meta-learned network rapidly learns to implement a specific function, all of its adapted parameter values can be concatenated into a single vector that we treat as representing the function. We find that such parameter vectors can be added and subtracted according to symbolic relationships among the functions they represent, yielding new parameter vectors that successfully represent the functions predicted by the corresponding symbolic manipulations: the networks specified by these artificially recombined vectors actually implement the intended functions without any direct training on them. Our results suggest that meta-learning can tune a network's starting point to organize subsequent learning along systematic, functionally meaningful trajectories through the space of possible parameter vectors, providing a geometric basis for realizing inductive biases in neural networks.

title: Sketching Language Models for Context Attribution
text: Context attribution asks how removing parts of a prompt changes a language model's output. We study leave-one-out (LOO) attribution for a prompt of $n$ tokens and a fixed measurement function. Computing all LOO values directly requires $n$ model evaluations. Under a stability assumption, our algorithm estimates all LOO values to error proportional to $\varepsilon$ with constant probability using $O(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ evaluation calls. To complement our upper bound, we prove a matching $Ω(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ lower bound on the number of evaluation calls in an oracle model. Empirically, we verify coefficient decay consistent with stability and evaluate the performance of our sketching algorithm on a small language-model retrieval task. Technically, our result is based on a sketching algorithm for arithmetic circuits whose Taylor coefficients satisfy the stability condition recently introduced by Gunn [Gun26]. A direct adaptation of their forward differentiation sketches would require $\widetilde{O}(\log(n)/\varepsilon^2)$ evaluation calls. Our key observation is that we can apply forward differentiation to the backpropagation circuit, with only constant overhead over a forward sketch of the same Taylor degree. This reduces the variance of the sketches and is key to our improved evaluation bound. Our lower bound builds on the techniques of Amsel, Chen, Duman Keles, Halikias, Musco, and Musco [ACDH+26, SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications] for lower bounding the number of matrix-vector queries to estimate the diagonal elements of random matrices.

title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression
text: Abstract Understanding the genetic basis of gene expression can shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases. Single cell-resolved measures of RNA levels and single-cell expression quantitative trait loci (sc-eQTLs) have revealed genetic regulation that drives sub-tissue cell states and types across diverse human tissues. Here, we describe the first phase of TenK10K, the largest-to-date dataset of matched whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq). We leverage scRNA-seq data from over 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, and matched WGS, from 1,925 individuals, which provides power to detect associations between rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterised in their impact on cell-specific gene expression. We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell type-specific manner using a recently introduced method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than relying on aggregated ‘pseudobulk’ counts. We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare variant signals for 47% of genes. We explore how genetic effects vary across cell type and state spectra, develop a framework to determine the degree to which sc-eQTLs are cell type-specific, and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types. By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we also further characterise the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations. Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states and functions, and effects that vary cell state abundance directly.

title: ANO6-mediated trogocytosis of cancer-associated fibroblasts promotes pancreatic cancer cell growth and immune suppression
text: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the fibroblastic stroma constitutes most of the tumor mass and is remarkably devoid of functional blood vessels, leaving unresolved how PDAC cells obtain essential metabolites and water-insoluble lipids. We find that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) acquire and transfer lipids from blood-borne particles to PDAC cells through trogocytosis of CAF plasma membranes, a process requiring the CAF-expressed phospholipid scramblase anoctamin 6 (ANO6) to promote PDAC cell survival. Cancer cells and CAFs form synapse-like contacts that induce cytosolic calcium influx in CAFs through Orai channels, activating ANO6 and driving phosphatidylserine exposure on CAF membranes, which initiates trogocytosis and transfer of membrane lipids, including cholesterol, to PDAC cells. This ANO6-dependent phosphatidylserine externalization also supports CAF-mediated immunosuppression of cytotoxic T cells through trogocytosis. Blockade of ANO6 antagonizes tumor growth, partly by disrupting cholesterol delivery to cancer cells, and attenuates immune suppression, identifying ANO6 as a candidate therapeutic target in PDAC.

title: Integrated manufacturing platform for cortical organoids reveals early phosphatase and prefoldin dysregulation in MAPT V337M neurons
text: Human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived cortical organoids are powerful models but are often limited by low efficiency, variability, and stress-related artifacts. To address these challenges, we developed a scalable organoid platform with end-to-end quality control (QC) metrics spanning manufacturing and single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq), developed using eight MAPT mutation isogenic line sets relevant to frontotemporal dementia (FTD-tau). Using a 96 slit-well format, we achieved ~100% organoid formation across 64 lines. Controlled-release FGF2 enhanced hPSC pluripotency and reduced mesendodermal contaminants, while optimized SB431542 dosing enhanced cortical patterning across lines with variable TGFBR1/ALK5 expression. The resulting organoids displayed transcriptomic profiles and low-stress signatures closely aligned with the developing human cortex. Applying a cortical organoid scRNA-seq index (CortiCOSI), we identified early dysregulation of phosphatase regulators ( PPP2CA, ANP32A ) and the prefoldin subunit PFDN6 in MAPT V337M excitatory neurons before tau hyperphosphorylation and oligomerization. This platform improves scalability, reproducibility, and mechanistic insight in cortical organoid studies.

title: A systematic fluorescently tagged protein toolkit for dissecting apical extracellular matrix patterning in C. elegans
text: Barrier epithelia are shielded from the external environment by their apical extracellular matrices (aECMs). The molecular complexity of aECMs has challenged understanding of their organization in vivo. To define the molecular architecture of a model aECM we generated a toolkit of 105 fluorescently tagged aECM components using gene editing in C. elegans , focusing on proteins secreted by the epidermis to form the collagen-rich cuticle. We developed efficient pipelines for modular protein tagging and rapid fluorophore swapping. Most tagged collagens were functional and exhibited exquisitely specific patterning across stages, cell types, and matrix substructures. We define multiple reference markers for key substructures including the little-understood cortical layer, as well as the helical crossed fiber arrays that function as a hydrostatic skeleton to maintain organismal shape. We further tagged 30 members of key aECM protein classes including proteases, protease inhibitors, and lipid transporters. Our standardized markers will allow dissection of the mechanistic basis of aECM spatiotemporal patterning in vivo.

title: An astrocyte-microglia MFG-E8 axis promotes synapse engulfment in early amyloid pathology
text: Region-specific synapse loss is an early hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, yet the upstream signals that render synapses vulnerable remain unclear. In a mouse model of amyloidosis, we identify an early astrocyte state that emerges in vulnerable brain regions before widespread plaque deposition and overt gliosis. These astrocytes exhibit bulbous-looking perisynaptic processes enriched in p62 and glycogen, impaired autophagic flux and calcium signaling, and diminished astrocyte-synapse coverage. Rather than exhibiting increased synapse engulfment, bulbous astrocytes show elevated milk fat globule-epidermal growth factor 8 (MFG-E8) and are associated with increased local microglial synapse engulfment. Astrocyte-specific gain- and loss-of-function experiments demonstrate that astrocyte-derived MFG-E8 is required for microglial synapse engulfment and acts through microglial β3 integrin signaling. Astrocytic Mfge8 deletion reduces microglial engulfment and synapse loss across amyloidosis models and is associated with reduced amyloid pathology, gliosis, and cognitive impairment. Together, these findings define an astrocyte-microglia MFG-E8 signaling axis that contributes to region-specific synaptic vulnerability during early amyloid pathology.

title: Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression
Planetary-scale metagenomic analysis reveals CRISPR targeting dynamics across ecosystems
text: Interactions between microorganisms and their mobile genetic elements (MGEs), including viruses and plasmids, impact microbiome dynamics. CRISPR-Cas systems are important regulators of these host-MGE interactions, but a global understanding of the diversity, activity and roles of CRISPR spacers across Earth's biomes is still lacking. Here we develop a computational approach to search short-read data and collect 794 million CRISPR spacers across 367,609 public metagenomes, from which we identified 1.18 billion hits between 41 million spacers and 2.5 million viruses and plasmids. While spacers were highly variable across samples, those matching known viruses were more prevalent and conserved, consistent with a positive selection pressure associated with phage targeting. Among these, however, we find evidence suggestive of recurrent entry of phage genomes into non-host microbial cells, further blurring the line between CRISPR targeting and virus-host interactions. These results highlight key drivers of CRISPR targeting patterns likely to influence strain-level diversification and selection processes in microbiomes.

title: Leveraging genomic deep learning models for the prediction of noncoding variant effects
Survey of the human proteostasis network: the ubiquitin-proteasome system
text: Modification by ubiquitination governs the half-lives of thousands of proteins that are fated for elimination by either the proteasome or autophagy pathways, depending on the intricate architectures of ubiquitin modification. This system mediates quality control for individual proteins, protein complexes, and organelles, as well as myriad purely regulatory functions. Here we provide a comprehensive survey of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), the scope of which is at present poorly defined. The UPS, with the inclusion of pathways involving ubiquitin-like modifiers, comprises in our estimate over 1430 distinct components in humans, a vast set of activities whose collective impact on the biology of the cell is pervasive. The UPS is an integral component of the proteostasis network (PN), the remainder of which is surveyed in the accompanying reports. With the addition of molecular chaperones, proteins from autophagy-lysosome pathway, and related activities, the PN includes in total over 3150 components by our estimates. Comprehensive and systematic definition of these pathways should facilitate a range of ongoing investigations in the areas of genomics, proteomics, biochemistry, cell biology, and disease research.Abbreviations: APC, anaphase promoting complex; CDD, Conserved Domain Database; CRL, cullin RING ligase; DSB, double-strand break; DUB, deubiquitinating enzyme; ERAD, ER-associated degradation; PN, proteostasis network; RBR, RING-between-RING; RCR, RING-Cys-Relay; SPOC, Structure Prediction and Omics-informed Classifier; UB, ubiquitin; UBL, ubiquitin-like; UBLM, ubiquitin-like modifier; UEV, ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme variant; UPS, ubiquitin-proteasome system

title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism
text: Abstract Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD 1–3 . Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge 4 . Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals 5 , and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts 6,7 ; however, the biological basis of this ‘female protective effect’ (FPE) has remained unknown 8,9 . Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST . Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals 10 , emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

title: Intellectual Property Law and Microbiology: Patenting Microorganisms and Genetic Material
text: The recruitment of electoral ad-hoc personnel is a large-scale and time-sensitive activity that requires effective applicant registration, screening, assessment, information management, and communication. Conventional recruitment procedures involving physical forms and manual processing can create difficulties in applicant-data management, geographical accessibility, processing, and candidate assessment. This study presents the design and implementation of a web-based e-recruitment support system for electoral ad-hoc staff. The proposed system integrates applicant registration, online application, centralized applicant-data management, eligibility screening, online assessment, application-status management, and attestation-letter generation within a unified platform. An Object-Oriented Analysis and Design Methodology (OOADM) was adopted for system analysis and development. The system was implemented using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, PHP, and MySQL. Its architecture comprises an applicant interface, administrative interface, authentication component, screening engine, assessment component, notification mechanism, document-generation component, and centralized database. A rule-based assessment mechanism was implemented to determine applicant qualification using a predefined 50% score threshold. The implemented system was subjected primarily to functional and system-level testing, focusing on applicant registration, application processing, eligibility screening, assessment computation, data storage, status management, and attestation-letter generation. The results demonstrated that the major functional components operated according to their specified requirements. The study demonstrates the technical feasibility of integrating electoral ad-hoc staff recruitment activities into a centralized web-based platform and provides a foundation for subsequent large-scale field evaluation and operational deployment.

title: Comprehensive degron mapping in human transcription factors
text: Gene expression is regulated by the targeted degradation of transcription factors through the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Transcription factors destined for degradation are recognized by E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases through motifs termed degrons, embedded within the sequence. In this study, we systematically map degrons in all 1626 human transcription factors. We find thousands of both known and previously unidentified degrons and characterize their sequence properties. Active degrons placed within exposed and intrinsically disordered regions contribute to modulating the abundance of the transcription factors, while the most common somatic mutations that are linked to skin cutaneous melanoma lead to unfolding and exposure of a latent degron buried in the zinc finger structure. We present examples of compartment-specific degrons and demonstrate that variant effects in transcription factors correlate with degron potency. Last, we show that while >60% of all predicted transcriptional activation domains overlap with strong degrons, acidic residues within the remaining transactivating regions counter the degron potency, showing how degrons can shape the transcription factor sequence landscape.

title: Transcriptomic reprogramming screen identifies SRSF1 as a regulator of aging
Disruption of cell-type-specific molecular programs of striatal spiny projection neurons in autism
Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia
text: SUMMARY The basal ganglia play essential roles in motor control, emotion, learning and reward processing. Their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. However, the gene regulatory programs defining basal ganglia cell-type identity and function remain poorly understood, limiting interpretation of disease-associated non-coding variants. Here, we present the first single-cell multiome atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical adult human donors. Joint profiling reveals cell-type-specific deployment of active and repressive cis -regulatory elements and gene regulatory networks, and suggests a combinatorial homeobox transcription factor code underlying cell identity. Integration with matched spatial transcriptomic MERFISH data uncovers regional heterogeneity of epigenomic landscapes. Comparative analysis between human and mouse medium spiny neurons uncovers conservation of core gene regulatory features. This atlas interprets non-coding risk variants of neuropsychiatric disorders and supports the development of a deep learning model to predict gene regulation and functional effects of disease-associated variants. HIGHLIGHTS Joint single-cell profiling of transcriptomes and three histone modifications across eight human basal ganglia regions characterizes active and repressive chromatin states at cell-type resolution. Cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs decode combinatorial homeobox TF grammar governing the identity and diversification of basal ganglia neurons. Intergrative analyses link noncoding neuropsychiatric risk variants to specific cell types, regulatory elements, and candidate target genes. A sequence-to-function deep-learning model predicts gene regulation from DNA sequence and prioritizes functional disease-associated variants.

title: Thermosensory pathway makes a U-turn to respond to heat
text: Plant organs exhibit a unimodal growth response to temperature, yet the mechanistic links connecting growth-promoting and growth-inhibiting thermal ranges remain unresolved. In Arabidopsis seedlings, warm temperatures promote hypocotyl elongation by relieving phytochrome B (phyB) inhibition, thereby activating the transcription factors PIF4 and PIF7 to drive auxin synthesis. Here, we demonstrate that temperatures beyond the growth optimum actively suppress growth by downregulating auxin levels, auxin signalling, and PIF4 abundance specifically within the cotyledons, the primary site of auxin production. Strikingly, whereas warm temperatures induce the shrinking of phyB nuclear bodies, heat stress causes phyB to assemble into enlarged condensates, a behaviour faithfully recapitulated in mammalian cells, demonstrating an intrinsic biophysical mechanism. Together, our findings indicate that heat-induced growth inhibition is not merely passive stress damage, but an active molecular reversal of the promotive pathway of thermomorphogenesis.

title: Optogenetic induction of TAD boundary pairing promotes gene activity
text: The genome folds inside the nucleus into distinct structures across multiple levels of organization. Topologically associating domains (TADs) are a ubiquitous architectural feature of genomes delineated by boundaries enriched in the CTCF protein and the cohesin complex. TADs are dynamic structures as their boundaries undergo continuous, short-lived pairing events. Whether the structural integrity of TADs contributes to regulation of the genes within the TAD is unclear. To directly test the structure-function relationship of TADs, we have developed OptoTet, an optogenetic tool to rapidly and directly manipulate chromatin contacts in a controlled fashion using light without the need for mutation or protein depletion. Using the TADs containing the ERRFI1 or MYC gene as model systems, we show that OptoTet promotes TAD boundary looping. When applied to probing the structure-function relationship of TADs, light-induced pairing of TAD boundaries promoted transcriptional activity of ERRFI1 as indicated by increased gene bursting. In contrast, bursting of MYC was insensitive to boundary pairing. Enhanced TAD boundary pairing also partially rescued the effect of depletion of cohesin components on ERRF1 but not on MYC. Our results suggest that TADs boundary pairing dynamics can contribute to gene regulation in a gene-specific manner.

title: Sperm phospholipase C signaling via PLCζ1 and PLCδ4 is essential for Ca2+ oscillations and fertility in mice
text: Fertilization-induced calcium (Ca2+) oscillations are essential for egg activation and embryonic development in mammals. The sperm-specific phospholipase C isoform, PLCζ1, is the primary trigger of these oscillations. Functional and clinical studies have linked mutations or reduced expression of PLCζ1 to male infertility. However, whether PLCζ1 alone accounts for Ca2+ release at fertilization in all mammals remains uncertain. Male mice lacking Plcζ1 exhibit subfertility and reduced litter sizes; their sperm induce delayed, low-frequency Ca2+ oscillations, indicating a compensatory mechanism. Notably, mouse sperm express high levels of PLCδ4, essential for completing the acrosome reaction (AR). In Plcζ1-null sperm, PLCδ4 is upregulated and retained post-AR. These observations suggest a secondary functional role for PLCδ4. Using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, we generated Plcδ4 knockout (KO) mice. Plcδ4-null sperm trigger attenuated, delayed Ca2+ oscillations and significantly reduced fertilization rates, indicating that PLCδ4 contributes to but does not independently drive Ca2+ signaling. We therefore generated a Double Knockout (DKO) mouse line lacking both sperm-enriched PLCs. DKO males were sterile, with sperm failing to induce Ca2+ oscillations, and the isolated residual Ca2+ rise was insufficient to activate eggs. These findings reveal that PLCζ1, the primary oscillator, and PLCδ4, a compensatory factor, work cooperatively within a complex, multi-component PLC system that ensures robust fertilization. This work reveals molecular specialization among mammals in initiating the fertilization Ca2+ signals. It has implications for understanding male infertility, improving assisted reproductive technologies, and developing contraceptive strategies.

title: Lipid-mediated GPR32 signaling reprograms macrophage metabolism to impair anti-tuberculous immunity
text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB), has evolved strategies to evade innate immunity and establish persistent infection. However, the mechanisms by which M. tuberculosis reprograms human macrophage metabolism remain incompletely defined. Tuberculous pleural effusion (TB-PE), a common extrapulmonary manifestation that frequently coexists with pulmonary TB, offers a unique, clinically relevant immunometabolic window into the TB microenvironment. Here, using patient-derived TB-PE samples, we show that this microenvironment induces a metabolic state in human macrophages that compromises their antimicrobial function. Lipidomic analysis identified an enrichment of the specialized pro-resolving mediator Resolvin D5 (RvD5), whose abundance was associated with reduced macrophage glycolytic activity. The acellular fraction of TB-PE promoted RvD5 production by monocytes, consistent with increased expression of RvD5 biosynthetic enzymes in pleural monocytes from TB patients. Exogenous RvD5 was sufficient to reduce glycolysis and impair intracellular control of M. tuberculosis in macrophages. Pharmacological blockade of GPR32 counteracted these effects, supporting the involvement of GPR32 signaling in the response to RvD5. RvD5 treatment was also associated with reduced HIF-1α levels, whereas pharmacological stabilization restored several macrophage functions impaired by RvD5.
