Together, these findings identified RvD5 as a biologically relevant lipid mediator capable of reproducing key features of TB-PE-induced macrophage dysfunction and support a role for GPR32- and HIF-1α-associated pathways in this process.

title: Edición génica in vivo de PCSK9 en la prevención cardiovascular aterosclerótica: de la validación genética a la clínica
text: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is the primary causal and modifiable risk factor.Available lipid-lowering therapies-statins, ezetimibe, anti-PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies, and RNA interference-have been shown to reduce cardiovascular events, but they require long-term administration and are limited by efficacy, adherence, cost, and access.Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is, to date, the most genetically validated target for the development of in vivo gene-editing strategies aimed at achieving a permanent reduction in LDL-C through a single therapeutic administration.This review describes the biology of PCSK9, the available gene-editing platforms-CRISPR-Cas9, base editing, and primer editing-and their delivery to hepatocytes via lipid nanoparticles.It summarizes preclinical data and ongoing clinical trials (VERVE-101, VERVE-102, and YOLT-101) showing sustained, dose-dependent reductions in LDL-C following a single infusion, with acceptable short-term safety profiles.Finally, the long-term safety, regulatory, economic, and ethical challenges that will determine the eventual translation of this technology into routine clinical practice are discussed.

title: NRF2 coordinates cystine import and glutathione use to sustain ferroptosis resistance and formaldehyde tolerance in cancer
text: Cancer cells must balance detoxification of reactive metabolic by-products while preserving redox homeostasis, but how this trade-off is managed remains unclear. The Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1)-nuclear factor-erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) pathway, a key regulator of antioxidant defenses, is frequently hyperactivated in cancer. Formaldehyde, a genotoxic one-carbon by-product, is typically detoxified via glutathione (GSH), which is also essential for suppressing ferroptotic cell death. Here, we show that NRF2 promotes formaldehyde tolerance through up-regulation of the cystine transporter SLC7A11, enabling a protective mechanism that is largely independent of GSH, which remains necessary for ferroptosis resistance. In NRF2-active cells, formaldehyde reacts with cysteine to form a thiazolidine conjugate, and the combination of formaldehyde stress and SLC7A11 inhibition activates the integrated stress response, suppresses global protein synthesis, and markedly compromises cell viability. Together, these findings reveal that NRF2 coordinates ferroptosis resistance and formaldehyde tolerance, exposing a cancer vulnerability through combined inhibition of cystine uptake and GSH synthesis.

title: ANO6-mediated trogocytosis of cancer-associated fibroblasts promotes pancreatic cancer cell growth and immune suppression
text: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the fibroblastic stroma constitutes most of the tumor mass and is remarkably devoid of functional blood vessels, leaving unresolved how PDAC cells obtain essential metabolites and water-insoluble lipids. We find that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) acquire and transfer lipids from blood-borne particles to PDAC cells through trogocytosis of CAF plasma membranes, a process requiring the CAF-expressed phospholipid scramblase anoctamin 6 (ANO6) to promote PDAC cell survival. Cancer cells and CAFs form synapse-like contacts that induce cytosolic calcium influx in CAFs through Orai channels, activating ANO6 and driving phosphatidylserine exposure on CAF membranes, which initiates trogocytosis and transfer of membrane lipids, including cholesterol, to PDAC cells. This ANO6-dependent phosphatidylserine externalization also supports CAF-mediated immunosuppression of cytotoxic T cells through trogocytosis. Blockade of ANO6 antagonizes tumor growth, partly by disrupting cholesterol delivery to cancer cells, and attenuates immune suppression, identifying ANO6 as a candidate therapeutic target in PDAC.

title: MapMyCells: High-performance mapping of cell-by-gene data to reference brain taxonomies
text: Abstract Single-cell mapping methods convert raw, heterogeneous single-cell datasets into interpretable and comparable representations of biological identity. As reference cell-type taxonomies mature, mapping new datasets to shared references has become a central strategy for enabling cross-study integration, reproducible annotation, and cumulative biological knowledge. Here we present MapMyCells , an open-source framework designed to align diverse single-cell omics datasets to hierarchical reference taxonomies with minimal preprocessing. MapMyCells provides out-of-the-box support for an expanding set of high-quality brain cell-type references generated by the Allen Institute for Brain Science, the BRAIN Initiative, and the Seattle Alzheimer’s Disease Brain Cell Atlas, including whole-brain mouse and human atlases, aging and Alzheimer’s disease cohorts, and a cross-species consensus taxonomy initially focused on the basal ganglia. MapMyCells enables efficient mapping of hundreds of thousands of cells on standard workstations without specialized hardware, providing a deterministic, scalable, and modality-agnostic approach that is robust across species and molecular assays. The framework produces interpretable confidence metrics and quantitative summaries of mapping performance, allowing users to evaluate assignment precision and accuracy. We demonstrate the mapping of unlabeled transcriptomic, epigenomic, and spatial datasets to reference taxonomies and describe a general workflow for preparing arbitrary hierarchical taxonomies for reference-based mapping. As the ecosystem of single-cell reference atlases expands, MapMyCells offers a practical and reproducible solution for community-scale cell-type annotation and cross-dataset integration, supporting the development of unified and extensible brain cell atlases.

title: Cross-species multiomic atlas of the primate basal ganglia
text: The basal ganglia (BG) are conserved brain regions essential for motor control, learning, emotion, and cognition, and are implicated in neurological and psychiatric disease. Yet a unified cross-species taxonomy of BG cell types is lacking, limiting translation of BG circuit mechanisms, interpretation of human genetic risk, and development of cell type-targeted tools. We present a multiomic consensus atlas of 1.8 million nuclei from human, macaque, and marmoset spanning eight BG structures. Integrating cross-species gene expression, open chromatin, and spatial profiling enables definition of conserved and divergent cell types. Alignment to existing mouse and human atlases identifies 61 homologous cell types conserved over 80 million years. We identify a STRd D2 StrioMat Hybrid medium spiny neuron (MSN) type with molecular, electrophysiological, and morphological features that clarify hybrid MSN identities. Comparative cis-regulatory analysis reveals conserved sequence grammars that encode cell identity and inform viral targeting strategies, providing a foundational resource for BG evolution, function, and disease.

title: Integrated manufacturing platform for cortical organoids reveals early phosphatase and prefoldin dysregulation in MAPT V337M neurons
text: Human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived cortical organoids are powerful models but are often limited by low efficiency, variability, and stress-related artifacts. To address these challenges, we developed a scalable organoid platform with end-to-end quality control (QC) metrics spanning manufacturing and single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq), developed using eight MAPT mutation isogenic line sets relevant to frontotemporal dementia (FTD-tau). Using a 96 slit-well format, we achieved ~100% organoid formation across 64 lines. Controlled-release FGF2 enhanced hPSC pluripotency and reduced mesendodermal contaminants, while optimized SB431542 dosing enhanced cortical patterning across lines with variable TGFBR1/ALK5 expression. The resulting organoids displayed transcriptomic profiles and low-stress signatures closely aligned with the developing human cortex. Applying a cortical organoid scRNA-seq index (CortiCOSI), we identified early dysregulation of phosphatase regulators ( PPP2CA, ANP32A ) and the prefoldin subunit PFDN6 in MAPT V337M excitatory neurons before tau hyperphosphorylation and oligomerization. This platform improves scalability, reproducibility, and mechanistic insight in cortical organoid studies.

title: A systematic fluorescently tagged protein toolkit for dissecting apical extracellular matrix patterning in C. elegans
text: Barrier epithelia are shielded from the external environment by their apical extracellular matrices (aECMs). The molecular complexity of aECMs has challenged understanding of their organization in vivo. To define the molecular architecture of a model aECM we generated a toolkit of 105 fluorescently tagged aECM components using gene editing in C. elegans , focusing on proteins secreted by the epidermis to form the collagen-rich cuticle. We developed efficient pipelines for modular protein tagging and rapid fluorophore swapping. Most tagged collagens were functional and exhibited exquisitely specific patterning across stages, cell types, and matrix substructures. We define multiple reference markers for key substructures including the little-understood cortical layer, as well as the helical crossed fiber arrays that function as a hydrostatic skeleton to maintain organismal shape. We further tagged 30 members of key aECM protein classes including proteases, protease inhibitors, and lipid transporters. Our standardized markers will allow dissection of the mechanistic basis of aECM spatiotemporal patterning in vivo.

title: An astrocyte-microglia MFG-E8 axis promotes synapse engulfment in early amyloid pathology
text: Region-specific synapse loss is an early hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, yet the upstream signals that render synapses vulnerable remain unclear. In a mouse model of amyloidosis, we identify an early astrocyte state that emerges in vulnerable brain regions before widespread plaque deposition and overt gliosis. These astrocytes exhibit bulbous-looking perisynaptic processes enriched in p62 and glycogen, impaired autophagic flux and calcium signaling, and diminished astrocyte-synapse coverage. Rather than exhibiting increased synapse engulfment, bulbous astrocytes show elevated milk fat globule-epidermal growth factor 8 (MFG-E8) and are associated with increased local microglial synapse engulfment. Astrocyte-specific gain- and loss-of-function experiments demonstrate that astrocyte-derived MFG-E8 is required for microglial synapse engulfment and acts through microglial β3 integrin signaling. Astrocytic Mfge8 deletion reduces microglial engulfment and synapse loss across amyloidosis models and is associated with reduced amyloid pathology, gliosis, and cognitive impairment. Together, these findings define an astrocyte-microglia MFG-E8 signaling axis that contributes to region-specific synaptic vulnerability during early amyloid pathology.

title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
text: Abstract Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment 1–8 , suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear 9–13 . Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.

title: Steroid hormones produced by coral-associated Endozoicomonas influence coral immune response during thermal stress
text: The coral microbiome is believed to play a crucial role in sustaining corals and enabling adaptation to perturbations. A ubiquitous group of coral-associated bacteria, known as Endozoicomonas, are hypothesized to provide essential metabolites to corals, although detailed dynamics of the interactions between host and microbe are poorly understood. Here multi-omics and laboratory validation experiments reveal that Endozoicomonas encodes genes for the metabolism of coral-derived testosterone and converts ubiquitous cholesterol into testosterone and progesterone, both important steroids that accumulate within the coral holobiont during thermal stress. Field sampling along a natural temperature gradient showed general suppression of coral steroid hormones under thermal stress and during white syndrome manifestation. Provision of testosterone or progesterone to corals during laboratory thermal stress induced transcriptional reprogramming of the coral innate immune response, suggesting microbial involvement in host immune modulation. These findings highlight a previously unrecognized potential mechanism of microbial contribution to coral resilience. Multi-omics and laboratory experiments reveal that a coral-associated bacterium can produce testosterone and progesterone; these two hormones alter the coral host’s innate immune responses during thermal stress.

title: A multi-tissue atlas of genetic regulatory effects in sheep
A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity
text: Abstract Cancer cells show highly heterogeneous and plastic states in glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour 1–5 . However, how these malignant states arise and whether they follow defined cellular trajectories across tumours is poorly understood. Here we generated a deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma that pairs transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling of 12 tumours across many regions. We identify that glioblastoma heterogeneity is driven by spatially patterned transitions of cancer cells from developmental-like states towards those defined by a glial injury response and hypoxia. This cellular trajectory regionalizes tumours into distinct tissue microenvironments and manifests in a molecularly conserved manner across tumours as well as genetically distinct tumour subclones. Consistently, using a new deep-learning framework to map cancer cell states jointly with clones in situ, we show that tumour subclones are finely spatially intermixed through glioblastoma tissue microenvironments. We validate this cellular trajectory by using somatic mutation-based hierarchies in vivo and an experimental patient-derived organoid model ex vivo. Finally, we show that this cancer cell trajectory is intimately linked to myeloid heterogeneity and unfolds across regionalized myeloid signalling environments. Our findings define a stereotyped trajectory of cancer cells in glioblastoma and unify glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity into a tractable cellular and tissue framework.

title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals organizational properties of the mouse spinal cord and alterations in neuropathic pain
text: The spinal cord integrates diverse somatosensory inputs and executes motor outputs through anatomically and functionally distinct circuits. Here, we employed spatially resolved single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the adult mouse spinal cord to gain insights into the organizational logic of the spinal cord. Our results reveal distinct spatial and laminar distributions of neuronal subtypes, including axial level and sex-specific differences. Many neuronal subtypes exhibit lamina-specific somatic proximities, suggesting potential regionally specific connectivity. Additionally, neuronal subtypes within the dorsal horn exhibit a wide range of predicted cell-cell communication motifs, as assessed by the spatial distribution of neuropeptide- and other ligand-receptor pairs. Finally, we identified several neuronal subtypes with altered transcriptomic states and predicted cell–cell communications in a model of neuropathic pain. This spatially resolved cellular and molecular map of the spinal cord will facilitate the decoding of circuit mechanisms underlying somatosensory and motor functions in health and disease.

title: Disruption of cell-type-specific molecular programs of striatal spiny projection neurons in autism
OpenDVP: an experimental and computational framework for community-empowered deep visual proteomics
text: Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics.

title: Conservative evolution of genetic and features in Caenorhabditis becei , an experimentally tractable gonochoristic worm
text: Caenorhabditis nematodes represent a promising model clade for evolutionary genetics and genomics, but research has focused on the three androdioecious species, those with self-fertile hermaphrodites, all in the Elegans Group of species. The majority of Caenorhabditis species are gonochorists, with males and females, characterized by inconveniently high heterozygosity and inbreeding depression. We have identified C. becei as an experimentally tractable gonochorist. We show that transmission-genetic properties known from the androdioecious Elegans Group species are conserved in this Japonica Group species: the organization of the genetic map, cosegregation of autosomal indels and sex chromosomes, and segregation distortion due to Medea elements, demonstrated here for the first time in a gonochoristic Caenorhabditis species. We describe a new chromosomal genome assembly of a healthy inbred C. becei reference strain, integrating data from PacBio HiFi reads, Illumina short reads, genetic linkage, and HiC chromatin contacts, and experimental gene annotation with short- and long-read data. Some aspects of the genome are highly conserved, including synteny across the six chromosomes and the distributions of repetitive sequences and genes along each chromosome. Other features are quite distinctive, including evolved shifts in GC composition & heterogeneity along the genome. Both codon & amino acid usage are shifted in concert with the species' genomic GC content. C. becei has an unusually large X chromosome, which we find is associated with multiple local gene family expansions. These findings and resources lay the foundation for further experimental and computational studies of Caenorhabditis genetics and genomics.

title: Human neocortical glutamatergic neurons revealed through multimodal profiling
text: The human neocortex underlies higher cognition and is the engine of complex thought. Yet our understanding of its neuronal diversity is limited by sparse access to tissue, inconsistent sampling across studies, and a lack of multiple modality data. Although single-cell transcriptomic taxonomies are an important framework for characterizing cell type diversity, transcriptomic information alone cannot reveal the cellular properties that define neuronal computations. To address this, we performed Patch-seq, a method for collecting Morphology, Electrophysiology, and Transcriptomic data from a single neuron. We focused on glutamatergic, neocortical, excitatory neurons, the principal long-range projecting neurons of the cortex, and systematically integrated their morphoelectric features with transcriptomic identity. In combination with spatial transcriptomic data, we interrogated 39 of 42 transcriptomically-defined neuron types with a layer-centric perspective. Morphoelectric properties, such as cortical depth, apical dendrite structure, and excitability clearly distinguish transcriptomic subclasses and support many finer transcriptomic types. Morphoelectric properties are influenced by spatial location in supragranular layers, while deeper layers exhibit greater heterogeneity. Cross-species comparisons reveal conserved subclass organization but pronounced differences in apical dendrite arborization between mouse and human, and surprising similarities between human and macaque. Together, these datasets provide a unified multimodal reference that advances our understanding of human cortical circuitry and establishes a foundation for experimental and computational studies of human brain function and disease.

title: Structural insights into bromodomain-containing complexes from Trypanosoma cruzi revealed by proximity labeling and stoichiometric space exploration
text: Trypanosoma cruzi , the etiological agent of Chagas disease, remains a major health concern due to the limited efficacy and toxicity of current treatments. Bromodomain factors (BDFs), which recognize acetylated lysine residues, are key components of epigenetic regulatory machinery and represent promising therapeutic targets. Despite their importance, structural organization of bromodomain-containing complexes in trypanosomatids is poorly understood. In this study, we combined experimental and computational approaches to investigate the composition and stoichiometry of BDF-containing complexes in T. cruzi . Using TurboID-based proximity labeling, we mapped interaction networks for five BDFs (BDF3, BDF4, BDF5, BDF6 and BDF8) and identified two major complexes, CRKT and NuA4. To further resolve their architecture, we applied structure prediction methods that explore multiple stoichiometric configurations. Our analyses indicate that CRKT is organized into three modules with distinct interaction dynamics, whereas NuA4 comprises two modules. The CRKT core module displays a symmetric arrangement containing two copies of BDF3, BDF5, and BDF8. Its catalytic module contains three subunits including HAT2, while the BET module contains BDF4 and BDF1. In NuA4, the catalytic module resembles the yeast piccolo-NuA4 complex and includes HAT1, with the TINTIN module associating via BDF6. These findings provide structural insights into epigenetic complexes in trypanosomatids and support their potential as drug targets.

title: Integrated Structural and Evolutionary Analysis of Petromyzon marinus Thyroglobulin: Identification of a Novel TG cysteine-rich motif
text: The thyroglobulin (TG) gene is a cornerstone of vertebrate endocrinology, serving as the macromolecular precursor for thyroid hormone biosynthesis. Here, we reconstructed the full-length TG sequence of the sea lamprey (Petromyzon marinus), a basal vertebrate of key evolutionary significance, and performed comparative analyses across 50 representative species. By integrating NCBI, UniProt, and Ensembl data, we identified a complete TG locus spanning ~120 kb, organized into 49 exons, which encodes a 24-residue signal peptide followed by a 2892-amino-acid polypeptide chain. Structural predictions confirmed the presence of canonical TG domains—including TG type 1, TG type 2, and TG type 3 repeats, the linker, hinge, and spacer modules, as well as the ChEL domain—preserving the overarching architecture observed in human TG despite a moderate sequence identity (32.5%). Comparative alignments revealed strong conservation of cysteine and tyrosine residues, underscoring the evolutionary stability of the functional core. The sea lamprey TG monomeric model generated via AlphaFold 3 achieved a pTM of 0.68 and a mean Cα pLDDT of 70.37, while predicted aligned error (PAE) matrices showed consistent low-error profiles. Notably, sea lamprey spacer 3 harbors a novel TG cysteine-rich motif preserved in lobe-finned and cartilaginous fishes but absent from ray-finned fishes, tetrapods, and other jawless vertebrates (Lampetra fluviatilis and Lampetra planeri). The spatial distribution of these 8 cysteines resembles a somatomedin B domain, suggesting that this motif constitutes a bona fide member of this module class. Transcriptomic and developmental profiling confirm that the TG cysteine-rich motif-bearing Exon 38 is a constitutively spliced, non-artifactual feature robustly expressed across all larval stages. Phylogenetic analyses confirmed a canonical TG organization across all surveyed taxa, with lineage-specific indels shaping domain variability. Conservation analysis of the 66 human TG tyrosine residues across vertebrates revealed heterogeneous preservation; mammals exhibited the highest conservation, whereas jawless vertebrates showed uniformly low values, though several ray-finned fishes scored even lower. Together, these findings establish the sea lamprey TG sequence as a critical reference point at the base of vertebrate evolution, highlighting structural conservation alongside lineage-specific adaptations.

title: Bioimaging and comparative genomics for characterization of surface-bacteria isolated from a blood bank facility
text: Blood banks represent highly controlled healthcare environments where microbiological surveillance has traditionally focused on Blood products rather than environmental microbial reservoirs. Despite their crucial role in transfusion safety, the ecology of surface-associated microorganisms remains poorly understood. This cross-sectional study characterized culturable bacteria recovered from Blood-bank surfaces. We combined scanning electron microscopy, culture-based microbiology, phenotypic characterization, MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, and whole-genome sequencing to investigate whether surfaces within a public blood bank facility (BBF) constitute reservoirs of environmentally derived bacteria with putative traits potentially relevant to environmental survival. Samples collected from a public BBF in Tucumán, Argentina yielded 36 culturable bacterial isolates, predominantly Gram-positive taxa together with a limited number of opportunistic Gram-negative species. Several isolates showed reduced susceptibility to various groups of antimicrobials; furthermore, several strains exhibited strong biofilm formation, production of amyloid-like fibers, motility, and hemolytic activity. Whole-genome sequencing of six representative isolates supported previous species affiliations, identified genes related to antimicrobial resistance, adhesion, biofilm formation, stress adaptation, and cytotoxicity, highlighting the importance of integrating genomic and phenotypic analyses. Notably, BS-018 showed a low ANI to the reported comparison genome, but its taxonomic assignment remains unresolved. Blood bank surfaces function as localized environmental conditions favoring bacteria with potential persistence-associated traits. This study identified environmental bacterial isolates exhibiting phenotypic and genomic characteristics potentially relevant to biosafety surveillance. Our results support incorporating integrated bioimaging, phenotypic characterization, and environmental surveillance with genomic resolution into infection prevention strategies and transfusion biosafety programs.

title: Neuroimmune-endocrine interactions in perinatal asphyxia: from brain injury to neuroprotection
text: Perinatal asphyxia (PA) remains a major cause of neonatal mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental disability worldwide. Although hypoxic–ischemic brain injury has traditionally been attributed to oxygen deprivation, excitotoxicity, and oxidative stress, accumulating evidence indicates that neurological outcomes are determined by complex interactions among metabolic, mitochondrial, neuroimmune, and neuroendocrine mechanisms. Following hypoxic–ischemic injury, primary energy failure rapidly triggers excitotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, calcium dysregulation, and oxidative damage, leading to activation of microglia and astrocytes, release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, disruption of blood–brain barrier integrity, and recruitment of peripheral immune cells. These events contribute to the development of secondary energy failure and persistent neuroinflammation. Simultaneously, activation of hypoxia-responsive pathways, including hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1), heat shock protein 70 (HSP70), glutathione-dependent antioxidant defenses, and neuroendocrine stress responses involving the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, promote endogenous adaptation and neuroprotection. Nitric oxide signaling further links mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative and nitrosative stress, inflammatory activation, and neuronal injury. Together, these mechanisms form an integrated neuroimmune-endocrine network that influences both injury progression and tissue repair. In this review, we propose Brain Energy Failure as a unifying conceptual framework linking mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative and nitrosative stress, neuroinflammation, endocrine adaptation, and endogenous neuroprotective responses following perinatal hypoxia. We further discuss the role of biomarkers associated with neuro-immuno-endocrine dysfunction, including inflammatory mediators, oxidative stress markers, endocrine factors, and indicators of neuronal and glial injury. Recent evidence has highlighted the therapeutic potential of multimodal neuroprotective approaches, including endogenous lipid mediators such as palmitoylethanolamide (PEA), which exert anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and mitoprotective effects. We also review current and emerging neuroprotective strategies targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling, and bioenergetic instability, and discuss their translational implications. Understanding the interactions among these interconnected pathways may facilitate biomarker-guided diagnosis, personalized neuroprotection, and the development of more effective therapies aimed at improving long-term neurological outcomes following perinatal asphyxia.

title: Beyond the Plasma Membrane: Nuclear G Protein‐Coupled Receptors With a Focus on Angiotensin Receptors
text: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) have traditionally been described as seven-transmembrane receptors located at the plasma membrane. However, it is now well established that these receptors can also signal from intracellular membrane compartments, including endosomes, mitochondria, the Golgi apparatus, and nuclear membranes. Importantly, such intracellular signaling can generate distinct functional outcomes even when similar G protein-mediated pathways and second messenger systems are engaged. In this context, increasing evidence indicates that angiotensin receptors, which are GPCRs, are not restricted to the cell surface but can also localize to intracellular compartments, particularly the nucleus. This intracellular distribution supports the concept of an intracrine renin-angiotensin system, in which nuclear angiotensin receptors may directly regulate gene expression and cellular function. Thus, nuclear GPCR signaling represents an additional layer of complexity in angiotensin receptor biology, extending beyond classical membrane-initiated pathways. This review focuses on nuclear angiotensin receptors, their signaling properties, and their functional relevance in regulating cellular responses.

title: Multi-receptor whole-brain modeling reveals affinity-driven chemoarchitectural mechanism of virtual atomoxetine action
text: Linking molecular mechanisms with large-scale brain dynamics remains a fundamental challenge in computational psychiatry. Receptor-informed whole-brain models have provided mechanistic insights into pharmacological interventions, yet they have largely relied on single-receptor topographies that cannot explain the collective response of multiple receptor systems. Here, we combined pharmacological resting-state fMRI with a whole-brain model incorporating cortical expression of adrenergic and dopaminergic receptors to investigate the effects of atomoxetine, a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor that globally elevates catecholaminergic signaling. Using receptor similarity, we first identified a catecholaminergic chemoarchitecture comprising frontal, posterior and temporal networks, providing the neurochemical scaffold for interpreting atomoxetine-induced brain dynamics. Empirically, atomoxetine selectively stabilized functional connectivity dynamics within the posterior catecholaminergic network. Whole-brain modeling revealed that although individual receptor parameters did not differ between conditions, their collective organization converged toward empirical receptor binding affinities. Remarkably, the simulated atomoxetine state was reconstructed from the placebo configuration through a negative reweighting along this receptor-affinity axis. In silico forward modeling showed that this affinity-driven redistribution gave rise to a cortical modulation pattern aligned with a frontal chemoarchitectural gradient, which was sufficient to simulate the observed dynamical and connectivity changes. Together, these findings suggest receptor binding affinity as a key organizing principle linking molecular receptor organization to brain dynamics, providing a model-based, biologically interpretable computational mechanism through which global catecholaminergic perturbations reshape whole-brain function.

title: P4HB/PDIA1: an emerging biomarker linking periprostatic adipose tissue and prostate cancer progression
text: Prolyl 4-hydroxylase subunit beta (P4HB), also known as protein disulfide isomerase A1 (PDIA1), is an endoplasmic reticulum oxidoreductase involved in protein folding, ER proteostasis, oxidative stress responses, collagen maturation, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Increasing evidence implicates P4HB in tumor progression and treatment resistance, although its role in the prostate cancer (PCa) microenvironment remains incompletely understood. Periprostatic adipose tissue (PPAT) is an active endocrine and paracrine compartment that undergoes metabolic remodeling during locally advanced PCa and participates in bidirectional communication with tumor cells through adipokines, cytokines, growth factors, extracellular matrix components, and metabolic mediators. Proteomic profiling of PPAT adjacent to pathological T3 tumors revealed enrichment of pathways involved in lipid mobilization and transport and identified P4HB within the PPAT secretome. Elevated tumoral P4HB expression has been associated with higher Gleason score, advanced disease stage, lymphovascular invasion, biochemical recurrence, residual disease, and radiotherapy resistance. Furthermore, experimental inhibition of PDI family proteins can suppress PCa growth, impair androgen receptor signaling, and enhance enzalutamide sensitivity. Collectively, these findings suggest that P4HB may link PPAT metabolic remodeling with aggressive PCa. PPAT-derived P4HB warrants further investigation as a biomarker and potential therapeutic target for microenvironment-directed treatment.

title: GSK3 Inhibition During Annelid Head Regeneration Results in a Hyper‐Proliferative Blastema and Impaired Differentiation
text: A major goal of regeneration biology is to uncover the molecular mechanisms that allow a wide range of animals to replace body parts through regeneration. Glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3) is known to have significant regulatory influence on developmental pathways that are integral to successful regeneration in several animal groups. Annelids include some of the most highly regenerative animals known and, although GSK3 has been studied during regeneration in several species, its major roles remain unclear. Here, we characterize the effects of 1-azakenpaullone (AZP), a known GSK3 inhibitor and Wnt signaling agonist, during anterior and posterior regeneration in the highly regenerative oligochaete annelid Pristina leidyi using morphological markers, cell proliferation assays, and RT-qPCR of stem cell and differentiation associated genes. Although posterior regeneration was only minorly affected by AZP treatment, anterior regeneration was strongly impaired, producing a persistent "hyper-blastema" that fails to differentiate anterior-specific structures through at least 13 days, more than twice the normal time period of complete regeneration. At time points when regeneration should be complete, this hyper-blastema still exhibits high levels of cell proliferation and stem cell-associated gene expression, resembling an early blastema. These results suggest that GSK3 inhibition suppresses anterior-specific differentiation pathways during later phases of regeneration, consistent with a conserved role for GSK3 in anterior development. The results also support GSK3's conserved role in promoting neural differentiation. More broadly, our study implicates GSK3 in opposing the blastema's pro-regenerative signals in annelids, broadening understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying animal regeneration.

title: ISLES’24: Final stroke infarct prediction with multimodal imaging and clinical data. Where do we stand?
text: Accurate estimation of brain infarction (i.e., irreversibly damaged tissue) is critical for guiding treatment decisions in acute ischemic stroke. Reliable infarct prediction informs key clinical interventions, including the need for patient transfer to comprehensive stroke centers, the potential benefit of additional reperfusion attempts during mechanical thrombectomy, decisions regarding secondary neuroprotective treatments, and, ultimately, prognosis of clinical outcomes. This work introduces the Ischemic Stroke Lesion Segmentation (ISLES) 2024 challenge, which focuses on the prediction of final infarct volumes from pre-interventional acute stroke imaging and clinical data. ISLES'24 provides a comprehensive, multimodal setting where participants can leverage all clinically and practically available data - including full acute CT imaging, sub-acute follow-up MRI, and structured clinical information - across a train set of N=150 cases. On the hidden test set (N=98), the top-performing model, a multimodal nnU-Net-based architecture, achieved a Dice score of 0.285 ± 0.213 and an absolute volume difference of 21.2 ± 37.2 mL, underlining the significant challenges posed by this task and the need for further advances in multimodal learning. This overview of the ISLES'24 challenge offers two primary contributions: first, it provides a standardized, clinically realistic benchmark for post-treatment infarct prediction, built on a comprehensive, open, and multimodal longitudinal stroke imaging dataset; second, it provides insights into the strengths and limitations of current algorithms and delineates key research directions to guide the development of next-generation infarct prediction models.

title: FLAb2: Benchmarking reveals that protein AI models cannot yet consistently predict developability properties
text: We introduce the Fitness Landscape for Antibodies (FLAb2), the largest public benchmark for therapeutic antibody design, comprising developability data for over 4 million antibodies across 32 studies and covering 7 properties: thermostability, expression, aggregation, binding affinity, pharmacokinetics, polyreactivity, and immunogenicity. Evaluating 30 AI and biophysical models, we find that most (80%) fail to produce statistically significant correlations. No model performs well across all properties. Some pretrained models (IgLM, ProGen2, Chai-1, ESM2, ISM, and IgFold) show significant zero-shot correlations for select properties. Fine-tuning with ≥10 2 points helps for thermostability, aggregation, and binding though polyreactivity and pharmacokinetics lack sufficient data. With enough data (10 3 points), a fine-tuned one-hot encoding model matches billion-parameter models. Training data matters more than architecture, and intrinsic properties (thermostability) are predicted more readily than extrinsic ones (immunogenicity and pharmacokinetics). Partial correlation analysis shows that germline distance accounts for ∼37% of language models' apparent predictive power.

title: How Proteins Work
text: How Proteins Work is an up-to-date and authoritative account of protein function. It covers the full breadth of protein science, from protein structure and organization through evolution, enzymes, regulation, dynamics, folding, allostery, and experimental and computational techniques, with chapters detailing how these features work together to support signaling and motion. It tackles challenging topics such as cooperativity, dynamics, and intrinsically disordered proteins, but always in an engaging style that puts clarity and understanding at the forefront. This text will enable undergraduate students in biochemistry and biophysics to understand the relationships between protein function, structure, and dynamics. It will also serve as a valuable resource for graduate students and researchers grappling with proteins and their functions. New to this second edition is a fuller account of enzyme kinetics and inhibition; more detail on protein folding and intracellular responses to unfolded proteins; a more coherent account of avidity and cooperativity; and discussion of new developments, including AlphaFold and cryo-electron microscopy. The text has been substantially reordered. Key Features: Chapters end with a problems section that aims to test the reader’s understanding of chapter content and its application. Top-quality full color illustrations help elucidate key concepts and mechanisms. High-resolution protein structures enhance understanding of molecular interactions and how structure relates to function. Extensive reference lists. Cross-referencing within the text to draw out the connections between different topics.

title: Biosafety level‐3 cryo‐electron tomography of active severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 virions
text: Understanding the structural properties of pathogenic viruses in their native, infectious state is critical for rational vaccine and drug development. However, conducting cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) under biosafety level 3 (BSL-3) containment presents significant challenges. Here, we established and validated a high-end cryo-EM workflow within a BSL-3 facility, comprehensively integrating facility design, containment measures, sample handling, cryo-transfer systems, and decontamination protocols. To demonstrate the utility and reproducibility of this workflow, we applied cryo-electron tomography to investigate severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 in its native, active state. Our observations confirm that unfixed viral particles display pleomorphic features comparable to those previously reported in fixed or inactivated preparations, validating that these structural characteristics represent native features rather than artifacts of chemical fixation. Furthermore, spatial redistribution of surface spikes was observed. The establishment of this robust BSL-3 cryo-EM workflow provides a practical blueprint for the structural characterization of emerging high-consequence pathogens, supporting pandemic preparedness, vaccine development, and antiviral discovery.

title: OpenDVP: an experimental and computational framework for community-empowered deep visual proteomics
text: Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics.

title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia
text: SUMMARY The basal ganglia play essential roles in motor control, emotion, learning and reward processing. Their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. However, the gene regulatory programs defining basal ganglia cell-type identity and function remain poorly understood, limiting interpretation of disease-associated non-coding variants. Here, we present the first single-cell multiome atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical adult human donors. Joint profiling reveals cell-type-specific deployment of active and repressive cis -regulatory elements and gene regulatory networks, and suggests a combinatorial homeobox transcription factor code underlying cell identity. Integration with matched spatial transcriptomic MERFISH data uncovers regional heterogeneity of epigenomic landscapes. Comparative analysis between human and mouse medium spiny neurons uncovers conservation of core gene regulatory features. This atlas interprets non-coding risk variants of neuropsychiatric disorders and supports the development of a deep learning model to predict gene regulation and functional effects of disease-associated variants. HIGHLIGHTS Joint single-cell profiling of transcriptomes and three histone modifications across eight human basal ganglia regions characterizes active and repressive chromatin states at cell-type resolution. Cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs decode combinatorial homeobox TF grammar governing the identity and diversification of basal ganglia neurons. Intergrative analyses link noncoding neuropsychiatric risk variants to specific cell types, regulatory elements, and candidate target genes. A sequence-to-function deep-learning model predicts gene regulation from DNA sequence and prioritizes functional disease-associated variants.

title: High-content morphological profiling by Cell Painting in 3D spheroids
text: Abstract Cell Painting is a popular high-content imaging assay that captures the shape and internal organization of 2D cell cultures at scale. While 3D cell cultures are more physiologically relevant models – especially for studying drug perturbations – they remain challenging to image because light scatters before it reaches the cultures’ interior. Here, we introduce a scalable method to adapt Cell Painting for 3D spheroids. We show that tissue-clearing, a technique that makes spheroids transparent, combined with a focusing routine that locates spheroids on the fly, enables Cell Painting at single-cell level inside intact spheroids. By profiling 52 clinically relevant drugs, we show that single-cell fingerprints clustered by biological pathway and resolved drug effects more robustly than those of flattened spheroid-wide views. Notably, the effect of two drugs, 5-fluorouracil and olaparib, nearly indistinguishable in 2D monolayers, diverged in spheroids. This finding was then corroborated by DNA-damage, cell-cycle, and gene-expression assays. The workflow runs on a spinning-disk confocal microscope in a standard 384-well plate format, making single-cell 3D profiling accessible to laboratories already performing Cell Painting.

title: Towards efficient large language models for scientific data: a review
text: Abstract The adaptation of large language models (LLMs) to scientific domains requires efficient strategies to mitigate high computational costs while preserving performance. We present a systematic survey of efficiency techniques for adapting LLMs to scientific applications. Our review analyzes 120 studies across seven scientific fields, including biomedicine, clinical medicine, biology, mathematics, chemistry, geo-environmental science, and cross-domain scientific research. Across the surveyed literature, we summarize 34 representative models and 30 scientific datasets for efficient scientific LLM research. Examining parameter-efficient fine-tuning, knowledge distillation, architectural optimization, and data-centric approaches, we introduce a dual-axis taxonomy that organizes efficiency techniques by both methodological strategy and scientific domain. We further provide practical guidance for selecting efficiency strategies under resource constraints and highlight open challenges including multimodal integration, catastrophic forgetting, and automated method selection. By synthesizing cross-domain evidence and outlining directions for sustainable model development, this survey supports the adoption of efficient scientific LLMs in resource-constrained research environments and promotes more accessible and responsible deployment across scientific disciplines.

title: Pharmacophore-Conditioned Diffusion Model for Ligand-Based De Novo Drug Design
text: Developing bioactive molecules remains a central, time- and cost-heavy challenge in drug discovery, particularly for novel targets lacking structural or functional data. Pharmacophore modeling presents an alternative for capturing the key features required for molecular bioactivity against a biological target. In this work, we present PharmaDiff, a pharmacophore-conditioned diffusion model for 3D molecular generation. PharmaDiff employs a transformer-based architecture to integrate an atom-based representation of the 3D pharmacophore into the generative process, enabling the precise generation of 3D molecular graphs that align with predefined pharmacophore hypotheses. Through comprehensive testing, PharmaDiff demonstrates superior performance in matching 3D pharmacophore constraints compared to ligand-based drug design methods. Additionally, it achieves higher docking scores across a range of proteins in structure-based drug design, without the need for target protein structures. By integrating pharmacophore modeling with 3D generative techniques, PharmaDiff offers a powerful and flexible framework for rational drug design.

title: Spatial proteomics reveals lipid droplet reorganization in symbiotic Paramecium bursaria cells
text: Endosymbiosis is an important adaptive mechanism allowing organisms to exploit previously inaccessible niches. The flexible relationship between the ciliate Paramecium bursaria and green algae represents a model system for studying early endosymbiosis evolution. However, the mechanisms underlying how P. bursaria cells maintain this endosymbiotic relationship remain unclear. Here, we use mass spectrometry–based proteomics to generate a spatial proteomic atlas of the host P. bursaria cells with and without endosymbionts. This atlas defines the protein composition of the endosymbiont-containing compartment (perialgal vacuole) and reveals pronounced remodeling of host lipid droplets upon symbiosis. Imaging analyses confirm that lipid droplets change in size, morphology, and positioning, accumulating near intracellular algae. Perturbing symbiotic cells with chemical inhibitors of lipid metabolism reduces endosymbiotic algal numbers, revealing a role for lipid droplets in the host-endosymbiont interaction. Our data provide a comprehensive resource for protein localization in P. bursaria cells and elucidate how those cells remodel an existing cellular compartment to maintain endosymbiosis.

title: A Water Compartment Cell Culture Lid Enables Stable Longitudinal Recording of Neuronal Networks In Vitro
text: Longitudinal electrophysiological recordings of neuronal networks are essential for studying network maturation, plasticity, and pharmacological responses. Yet, current microelectrode array (MEA) approaches are limited by evaporation-induced drift in culture conditions, exacerbated by heat dissipation from active recording electronics on CMOS-based high-density MEAs. We present a cell culture lid featuring a water compartment at its interface that eliminates evaporation whilst maintaining gas exchange. Combined with a custom incubator that uses independent temperature control of the MEA to prevent condensation, the system enables stable, uninterrupted recordings for weeks. We show that perturbations in firing rate and functional connectivity following medium exchange are significantly reduced by suppressing evaporation. We demonstrate continuous 35-day recordings of patterned human iPSC-derived neuronal networks with a single half-medium exchange, revealing multiple spatiotemporal firing patterns that are held concurrently and evolve over weeks. All design files are provided, enabling adoption across culturing platforms for longitudinal studies of development within individual cultures, and establishing the conditions required for studies of plasticity and chronic pharmacology.

title: Boltzmann generators for amorphous particle systems
text: Sampling configurations in thermodynamic equilibrium is a long-standing challenge in statistical physics. Boltzmann generators address this problem by employing generative models to propose independent configurations, which are then reweighted via importance sampling using exact likelihood evaluations. Recent Boltzmann generators based on continuous normalizing flows and flow matching have achieved significant success for particle systems and biomolecules. However, these approaches have not been extended to amorphous materials (glasses), for which equilibrium sampling is notoriously slow. Because of their disordered structure, the invariances and geometrical constraints of amorphous materials differ from those of crystals and biomolecules, preventing the direct use of existing generative models. Here, we develop Boltzmann generators tailored to amorphous materials by building the required equivariances directly into Riemannian stochastic interpolants. Our framework incorporates periodic boundary conditions and particle symmetries using equivariant graph neural networks. Numerical experiments demonstrate that enforcing physical symmetries significantly improves the accuracy of Boltzmann generators but also reveal an intrinsic limitation of the continuous-flow formulation: accumulated numerical errors during likelihood integration break time-reversibility, compromising exact thermodynamic reweighting. These results reveal a fundamental challenge for continuous-flow generative models in statistical mechanics and call for alternative approaches that preserve exact thermodynamic consistency.

title: Tryptoline stereoprobe elaboration identifies inhibitors of the GRPEL1–HSPA9 complex
text: Activity-based protein profiling has identified hundreds of human proteins from diverse classes that react at cysteine residues with stereochemically defined electrophilic compounds (stereoprobes). The structure-activity relationships underlying these stereoprobe-protein interactions, however, remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the protein interaction landscape of tryptoline acrylamide stereoprobes can be profoundly altered by structural modifications distal to the acrylamide reactive group. Most stereoprobe liganding events occurred at nonorthosteric sites and evaded assignment by the machine learning-based cofolding model Boltz-2, which instead tended to misplace stereoprobes in orthosteric pockets (an outcome we term 'orthostery burnout'). We found that stereoprobes reacting with C124 in the nucleotide exchange factor GRPEL1 disrupt interactions with the mitochondrial HSP70 chaperone HSPA9/mortalin, leading to impairments in mitochondrial protein import and mitophagy induction. Our results highlight tryptoline acrylamides as a versatile source of covalent ligands targeting nonorthosteric sites on proteins, including tool compounds that perturb the mitochondrial HSP70 chaperone system.

title: Programmable and selective silencing of oncogenic fusion transcripts by CRISPR-Cas13b via breakpoint sequence recognition
text: Oncogenic gene fusions are key drivers of cancer, yet most remain undruggable by current therapies. Here, we establish CRISPR- Psp Cas13b as a personalizable platform for systematic silencing of various fusion transcripts. We reveal that recognition and cleavage of the breakpoint sequence by Psp Cas13b disrupt the fusion transcript, resulting in efficient protein depletion. Psp Cas13b cleavage produces aberrant, translation-incompetent target RNA species, a subset of which harbors internal deletions proximal to the cleavage site. We demonstrate that targeting the BCR::ABL1 breakpoint sequence efficiently degrades both wild-type and drug-resistant BCR::ABL1 mutants, which are the primary drivers of tyrosine kinase inhibitor resistance and relapse in chronic myeloid leukemia. Molecular profiling revealed that Psp Cas13b impairs BCR::ABL1 tyrosine phosphokinase activity and triggers extensive transcriptomic and proteomic remodeling, leading to erythroid differentiation and apoptosis in drug-resistant cells. Beyond BCR::ABL1, personalized design of Psp Cas13b effectively silences other undruggable oncogenic fusions. Collectively, this study establishes a molecular framework for precise targeting of undruggable or drug-resistant oncogenic transcripts.

title: Embedded Morgan Fingerprints for More Efficient Molecular Property Predictions With Machine Learning
text: High‐dimensional molecular fingerprints have become a quiet bottleneck for chemical machine learning, where bit collisions in large, chemically diverse datasets and escalating computational costs constrain model discovery. This work introduces the embedded Morgan Fingerprint (eMFP), a postprocessing scheme that compresses standard Morgan Fingerprints into continuously valued, lower‐dimensional representations governed by a compression factor. Applied to three molecular datasets of increasing size (RedDB, Non‐Fullerene Acceptors, and QM9), five regression models, and four encoding configurations under scaffold‐aware nested cross‐validation, eMFP maintains the predictive power of full‐length fingerprints for tree‐based methods at moderate compression (), while exhibiting more model‐ and setting‐dependent behavior elsewhere. Its continuous outputs pair favorably with Fourier Feature Neural Networks, where they interact more naturally with sinusoidal feature mappings than the original binary fingerprints, and consistently shorten training times per trial. Together, these results position eMFP as a simple, drop‐in route to more scalable molecular representations that retain accuracy while easing the computational burden of model development.

title: A Latin American consensus on the use of L-asparaginase in pediatric and adolescent/young adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia – part 1
text: Background L-asparaginase remains a fundamental component of curative therapy for children, adolescents and young adults (AYA; 15–39 years) with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). However, optimal treatment remains challenging across Latin America due to shortages, heterogeneous product quality, limited access to therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM), and toxicities. This study aimed to develop regionally adapted, evidence-informed recommendations for L-asparaginase use in ALL. Methods A multinational modified Delphi process involved 19 experts from 10 Latin American countries. Following a literature review, candidate statements were developed. Consensus was predefined as ≥80% of respondents assigning scores of 7–9 on a 9-point Likert scale. Statements not reaching consensus underwent iterative discussion, revision, and reevaluation. Results Ninety-three statements were evaluated in the first anonymous voting round and grouped post hoc into five thematic blocks; this first part reports the 46 statements of blocks 1–3: treatment continuity, pharmacokinetic and dosing principles, and TDM and treatment optimization. Round-level participation was 94.7%, 84.2%, and 84.2% in Rounds 1–3. Thirty-two statements achieved consensus in the first round. The 14 that did not were subdivided, merged, reformulated, or withdrawn, yielding 14 revised statements; six achieved consensus in the second round, one was withdrawn, and the remaining seven were consolidated into six third-round statements, all achieving consensus. The process resulted in 44 final consensus statements. Key recommendations emphasize preservation of therapeutic exposure, avoidance of unnecessary discontinuation, formulation-specific pharmacokinetics and dosing, linkage of dose and dosing intervals to the desired duration of exposure, and expansion of TDM, with serum asparaginase activity ≥0.1 IU/mL at a formulation- and schedule-appropriate sampling time endorsed as the minimum therapeutic target. Conclusions This consensus provides a multinational Latin American framework for L-asparaginase use in ALL. The recommendations support exposure-centered treatment strategies and identify priorities for regional collaboration, including pharmacokinetic monitoring, toxicity management, and access to high-quality L-asparaginases.

title: Bioimaging and comparative genomics for characterization of surface-bacteria isolated from a blood bank facility
text: Blood banks represent highly controlled healthcare environments where microbiological surveillance has traditionally focused on Blood products rather than environmental microbial reservoirs. Despite their crucial role in transfusion safety, the ecology of surface-associated microorganisms remains poorly understood. This cross-sectional study characterized culturable bacteria recovered from Blood-bank surfaces. We combined scanning electron microscopy, culture-based microbiology, phenotypic characterization, MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, and whole-genome sequencing to investigate whether surfaces within a public blood bank facility (BBF) constitute reservoirs of environmentally derived bacteria with putative traits potentially relevant to environmental survival. Samples collected from a public BBF in Tucumán, Argentina yielded 36 culturable bacterial isolates, predominantly Gram-positive taxa together with a limited number of opportunistic Gram-negative species. Several isolates showed reduced susceptibility to various groups of antimicrobials; furthermore, several strains exhibited strong biofilm formation, production of amyloid-like fibers, motility, and hemolytic activity. Whole-genome sequencing of six representative isolates supported previous species affiliations, identified genes related to antimicrobial resistance, adhesion, biofilm formation, stress adaptation, and cytotoxicity, highlighting the importance of integrating genomic and phenotypic analyses. Notably, BS-018 showed a low ANI to the reported comparison genome, but its taxonomic assignment remains unresolved. Blood bank surfaces function as localized environmental conditions favoring bacteria with potential persistence-associated traits. This study identified environmental bacterial isolates exhibiting phenotypic and genomic characteristics potentially relevant to biosafety surveillance. Our results support incorporating integrated bioimaging, phenotypic characterization, and environmental surveillance with genomic resolution into infection prevention strategies and transfusion biosafety programs.

title: Neuroimmune-endocrine interactions in perinatal asphyxia: from brain injury to neuroprotection
text: Perinatal asphyxia (PA) remains a major cause of neonatal mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental disability worldwide. Although hypoxic–ischemic brain injury has traditionally been attributed to oxygen deprivation, excitotoxicity, and oxidative stress, accumulating evidence indicates that neurological outcomes are determined by complex interactions among metabolic, mitochondrial, neuroimmune, and neuroendocrine mechanisms. Following hypoxic–ischemic injury, primary energy failure rapidly triggers excitotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, calcium dysregulation, and oxidative damage, leading to activation of microglia and astrocytes, release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, disruption of blood–brain barrier integrity, and recruitment of peripheral immune cells. These events contribute to the development of secondary energy failure and persistent neuroinflammation. Simultaneously, activation of hypoxia-responsive pathways, including hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1), heat shock protein 70 (HSP70), glutathione-dependent antioxidant defenses, and neuroendocrine stress responses involving the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, promote endogenous adaptation and neuroprotection. Nitric oxide signaling further links mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative and nitrosative stress, inflammatory activation, and neuronal injury. Together, these mechanisms form an integrated neuroimmune-endocrine network that influences both injury progression and tissue repair. In this review, we propose Brain Energy Failure as a unifying conceptual framework linking mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative and nitrosative stress, neuroinflammation, endocrine adaptation, and endogenous neuroprotective responses following perinatal hypoxia. We further discuss the role of biomarkers associated with neuro-immuno-endocrine dysfunction, including inflammatory mediators, oxidative stress markers, endocrine factors, and indicators of neuronal and glial injury. Recent evidence has highlighted the therapeutic potential of multimodal neuroprotective approaches, including endogenous lipid mediators such as palmitoylethanolamide (PEA), which exert anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and mitoprotective effects. We also review current and emerging neuroprotective strategies targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling, and bioenergetic instability, and discuss their translational implications. Understanding the interactions among these interconnected pathways may facilitate biomarker-guided diagnosis, personalized neuroprotection, and the development of more effective therapies aimed at improving long-term neurological outcomes following perinatal asphyxia.

title: Multi-receptor whole-brain modeling reveals affinity-driven chemoarchitectural mechanism of virtual atomoxetine action
text: Linking molecular mechanisms with large-scale brain dynamics remains a fundamental challenge in computational psychiatry. Receptor-informed whole-brain models have provided mechanistic insights into pharmacological interventions, yet they have largely relied on single-receptor topographies that cannot explain the collective response of multiple receptor systems. Here, we combined pharmacological resting-state fMRI with a whole-brain model incorporating cortical expression of adrenergic and dopaminergic receptors to investigate the effects of atomoxetine, a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor that globally elevates catecholaminergic signaling. Using receptor similarity, we first identified a catecholaminergic chemoarchitecture comprising frontal, posterior and temporal networks, providing the neurochemical scaffold for interpreting atomoxetine-induced brain dynamics. Empirically, atomoxetine selectively stabilized functional connectivity dynamics within the posterior catecholaminergic network. Whole-brain modeling revealed that although individual receptor parameters did not differ between conditions, their collective organization converged toward empirical receptor binding affinities. Remarkably, the simulated atomoxetine state was reconstructed from the placebo configuration through a negative reweighting along this receptor-affinity axis. In silico forward modeling showed that this affinity-driven redistribution gave rise to a cortical modulation pattern aligned with a frontal chemoarchitectural gradient, which was sufficient to simulate the observed dynamical and connectivity changes. Together, these findings suggest receptor binding affinity as a key organizing principle linking molecular receptor organization to brain dynamics, providing a model-based, biologically interpretable computational mechanism through which global catecholaminergic perturbations reshape whole-brain function.

title: Design, synthesis and larvicidal activity of novel imidazo[2,1‐ b ][1,3,4]thiadiazole carboxamides against Anopheles arabiensis and in silico target exploration
text: Abstract BACKGROUND Widespread resistance among malaria vectors to conventional insecticides, coupled with the limited availability of insecticides with novel mechanisms of action, necessitates the discovery of new chemical scaffolds for vector control. Anopheles arabiensis is an important malaria vector in sub‐Saharan Africa and poses additional control challenges due to its behavioral adaptability and rising insecticide resistance. This study aimed to design, synthesize, characterize, and evaluate novel 6‐(4‐substituted phenyl)imidazo[2,1‐ b ][1,3,4]thiadiazole‐2‐carboxamide derivatives ( 6a–6i ) as potential larvicidal agents. RESULTS Novel derivatives were synthesized and evaluated against third‐instar A. arabiensis larvae. At 4 μg/ mL , mortality ranged from 18% to 97% after 48 h. Compound 6e , bearing a sulfolane substituent, was the most active, producing 93% and 97% mortality at 24 and 48 h, respectively, comparable to temephos (99% at both time points). Its median lethal concentration ( LC 50 ) values were 1.17 and 1.03 μg/ mL , respectively, compared with 1.41 and 1.21 μg/ mL for temephos, corresponding to an efficiency ratio of 0.9 at both time points. Structure–activity relationship ( SAR) analysis indicated that the C‐6 trifluoromethyl group and polar hydrogen‐bond‐accepting substituents were favorable. Molecular docking identified adenosine kinase as a potential target, with recurrent interactions involving Gly64, Asn221, and Leu133. CONCLUSION The findings identify imidazo[2,1‐ b ][1,3,4]thiadiazole as a promising scaffold for developing new larvicidal chemotypes. Compound 6e represents the most promising lead and provides a basis for further optimization and validation of this scaffold for innovative malaria‐vector control strategies. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

title: MASLD-Mitochondrial Digital Twin: Mapping mitonuclear epistasis to predict disease trajectory and systemic bioenergetic homeostasis
text: Abstract Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent chronic disorder with marked clinical heterogeneity and divergent outcomes. Current pathophysiological models fail to fully account for inter-individual variation in progression toward steatohepatitis and systemic multimorbidity. This Perspective posits the mitochondrion as an integrative functional hub where genomic predisposition, epigenomic plasticity, and bioenergetic signaling converge to shape the disease's longitudinal trajectory. We synthesize evidence from the mitonuclear interactome—the co-evolutionary and functional coordination between nuclear and mitochondrial genomes, hepatic epigenomic remodeling, and circulating mitochondrial metabotypes to propose a unified systems biology framework: the MASLD-Mitochondrial Digital Twin (MASLD-MDT). This multiscale platform integrates high-resolution biological data—including single-cell mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) heteroplasmy, NAD+ redox dynamics, and the systemic efflux of mitochondrial-derived peptides (MDPs)—to simulate individualized disease kinetics. By reframing MASLD as a systemic mitochondriopathy, the MASLD-MDT could quantify critical bioenergetic thresholds, providing a novel metric for risk stratification and the in silico optimization of therapeutic deployment. This hypothesis-oriented instrument aims to advance the field toward a mitochondrial precision medicine strategy, enabling the discovery of targeted interventions to intercept multi-organ compromise.

title: Schizophrenia research in 2026: report from the annual meeting of the Schizophrenia International Research Society
text: Abstract SIRS 2026, held under the theme “Schizophrenia Research in the Era of Artificial Intelligence,” brought together researchers, clinicians, and persons with lived experience to take stock of a field whose tools for measuring, predicting, and intervening in psychosis have expanded rapidly. Themes spanned artificial intelligence, automated speech analysis, retinal imaging, computational modelling, and novel psychosocial and pharmacological targets, with evidence that, individually, warrants cautious but serious attention and that, collectively, points toward a more mechanistically grounded psychiatry. A recurring call across the meeting was for rigorous external validation, equitable implementation, and sustained scrutiny of underlying assumptions, including whether existing diagnostic categories and treatment targets remain adequate. Some areas remained underworked relative to their importance, including translating basic neuroscience advances into questions relevant to patients and families, and the structural determinants of illness onset and treatment access. Perhaps the most significant development at SIRS 2026 was not any single scientific finding but the broadening of whose voices and experiences are treated as evidence worth taking seriously in this era of AI, a shift whose consolidation remains a question for the field as much as for any individual programme of work.

title: Landscape and training opportunities in artificial intelligence for biosciences in Latin America: the BiotrAIn project
text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is redefining biosciences by enabling the analysis of complex, large-scale biological and medical data. Latin America has demonstrated remarkable potential through studies applying AI to biomedical sciences often using locally generated data and addressing regional needs. However, the integration of AI into research and healthcare in this region faces several structural challenges, including insufficient infrastructure, lack of specialized training, fragmented research systems, and continuously constrained funding. To overcome existing limitations, capacity building at the regional level is crucial. This includes developing localized AI training programs and the reinforcement of a collaborative research framework. Collaboration across institutions and countries, along with engagement from industry and government, is key to fostering an enabling environment for the responsible and effective use of AI. One promising response to these challenges is the BiotrAIn project, a partnership involving EMBL-EBI, the University of Costa Rica, and CABANAnet, with support from the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. The project is structured around three pillars: knowledge exchange, curriculum development, and regional training. BiotrAIn exemplifies how strategically designed, regionally adapted programs can build AI capacity in biosciences and foster more equitable scientific development across Latin America. Strategic efforts like BiotrAIn serve as essential building blocks toward a more robust, ethical, and sustainable AI ecosystem in the region, while offering a model that could be adapted by other regions globally. Ultimately, with coordinated investment, inclusive policies, and collaborative networks, Latin America can position itself as a significant contributor to global AI-driven bioscience.
