Decalogue of Ibero-American Community Pharmacy: Declaration of Abarán, Spain
text: Introduction: It is well known that community pharmacy in Latin America exhibits conceptual, regulatory and care-related heterogeneity, making it difficult to integrate community pharmacists into health systems in a uniform manner. The objective of this study was to present the Decalogue of Ibero-American Community Pharmacy, developed by the Scientific-Professional Society of Ibero-American Community Pharmacy (SOCFIC by its Spanish acronym), and its operationalization as a preliminary tool to evaluate regional development, identify and prioritize gaps, establish levels of maturity, and guide public policies, national plans, and strengthening strategies. Method: A methodological study was carried out in two stages: development and validation of the Decalogue by experts from 17 Ibero-American countries, and its operationalization through a matrix of indicators, categories of compliance, and progressive levels of maturity. Results: The Decalogue of Ibero-American Community Pharmacy was developed along with a preliminary Evaluation Matrix, four levels of maturity, and an implementation roadmap focused on monitoring, comparison, and regional strengthening. Conclusions: The Decalogue and its operationalization provide a common framework for evaluating, monitoring, and guiding policies and strategies to strengthen Ibero-American community pharmacies.

title: Global Mental Wealth: A Multidimensional Analysis of Social, Financial, and Emotional Well-Being in 92 Countries
text: Abstract Governments and organizations increasingly endorse the importance of mental health in all forms of policy, though emphasis in measurement still remains on indicators such as GDP, depression, and other common disorders. In this study of 92 countries ( n = 53,799), we assess the mental health of individuals around the world alongside measures of financial and social well-being. Findings include a trend of languishing mental health across many groups, particularly among younger adults and within higher-income countries. While positive trends are observed for education and income, a number of concerning trends also emerge, particularly the poor results for young adults and generally moderate results for employed individuals. In sum, we find an alarming but perhaps unsurprisingly low level of positive mental health in a substantial number of countries, but also identify specific economic, social, and other indicators that policymakers could target in improving the well-being of the populations they serve.

title: So close, yet so far: can AI succeed where health systems are failing?
text: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned as a transformative tool in health, including in sexual, reproductive, and maternal health (SRMH). Yet this momentum coexists with a more uncomfortable reality: many health systems continue to face foundational challenges, weak infrastructure, fragmented services, workforce shortages, poor data quality, and persistent inequities that are not technological in origin. This article argues that AI's potential contribution to SRMH will be shaped more by the conditions under which it is introduced than by its technical sophistication. Four interconnected arguments are developed. First, rapid adoption should not be mistaken for demonstrated value; the evidence base for scalable, equitable impact remains limited. Second, effective AI integration requires starting from health system bottlenecks rather than technological possibilities, since many SRMH barriers are organizational, political, and cultural before they are computational. Third, institutional readiness, governance, absorptive capacity, and implementation infrastructure are central determinants of whether AI improves or complicates care. Fourth, without deliberate policy decisions, AI is likely to benefit populations already better served, amplifying existing inequities. A pragmatic agenda for AI in SRMH must therefore begin with what health systems need, not what technology can offer.

title: Structure, resourcing, and data capture across international colorectal cancer outcomes registries: an international comparative study
text: Introduction There are many differences internationally in infrastructure between colorectal cancer outcomes registries. Understanding them is crucial in identifying common challenges and opportunities to improve and collaborate. This study compares the registries regarding scope, governance, funding, data capture and linkage, reporting, and research. Method Representatives from the registries included in the International Colorectal Cancer Outcomes Registry Collaborative provided data on their infrastructure. Other members of the registries validated the accuracy of the reported information by reviewing and confirming the results. Results Eight registries contributed to this study, from Australia and New Zealand, England and Wales, the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Argentina, Italy, and Scotland. The infrastructure of each registry influenced its scope and coverage of colorectal cancer cases. All registries utilised a form of web-based data entry and promote quality improvement by disseminating data back to relevant stakeholders and, in some cases, in public forums. More extensive linkages to other relevant domestic databases have been formed in more mature registries across numerous countries, while being explored in the Scottish registry. Legislative barriers largely limit international data linkage. Conclusion Cancer outcomes registries face many similar challenges internationally. Cross-registry collaboration can identify strategies to improve data collection internationally and support data-driven quality improvement. Leveraging technological advances in the evolution of outcomes registries would enhance efficiency and efficacy, but continual advancement requires adequate funding and stakeholder involvement.

title: Artificial intelligence in odontology education
text: Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored in dental education as a tool to support teaching, learning, assessment, and clinical decision-making. This systematic review synthesized current evidence on the implementation and educational impact of AI technologies in undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing dental education. Methodology: A PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted using Scopus, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Studies published between 2020 and 2025 evaluating AI applications in dental education were identified using predefined PICO criteria. Educational outcomes included knowledge acquisition, diagnostic accuracy, clinical reasoning, procedural skills, learner engagement, and perceptions of AI-assisted learning. Results: The included literature reflects an expansion from machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision systems primarily evaluated for diagnostic support toward generative AI platforms, including large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems. Across the included studies, AI applications were frequently associated with favorable diagnostic and examination performance and, in selected educational contexts, with supportive findings related to clinical reasoning, technical competency, feedback, and self-directed learning. However, the evidence was predominantly based on technical performance assessments and observational or cross-sectional designs. Discussion: AI is increasingly being explored as a potential complementary educational resource, with applications including interactive tutoring, adaptive learning, and support for clinical reasoning. Nevertheless, heterogeneous methodologies and limited longitudinal evidence indicate the need for standardized educational evaluation and responsible curricular integration. Conclusion: AI shows potential as a complementary resource in dental education. Its integration should remain pedagogically guided and ethically supervised while future research establishes its educational effectiveness through standardized and longitudinal evaluation.

title: Arquitetura Blockchain para gestão de dados no contexto do SUS
text: Dados de saúde são sensíveis a questões de segurança e privacidade. Normalmente, sistemas de registros médicos são centralizados, o que implica um ponto único de vulnerabilidade. A tecnologia Blockchain tem sido utilizada para ampliar a segurança por meio de suas características de descentralização e imutabilidade em um ambiente criptografado. Neste trabalho, propõe-se uma arquitetura baseada em Blockchain para armazenamento e intercâmbio de dados em sistemas de Registros Eletrônicos de Saúde (EHR). A pesquisa caracteriza-se como estudo de natureza técnica e exploratória, estruturado em duas etapas: a realização de três revisões sistemáticas da literatura e o desenvolvimento de uma proposta arquitetural. Este artigo apresenta a terceira revisão, sobre arquiteturas de sistemas EHR baseados em Blockchain, complementando duas revisões publicadas anteriormente pelos autores, que investigaram o estado da arte das plataformas Blockchain e o uso de sistemas de gerenciamento de registros médicos baseados nessa tecnologia. As três revisões fundamentaram a proposição de uma arquitetura conceitual voltada à integridade e à rastreabilidade de dados sensíveis de registros médicos, promovendo a interoperabilidade entre os diversos atores do setor. Como resultado, apresenta-se uma arquitetura conceitual que integra tecnologias destinadas a contribuir para a segurança e a governança dos dados. O estudo também inclui uma análise conceitual da aplicabilidade da proposta no contexto do Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS), discutindo seu potencial para aprimorar a gestão pública, contribuir para a conformidade com as leis de proteção de dados e fortalecer a confiança entre pacientes e profissionais de saúde. Entretanto, a proposta ainda não foi validada empiricamente.

title: From Local Initiatives to National Systems: Mapping the Landscape of Landslide Early Warning in Latin America
text: Abstract Rainfall-induced landslides are among the most damaging geophysical processes in Latin America, and landslide early warning systems (LEWS) have become the region's principal non-structural response. Yet how these systems are operated, financed and sustained remains largely undocumented, because regional research has concentrated on hazard analysis, susceptibility modelling and technical development rather than on deployed systems. This paper maps that operational landscape. Twenty-five warning services across ten countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua and Peru) were documented by researchers and practitioners directly involved in them, using a common template, and compared along two axes: the nine assumptions underpinning geographical LEWS, and five operational dimensions (hazard monitoring, forecasting, dissemination, governance and community engagement) rated through structured expert judgement. Three patterns emerged. First, historical records and rainfall thresholds remain the backbone of nearly every system, yet several countries now challenge the assumption that rainfall alone represents subsurface conditions, incorporating soil moisture, pore pressure, deformation and machine learning. Second, insufficient monitoring density in complex terrain is the dominant technical constraint region-wide. Third, and most consequentially, forecasting capability does not translate automatically into risk reduction. The most consolidated profiles, Brazil and Colombia, retain gaps at the municipal and land-use interface, while documented discontinuities elsewhere followed legal and ownership vacuums rather than technical failure. Sustained institutional ownership, predictable financing and locally actionable warnings, not further technological sophistication, define the region's frontier. We therefore call for greater investment in the continued monitoring of unstable hillslopes and catchments throughout the region.

title: Machine psychology for language models
text: Large language models (LLMs) show increasingly advanced emergent capabilities and are being incorporated across various societal domains. Understanding their behavior and reasoning abilities is therefore important. We argue that a fruitful direction for research is engaging LLMs in experiments inspired by psychology that have traditionally been aimed at understanding human cognition and behavior. Here, we highlight and summarize theoretical perspectives, experimental paradigms, and computational analysis techniques that this approach brings to the table. It paves the way for a "machine psychology" for LLMs that goes beyond performance measurements and focuses instead on computational insights that move us toward a better understanding and discovery of emergent abilities and behavioral patterns in LLMs. We review existing work taking this approach, synthesize best practices, and highlight promising future directions. We also describe the important caveats of applying methodologies designed for understanding humans to machines. We posit that leveraging tools from experimental psychology to study LLMs will become increasingly valuable as models evolve to be more powerful, opaque, multimodal, and integrated into complex agentic real-world settings.

title: 3D Segmentation in the Clinic: A Grand Challenge
text: This paper describes the set-up of a segmentation competition for automatic and semi-automatic extraction of the liver from computed tomography scans and the caudate nucleus from brain MRI data. This competition was held in the form of a workshop at the 2007 Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention conference. The rationale for organizing the competition is discussed, the training and test data sets for both segmentation tasks are described and the scoring system used to evaluate the segmentation is presented.

title: Generating interesting scientific ideas using knowledge graphs and LLMs: Evaluations with 100 research group leaders
text: The rapid growth of scientific literature makes it increasingly challenging for researchers to identify novel and impactful ideas, especially across disciplines. Modern AI systems offer new opportunities for scientific ideation, but how compelling are AI-generated ideas, and how can their quality be improved? Here, we introduce SCIMUSE , which generates personalized research ideas using a knowledge graph of 58 million papers and a large language model (LLM). A central focus of this work is to understand how interesting these ideas are. Therefore, we conducted a large-scale evaluation in which more than 100 research group leaders—spanning the natural sciences to the humanities—rated over 4,400 personalized ideas according to their level of interest. Overall, expert ratings were modest (mean 2.40 on a 5-point scale, most common rating 1), while 24.9% of ideas were rated 4 or 5. We find that supplying concept pairs selected using the knowledge graph does not improve expert-rated interest over a titles-only GPT baseline. High-citation-predicted pairs even showed a weak tendency (1.94 σ ) toward lower interest than random pairs. Nevertheless, graph features can be used to control properties of ideas, and, using this unique evaluation dataset, we show that idea interest can be predicted with both a supervised neural network based on graph features and a zero-shot ranking approach based on an LLM. Our work provides an AI methodology for generating scientific ideas and a large-scale interdisciplinary expert evaluation, paving the way to study and improve difficult-to-measure metrics such as expert-perceived scientific interestingness.

title: Federated Distillation: A Survey
text: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without centralizing clients’ raw data, but parameter exchange can impose substantial communication costs and usually requires compatible model architectures. Federated distillation (FD) instead transfers predictive or intermediate knowledge through knowledge distillation (KD), which can support heterogeneous models and reduce communication in suitable settings. These benefits are not automatic: their magnitude depends on the transmitted knowledge, reference data, communication schedule, and threat model. This survey provides a challenge-centered synthesis of FD. We first formalize a representative public-data, response-based FD protocol and then organize existing methods by the FL challenges they address, including data, system, and model heterogeneity, client drift, catastrophic forgetting, communication cost, and privacy risk. We further review applications in industrial engineering, computer vision, natural language processing, and healthcare, including recent federated adaptation of large language models. Finally, we identify five research priorities: richer transferred knowledge, joint treatment of interacting forms of heterogeneity, communication-aware distillation, threat-model-driven privacy protection, and standardized theory, benchmarks, and evaluation.

title: A statistical framework for evaluating the repeatability and reproducibility of large language models
text: OBJECTIVES: Systematic evaluation of variability in large language model (LLM)-generated outputs is critical for assessing their reliability. We developed a general statistical framework and Python package (llmReproScore) for quantifying the repeatability and reproducibility of LLM outputs. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Following US Food and Drug Administration terminology, our framework establishes four metrics for quantifying LLM repeatability and reproducibility along two dimensions: semantic and internal. Semantic metrics quantify variability in the meaning of LLM-generated outputs, whereas internal metrics quantify variability in token-generation certainty. We validated these metrics, and as an illustrative use case, applied them to diagnostic reasoning outputs generated across LLMs and prompting strategies using US Medical Licensing Examination questions and 90 real-world rare disease cases from the Undiagnosed Diseases Network. RESULTS: Validation results showed that semantic scores aligned with human ratings (Spearman ρ = 0.88 for repeatability and 0.66 for reproducibility) and confirmed that internal metrics capture variability in token-generation certainty. In the illustrative use case, LLM repeatability was generally not associated with accuracy, suggesting that LLM output variability and accuracy capture distinct dimensions of model performance. DISCUSSION: The proposed metrics can be used to characterize LLM output variability and systematically compare models, prompts, and generation settings. These comparisons can inform more rigorous selection of LLM configurations based on repeatability and reproducibility. CONCLUSION: We developed and validated generalizable metrics for quantifying LLM output variability. The proposed metrics can complement accuracy-based evaluation to inform experimental design and support more rigorous comparison and selection of models, prompts, and generation settings.

title: Language modeling on tabular data: a survey of foundations, techniques and evolution
text: Tabular data, a prevalent data type across various domains, presents unique challenges due to its heterogeneous nature and complex structural relationships. Achieving high predictive performance and robustness in tabular data analysis holds significant promise for numerous applications. Influenced by recent advancements in natural language processing, particularly Transformer architectures, new methods for tabular data modeling have emerged. Early techniques concentrated on pre-training Transformers from scratch, often encountering scalability issues. Subsequently, methods leveraging pre-trained language models like BERT have been developed, which require less data and yield enhanced performance. The recent advent of large language models, such as GPT and LLaMA, has further revolutionized the field, facilitating more advanced and diverse applications with minimal fine-tuning. Despite the growing interest, a comprehensive survey of language modeling techniques for tabular data remains absent. This paper fills this gap by providing a systematic review of the development of language modeling for tabular data, encompassing: (1) a categorization of different tabular data structures and data types; (2) a review of key datasets used in model training and tasks used for evaluation; (3) a summary of modeling techniques including widely-adopted data processing methods, popular architectures, and training objectives; (4) the evolution from adapting traditional Pre-training/Pre-trained language models to the utilization of large language models; (5) an identification of persistent challenges and potential future research directions in language modeling for tabular data analysis. GitHub page associated with this survey is available at: https://github.com/lanxiang1017/Language-Modeling-on-Tabular-Data-Survey.git .

title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Tool Descriptions Are Smelly! Towards Improving AI Agent Efficiency with Augmented MCP Tool Descriptions,
text: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) introduces a standard specification that defines how Foundation Model (FM)-based agents should interact with external systems by invoking tools. However, to understand a tool’s purpose and features, FMs rely on natural-language tool descriptions, making these descriptions a critical component in guiding FMs to select the optimal tool for a given (sub)task and to pass the right arguments to the tool. While defects or smells in these descriptions can misguide FM-based agents, their prevalence and consequences in the MCP ecosystem remain unclear. Hence, we examine 856 tools spread across 103 MCP servers empirically, assess their description quality, and their impact on agent performance. We identify six components of tool descriptions from the literature, develop a scoring rubric utilizing these components, and then formalize tool description smells based on this rubric. By operationalizing this rubric through an FM-based scanner, we find that 97.1% of the analyzed tool descriptions contain at least one smell, with 56% failing to state their purpose clearly. While augmenting these descriptions for all components improves task success rates by a median of 5.85 percentage points and improves partial goal completion by 15.12%, it also increases the number of execution steps by 67.46% and regresses performance in 16.67% of cases. These results indicate that achieving performance gains is not straightforward; while execution cost can act as a trade-off, execution context can also impact. Furthermore, component ablations show that compact variants of different component combinations often preserve behavioral reliability while reducing unnecessary token overhead, enabling more efficient use of the FM context window and lower execution costs.

title: ISLES’24: Final stroke infarct prediction with multimodal imaging and clinical data. Where do we stand?
text: Accurate estimation of brain infarction (i.e., irreversibly damaged tissue) is critical for guiding treatment decisions in acute ischemic stroke. Reliable infarct prediction informs key clinical interventions, including the need for patient transfer to comprehensive stroke centers, the potential benefit of additional reperfusion attempts during mechanical thrombectomy, decisions regarding secondary neuroprotective treatments, and, ultimately, prognosis of clinical outcomes. This work introduces the Ischemic Stroke Lesion Segmentation (ISLES) 2024 challenge, which focuses on the prediction of final infarct volumes from pre-interventional acute stroke imaging and clinical data. ISLES'24 provides a comprehensive, multimodal setting where participants can leverage all clinically and practically available data - including full acute CT imaging, sub-acute follow-up MRI, and structured clinical information - across a train set of N=150 cases. On the hidden test set (N=98), the top-performing model, a multimodal nnU-Net-based architecture, achieved a Dice score of 0.285 ± 0.213 and an absolute volume difference of 21.2 ± 37.2 mL, underlining the significant challenges posed by this task and the need for further advances in multimodal learning. This overview of the ISLES'24 challenge offers two primary contributions: first, it provides a standardized, clinically realistic benchmark for post-treatment infarct prediction, built on a comprehensive, open, and multimodal longitudinal stroke imaging dataset; second, it provides insights into the strengths and limitations of current algorithms and delineates key research directions to guide the development of next-generation infarct prediction models.

title: A survey of graph unlearning
text: Graph unlearning emerges as a crucial advancement in the pursuit of responsible AI, providing the means to remove sensitive data traces from trained models, thereby upholding the right to be forgotten . It is evident that graph machine learning exhibits sensitivity to data privacy and adversarial attacks, necessitating the application of graph unlearning techniques to address these concerns effectively. In this comprehensive survey paper, we present the first systematic review of graph unlearning approaches, encompassing a diverse array of methodologies and offering a detailed taxonomy and up-to-date literature overview to facilitate the understanding of researchers new to this field. To ensure clarity, we provide lucid explanations of the fundamental concepts and evaluation measures used in graph unlearning, catering to a broader audience with varying levels of expertise. Delving into potential applications, we explore the versatility of graph unlearning across various domains, including but not limited to social networks, adversarial settings, recommender systems, and resource-constrained environments like the Internet of Things, illustrating its potential impact in safeguarding data privacy and enhancing AI systems’ robustness. Finally, we shed light on promising research directions, encouraging further progress and innovation within the domain of graph unlearning. By laying a solid foundation and fostering continued progress, this survey seeks to inspire researchers to further advance the field of graph unlearning, thereby instilling confidence in the ethical growth of AI systems and reinforcing the responsible application of machine learning techniques in various domains.

title: Retrieval-augmented generation in biomedicine: a survey of technologies, datasets, and clinical applications
text: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) in biomedicine face a fundamental conflict between static parameter knowledge and the dynamic nature of clinical evidence. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) addresses this by grounding generation in external data, yet it introduces new complexities in latency and architecture. This survey synthesizes the biomedical RAG landscape from 2020 to 2025 through a structured literature mapping of 178 screened records, yielding 94 representative studies classified into naive RAG (38 studies, 40.4%), advanced RAG (46 studies, 48.9%), and modular RAG (10 studies, 10.7%). Beyond a technological taxonomy, we formalize the biomedical RAG trilemma, identifying the inherent trade-offs between reasoning depth, inference latency, and data privacy that constrain current clinical deployment. We analyze how recent agentic workflows enhance diagnostic reasoning but risk prohibitive latency, and how privacy constraints dictate the choice between powerful cloud-based models and local deployment. Finally, we outline the alignment gap in multimodal RAG and propose future directions for self-correcting, verifiable clinical agents.

title: From Frege to ChatGPT: Compositionality in Language, Cognition, and Deep Neural Networks
text: Unlike classical symbolic AI systems, however, the neural networks powering recent advances are not designed to embody a strong assumption of compositionality, relying instead on acquiring capabilities by learning statistical regularities from data (Fodor & Pylyshyn, 1988;McClelland et al., 1986b;Rumelhart et al., 1986b;Smolensky et al., 2022).Whereas compositionality is integral to certain fundamental design features of classical computational architectures (e.g., predicate-argument structure, variable binding, constituent structure), these features are not native to standard DNNs.Traditionally, this has been lodged as an objection to the viability of neural networks as cognitive models (Fodor & Pylyshyn, 1988).However, modern DNNs' impressive performance in domains traditionally thought to require compositionality (e.g., language) calls this into question.Have today's models overcome previously hypothesized limitations?Or are they merely imitating compositional be hav iors through useful but imperfect heuristics?Do DNNs instantiate a novel form of nonclassical compositionality?Or does their success in reproducing sophisticated cognitive be haviors show that there is a new game in town and that compositionality is negotiable after all?In this chapter, we review and contextualize recent studies of compositionality in DNNs, with a par tic u lar focus on language.We begin in section 11.2.1 with a historical overview of the explanatory role of compositionality in philosophy, linguistics, and psy chol ogy, outlining its evolution from a property of interest primarily to logicians and philosophers to an empirically motivated psychological construct central to con temporary cognitive science.We then briefly describe the rise of connectionism in the 1980s and 1990s (section 11.2.2) and the challenge that compositionality poses for neural networks (section 11.2.3).With this crucial context in place, we move to today's deep neural networks, reviewing key recent breakthroughs in replicating compositional be hav iors (section 11.3).In par tic u lar, we argue that meta-learning (section 11.3.2),or learning to learn, offers a novel perspective on how neural networks like LLMs (section 11.3.3)can come to reproduce the behavioral signatures of compositionality.To close, we discuss potential implications that this work may have for our understanding of human compositionality and suggest ave nues for future empirical and philosophical work (section 11.4).

title: Comparative analysis of end-to-end learning and foundation models for clinical-grade prostate pathology
text: Abstract Foundation models (FMs) using self-supervised pre-training are widely advocated as a universal solution for pathology, yet their advantages over task-specific (TS) models remain unclear. Here we show, using over 100,000 prostate biopsies from 6268 patients across 15 sites, that while FMs demonstrate utility in data-scarce scenarios, their performance converges with—and is in some cases surpassed by—TS models with sufficient labeled training data. Concordance with pathologists’ grading reaches quadratic Cohen’s kappas of 0.91 (95% CI 0.90-0.92; all models) on internal and 0.87 (0.86-0.88; TS), 0.86 (0.84-0.87; UNI FM) and 0.85 (0.84-0.86; Virchow2 FM) on external cohorts at full training. Task-specific training markedly reduces misgrading, misdiagnosis of challenging morphologies, and technical variability. Notably, FMs consume up to 35 times more energy. We advocate for considering both FMs and end-to-end learning for robust, resource-efficient, and clinically applicable AI pathology.

title: A generalist model for diverse text-guided medical image synthesis
text: Deep learning requires extensive data to achieve robust performance. However, data availability is often restricted in medicine due to patient privacy concerns. Synthetic data from medical image generative models present a possible solution to these challenges. Unfortunately, many models are often task-specific or trained on private datasets, limiting scalability and reproducibility. To address this, we introduce MediSyn: an open-access, generalist, text-guided latent diffusion model. MediSyn can generate images across 6 medical specialties and 10 imaging modalities, while being trained exclusively on public data. Our study provides several key contributions using MediSyn. First, we demonstrate that a generalist model can generate images of comparable quality to task-specific models across multiple specialties. Second, we show that this generalist approach is more computationally efficient than a suite of task-specific models. Third, we establish that a generalist model can produce realistic, text-aligned images across visually and medically distinct modalities. Fourth, we empirically demonstrate that these synthetic images are visually distinct from real images used in training. Finally, we show that a generalist model can produce images that improve classifier performance in data-limited settings across multiple specialties. Altogether, our findings highlight the potential of generalist image generative models to accelerate medical algorithmic research and development.

title: FLAb2: Benchmarking reveals that protein AI models cannot yet consistently predict developability properties
text: We introduce the Fitness Landscape for Antibodies (FLAb2), the largest public benchmark for therapeutic antibody design, comprising developability data for over 4 million antibodies across 32 studies and covering 7 properties: thermostability, expression, aggregation, binding affinity, pharmacokinetics, polyreactivity, and immunogenicity. Evaluating 30 AI and biophysical models, we find that most (80%) fail to produce statistically significant correlations. No model performs well across all properties. Some pretrained models (IgLM, ProGen2, Chai-1, ESM2, ISM, and IgFold) show significant zero-shot correlations for select properties. Fine-tuning with ≥10 2 points helps for thermostability, aggregation, and binding though polyreactivity and pharmacokinetics lack sufficient data. With enough data (10 3 points), a fine-tuned one-hot encoding model matches billion-parameter models. Training data matters more than architecture, and intrinsic properties (thermostability) are predicted more readily than extrinsic ones (immunogenicity and pharmacokinetics). Partial correlation analysis shows that germline distance accounts for ∼37% of language models' apparent predictive power.

title: How Proteins Work
text: How Proteins Work is an up-to-date and authoritative account of protein function. It covers the full breadth of protein science, from protein structure and organization through evolution, enzymes, regulation, dynamics, folding, allostery, and experimental and computational techniques, with chapters detailing how these features work together to support signaling and motion. It tackles challenging topics such as cooperativity, dynamics, and intrinsically disordered proteins, but always in an engaging style that puts clarity and understanding at the forefront. This text will enable undergraduate students in biochemistry and biophysics to understand the relationships between protein function, structure, and dynamics. It will also serve as a valuable resource for graduate students and researchers grappling with proteins and their functions. New to this second edition is a fuller account of enzyme kinetics and inhibition; more detail on protein folding and intracellular responses to unfolded proteins; a more coherent account of avidity and cooperativity; and discussion of new developments, including AlphaFold and cryo-electron microscopy. The text has been substantially reordered. Key Features: Chapters end with a problems section that aims to test the reader’s understanding of chapter content and its application. Top-quality full color illustrations help elucidate key concepts and mechanisms. High-resolution protein structures enhance understanding of molecular interactions and how structure relates to function. Extensive reference lists. Cross-referencing within the text to draw out the connections between different topics.

title: Exploring clinician interpretability of AI decision support systems for surgical anatomy recognition
text: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) decision support systems for surgery hold promise but face barriers to adoption, particularly around the interpretability of their outputs. We conducted an international cross-sectional survey of 47 neurosurgeons to evaluate perspectives on literature-derived explanatory techniques for AI-generated anatomical segmentations, using endoscopic pituitary surgery as a high-risk exemplar. Participants ranked certainty scores, certainty maps, saliency maps, scene similarity scores, and nearest-neighbour illustrations, and rated them using a modified Explanation Satisfaction Scale alongside free-text feedback. Certainty-based techniques were consistently ranked and rated highest - valued for aligning with surgical decision-making by conveying confidence (via scores) and anatomical boundaries (via maps). Saliency- and similarity-based methods were judged less clinically relevant and better suited to educational settings. Therefore, certainty-based techniques appear most acceptable to surgeons for improving the interpretability of AI-assisted anatomical navigation systems, though their impact on trust calibration and performance requires prospective evaluation across surgical domains.

title: Evaluation of Sequential Organ Failure Assessment-2 Performance Across Demographic Subgroups: An External Validation Using MIMIC-IV
text: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the discrimination and calibration of the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)-2 score for ICU mortality across demographic subgroups defined by age, sex, race and ethnicity, primary language, and insurance status. DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study. SETTING: Single academic medical center in the northeastern United States (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA), using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV database (version 3.1), 2008-2022, a dataset external to the SOFA-2 development cohort. PATIENTS: Adult patients (≥ 18 yr) with at least one ICU admission. The first ICU admission of the first qualifying hospitalization per patient was analyzed. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: First-day SOFA-2 scores were calculated from the worst values recorded during the first 24 hours of ICU admission across six organ systems, with ICU mortality as the primary outcome. Discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and calibration using intercept and slope, with subgroup differences in AUROC estimated by bootstrap resampling. Among 64,015 ICU patients (mean [sd] age, 64.6 [17.1] yr; 56.1% male; 66.1% White), overall AUROC was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.76-0.77). Discrimination declined significantly with age: AUROC, 0.85 (0.83-0.87) for ages 18-44 years vs. 0.72 (0.70-0.73) for ages 75 or older (ΔAUROC, -0.14 [95% CI, -0.16 to -0.11]), with systematic underprediction in older patients. Discrimination was significantly decreased among non-English speakers (ΔAUROC, -0.04) but did not differ across documented racial/ethnic groups. Patients with missing demographic information had markedly higher mortality than the overall cohort rate of 7.2% (14.1% for missing race/ethnicity; 23.1% for missing language). CONCLUSIONS: SOFA-2 demonstrated good overall performance but with clinically meaningful variation across subgroups, particularly with age and language. Patients with missing demographic data experienced markedly higher mortality. These findings argue for routine equity evaluation as a complement to traditional validation of clinical prediction tools.

title: Arterial energy dissipation as an emergent consequence of multi-scale mechanobiological regulation: a thermodynamic framework for arterial function
text: The mechanical behaviour of arteries is commonly described using predominantly elastic models that overlook the thermodynamic significance of viscous energy loss. Here, we examine whether arterial energy dissipation should be interpreted as a passive loss or as a consequence of physiological processes that regulate arterial function. Building on an intellectual lineage extending from Leonardo da Vinci to modern non-equilibrium thermodynamics, we integrate evidence from in vivo pressure-diameter hysteresis measurements, vascular smooth muscle energetics, endothelial signalling and systemic pressure-volume loop analysis. Together, these observations indicate that arterial dissipation is closely linked to the dynamic regulation of arterial mechanical state, including arterial diameter, stiffness, viscoelasticity, pulse wave velocity and vascular impedance. Experimental and modelling evidence further suggests that viscous energy loss contributes to the stabilization of pulsatile flow and the modulation of ventricular-arterial coupling, while providing a unified thermodynamic interpretation of vascular ageing, hypertension, exercise-induced adaptation and arterial mechanical remodelling. We propose that arterial energy dissipation is best understood not as a directly regulated variable, but as a thermodynamic consequence of the distributed mechanobiological regulation of arterial mechanical state and vascular impedance throughout the arterial network. This framework opens the possibility of defining vascular energetic phenotypes that capture how differences in arterial mechanical regulation shape cardiovascular function and adaptation.

title: Simplifying CT / MRI LI ‐ RADS v2018 Maintains Diagnostic Performance: An Individual Participant Data Meta‐Analysis
text: BACKGROUND: The Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) diagnostic algorithm assesses hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) probability of liver observations in high-risk individuals, but complexity may limit its adoption. PURPOSE: To evaluate whether LI-RADS v2018 can be simplified without impairing diagnostic performance by removing threshold growth (TG) and reducing size cut-offs. STUDY TYPE: Retrospective meta-analysis. POPULATION: Eight thousand five hundred eighty-two patients (mean age: 59 ± 11 years; 6610 male) at risk for HCC with CT/MRI (986 CT, 6554 MRI, and 1042 CT/MRI). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: Field strength: 1.5T and 3.0T; sequences varied by institution per LI-RADS technical requirements. ASSESSMENT: LI-RADS v2018 using major features only was compared with seven simplifications removing TG and/or applying single size cut-offs (≥ 10, ≥ 15, and ≥ 20 mm) in individual participant data (IPD) of 64 studies (29 institutions, 11 countries) from the LI-RADS Living Systematic Review and IPD Meta-analysis Project. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2. STATISTICAL TESTS: Summary receiver operating characteristic curves estimated area under the curve (AUC) across LR-3 to LR-5; LR-5 sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive value (PPV) were estimated using a one-step bivariate mixed-effects model. Differences were assessed by cluster bootstrap. p < 0.05 indicated significance, uncorrected for multiple comparisons. RESULTS: Nine thousand four hundred six observations were included. Excluding TG with a 10-mm cut-off showed AUC similar to LI-RADS v2018 (0.80 vs. 0.81, p = 0.44) and significantly higher LR-5 sensitivity (73.8% vs. 71.8%) with similar specificity (72.5% vs. 73.7%, p = 0.13) and PPV (97.8% vs. 97.8%, p = 0.73). Removing TG with 15-mm and 20-mm cut-offs had significantly lower AUC than v2018 (-0.03 [95% CI: -0.041, -0.019]; -0.043 [-0.054, -0.032], respectively) and sensitivity (-13.2% [95% CI: -14.5%, -12.0%]; -30.1% [-31.7%, -28.5%], respectively). Of the 64 studies, 17 had low-risk of bias, and 56 had low applicability concerns. CONCLUSION: Simplifying LI-RADS v2018 by removing TG and using a 10-mm size cut-off preserved diagnostic table AUC while improving LR-5 sensitivity without loss of specificity or PPV. PROTOCOL REGISTRATION: Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/cjwgp). EVIDENCE LEVEL: 3. TECHNICAL EFFICIENCY: Stage 2.

title: Bridging the dementia diagnostic gap by addressing cognitive assessments globally
text: Over 70% of projected dementia cases in the next 25 years will occur in low- and middle-income countries, yet diagnosis remains limited by absent culturally validated tools, inadequate biomarker infrastructure, and sociocultural barriers. This perspective examines these barriers and proposes solutions, including adapting cognitive tools culturally, integrating dementia screening into existing care platforms, and developing national policy, arguing that closing the diagnostic gap demands policies prioritizing equity and local ownership.

title: BEYOND RECOMMENDATIONS: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF VALUES, OUTCOMES AND IMPACT OF HEALTH TECHNOLOGY ASSESSMENT AGENCIES WORLDWIDE
text: IntroductionHealth Technology Assessment (HTA) agencies are increasingly required to demonstrate their added value for health systems, yet evidence on their real-world performance remains limited and heterogeneous.This systematic review aimed to describe the characteristics, perceived value, outcomes and impact of governmental HTA bodies worldwide. MethodsWe searched biomedical databases, registries, grey literature and websites of HTA agencies and international networks, without language or date restrictions, following Cochrane and PRISMA guidance.Eligible documents reported empirical data or structured opinions on governmental HTA agencies whose role is defined in law or equivalent regulation and/or whose recommendations are binding or otherwise mandatory for at least one health subsystem; purely theoretical pieces and non-governmental initiatives were excluded.A qualitative narrative and thematic synthesis was undertaken. ResultsWe identified 56 governmental HTA agencies, 43 established by law, operating across diverse regions and health-system arrangements.Stakeholders consistently valued these agencies for credibility, scientific rigor and their contribution to transparent, equity-oriented priority setting.Quantitative evidence showed wide variation in HTA report production, economic effects and influence on technology adoption, clinical practice and budgetary outcomes, with some agencies generating substantial savings and shaping coverage and disinvestment decisions.Impact was often indirect, context-dependent, more frequently documented at policy than clinical level.Long-term and equity-focused outcomes were sparsely reported. DiscussionOverall, HTA agencies mandates and binding recommendations by law are perceived as key contributors to evidence-based, equitable resource allocation, but https://doi.org/10.

title: Closed-loop acoustic stimulation promotes local slow oscillation train initiation and persistence in elderly adults
text: Abstract Slow oscillations (SOs) during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep support memory consolidation and metabolic waste clearance. Aging is associated with reduced SO amplitude and density and disrupted temporal organization, characterized by more isolated events and shorter SO trains. We investigated whether closed-loop acoustic stimulation (CLAS) could enhance the initiation and persistence of rhythmic SO activity in elderly adults. Twenty-seven participants underwent a baseline night followed by an experimental night, during which online-detected SOs were either stimulated using CLAS (STIM; n = 16) or left unstimulated (SHAM; n = 11). We quantified the proportions of isolated and consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and SO train length. Analyses assessed local effects around online-detected SOs and global effects across NREM sleep using offline detection. Locally, CLAS reduced the proportion of isolated SOs and increased the proportion of consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and mean train length. Global overnight effects were weaker but directionally consistent, primarily reflecting a shift toward longer SO trains. These changes occurred without a significant between-group difference in the change in SO density, and local effects remained significant after adjustment for SO density. Thus, CLAS promoted sustained rhythmic activity beyond changes in SO occurrence. These findings suggest that CLAS can modify the temporal organization of SOs in elderly adults, supporting its potential to mitigate age-related disruptions in SO dynamics. Temporal organization measures may complement conventional amplitude and density measures when evaluating CLAS effects. Further studies should establish whether these changes translate into cognitive benefits or improvements in other aspects of brain health.

title: Detection Technology of Peripheral Blood ctDNA Based on CRISPR/Cas and Gold Nanoparticles
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This study tests a new, fast blood test that may help detect very small traces of tumor DNA in the bloodstream. When tumor cells die, they release small pieces of DNA called circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) into the blood. Finding these pieces can help doctors diagnose cancer, monitor how well treatment is working, and detect cancer recurrence earlier. However, ctDNA is present in very small amounts and is hard to detect with current methods. Newer techniques such as next-generation sequencing (NGS) can find ctDNA, but they are expensive, require specialized laboratories, and take days to return results. This study evaluates a new testing method called "CRISPR/Cas12a combined with gold nanoparticle detection." This method uses a gene-editing protein (Cas12a) that can recognize a specific mutation in the BRCA1 gene and a gold nanoparticle-based readout that shows results within about 30 minutes, using portable equipment. The main purpose of this study is to find out how accurate, sensitive, and specific this new test is compared with NGS, which is considered the gold standard. The study will also check whether the portable device works consistently across different hospitals and whether the test results match patients' responses to treatment. The study will enroll adult cancer patients treated at participating hospitals and a group of healthy volunteers. All participants will provide about 3 mL of blood (less than one teaspoon). No additional invasive procedures or extra hospital visits are required beyond routine blood draws. For cancer patients, part of the blood sample will be tested with the new method and part will be tested with standard NGS, and the two results will be compared. Healthy volunteers' blood will be used to confirm that the test does not produce false positive results. There is no direct physical harm from the test itself, since it is performed on blood samples in the laboratory. Participants will receive the ctDNA test free of charge, and their test results may help their doctors better understand their disease. The results of this study may help develop a rapid, low-cost, bedside test for tumor DNA, which could improve cancer diagnosis and monitoring in the future.

title: A Safety and Efficacy Study Evaluating CTX112 in Adult Subjects With Refractory Autoimmune Disease
text: [Fase: PHASE1; Estado: RECRUITING] This is a single-arm, open-label, multicenter, ascending dose Phase 1 study evaluating the safety and preliminary efficacy of CTX112 in adult subjects with refractory autoimmune diseases, including active systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), systemic sclerosis (SSc), or idiopathic inflammatory myopathy (IIM).

title: EDIT-401 in Adults Who Require Additional Lowering of Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol (LDL-C)
text: [Fase: PHASE1,PHASE2; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] A phase 1/2, two-part trial consisting of an open label dose-escalation part and a randomized, double blind, placebo-controlled part to investigate safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy with EDIT-401 gene editing in adult male and female participants 18 to 65 years of age who require additional lowering of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) such as those with clinical diagnosis of Heterozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia (HeFH).

title: Combining Gene Editing and iPS to Study and Treat Monogenic Autoinflammatory Diseases
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] Type I interferonopathies (T1I) are rare autoinflammatory diseases characterized by dysregulated type I interferon signaling, leading to severe multisystem inflammation, including skin and lung involvement. STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy (SAVI) is an autosomal dominant T1I associated with severe systemic inflammation, skin ulcers, and progressive interstitial lung disease. Current treatments are often insufficient, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies. This project aims to develop patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models, combined with somatic cell differentiation and 3D organoid technologies, to investigate SAVI pathogenesis and assess the feasibility and efficacy of gene editing (GE). By enabling precise correction of disease-causing mutations, GE may overcome the limitations of conventional gene replacement approaches and provide a proof of concept for future targeted therapies.

title: A Safety and Efficacy Study Evaluating CTX112 in Subjects With Refractory Neurologic Autoimmune Disease
text: [Fase: PHASE1,PHASE2; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This is a single-arm, open-label, multicenter, ascending dose Phase 1/2 trial evaluating the safety and preliminary efficacy of CTX112 in adult participants with neurological autoimmune diseases (AIDs), including Progressive Multiple Sclerosis, relapsing Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder, relapsing Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein Antiody-Associated Disease, refractory AutoImmune Encephalitis, and refractory Stiff Person Syndrome

title: Transplantation of Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats Modified Hematopoietic Progenitor Stem Cells (CRISPR_SCD001) in Patients With Severe Sickle Cell Disease
text: [Fase: PHASE1,PHASE2; Estado: RECRUITING] This is an open label, non-randomized, 2-center, phase 1/2 trial of a single infusion of sickle allele modified cluster of differentiation (CD34+) hematopoietic stem progenitor cells (HSPCs) in subjects with in subjects ≥12 years old to 35 years old severe Sickle Cell Disease (SCD). The study will evaluate the hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) using CRISPR/Cas9 edited red blood cells (known as CRISPR\_SCD001 Drug Product).

title: Safety and Preliminary Efficacy of CTX112 in Adult Participants With Relapsed/Refractory Hematologic Autoimmune Disease
text: [Fase: PHASE1,PHASE2; Estado: RECRUITING] This is a single-arm, open-label, multicenter, ascending dose Phase 1/2 trial evaluating the safety and preliminary efficacy of CTX112 or Zugocabtagene geleucel (zugo-cel) in adult participants with relapsed/refractory primary Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP) and relapsed/refractory primary Warm Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (wAIHA).

title: Treatment of a Single Patient With CRD-TMH-001
text: [Fase: PHASE1; Estado: COMPLETED] The study is a single patient study intended to understand the effects of a gene-editing therapeutic to treat a rare mutation of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

title: Phase 1/2 Study of ABO-101 in Primary Hyperoxaluria Type 1 (redePHine)
text: [Fase: PHASE1,PHASE2; Estado: RECRUITING] The goal of the redePHine study is to evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of ABO-101 in participants with primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (PH1). The trial will consist of 2 Study Periods. During the first Study Period, there will be 2 parts. In Part A, adult participants will be treated with a single ascending dose to identify a recommended dose. In Part B, pediatric participants will be treated with the recommended dose. Following the first Study Period, participants will start Study Period 2, a long-term monitoring program to comply with local and national requirements.

title: Gene Editing For Sickle Cell Disease
text: [Fase: PHASE1; Estado: RECRUITING] This study is being done to test the safety of a new treatment called gene editing in Sickle Cell Disease (SCD) patients and to see if a single dose of this genetically modified cellular product will increase the amount of a certain hemoglobin called fetal hemoglobin (HbF) and help reduce the symptoms of SCD. Primary Objective * To assess the safety of autologous infusion of clustered regularly interspaced palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/ CRISPR associated protein (Cas9)-edited CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) in patients with severe SCD. Secondary Objective * To assess the efficacy autologous infusion of CRISPR/Cas9 genome-edited CD34+ HSPCs into patients with severe SCD.

title: Safety and Tolerability Study of Gene Editing Drug ZVS203e in Participants With Retinitis Pigmentosa
text: [Fase: EARLY_PHASE1; Estado: RECRUITING] The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety, tolerability and efficacy of a single escalating doses of ZVS203e administered via subretinal injection in participants with RP caused by RHO site-specific gene mutation (RHO-RP). This is a single-arm, open-label, single ascending dose study.

title: Molecular Characterization of Tumor-Microenvironment Interactions to Predict Drug Resistance in Gastric and GEJ Adenocarcinoma
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Surgical resection remains the only curative option for resectable gastric cancer, but perioperative FLOT chemotherapy is associated with substantial rates of chemoresistance and recurrence, largely driven by marked tumor heterogeneity. Recent data from the MATTERHORN phase III trial have shown that adding durvalumab to perioperative FLOT improves pathological complete response and survival, supporting this combination as a new standard of care for resectable gastric and gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. This observational multicenter study aims to characterize angiogenic and immune profiles within the tumor microenvironment and peripheral blood, in order to identify cellular and molecular signatures associated with response or resistance to perioperative FLOT plus durvalumab. Longitudinal biospecimen collection (PBMCs, serum, plasma, endoscopic biopsies, surgical specimens) will be integrated with multiparametric flow cytometry, single-cell transcriptomics and TCR/BCR sequencing, immunohistochemistry, pathomics and multiplex immunoassays, to provide mechanistic insights and potential predictive biomarkers.

title: Registry of an Integrated Longitudinal Multimodal Biospecimen Biobank for Primary CNS Lymphoma in China
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] This project aims to establish and prospectively register a longitudinal, multimodal biobank for primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL). The study will primarily enroll patients undergoing needle biopsy or surgical resection of lesions involving the brain, spinal cord, or meninges, with a pathological diagnosis of central nervous system lymphoma. To ensure population homogeneity, patients with PCNSL will constitute the core analysis cohort. Patients with imaging findings suggestive of PCNSL but a final pathological diagnosis other than PCNSL will serve as disease controls, and matched healthy volunteers will be recruited as baseline controls. At baseline, biopsy tissue, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), peripheral blood, urine, saliva, and stool samples will be collected. Follow-up visits will be scheduled at 1 month after biopsy and every 3-6 months thereafter, with contrast-enhanced brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and serial collection of CSF and peripheral blood. After the requirements of routine pathological diagnosis have been met, biopsy specimens will undergo tiered multi-omics profiling according to sample availability and freshness, including whole-exome sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, single-cell RNA sequencing, metabolomics, spatial transcriptomics, and spatial metabolomics. Analyses of CSF and blood samples will focus on circulating tumor DNA and cell-free RNA (ctDNA/cfRNA), supplemented by conventional cytology, flow cytometry, and other clinical data for longitudinal disease monitoring. The project will develop an integrated database incorporating clinical, imaging, pathological, molecular, and biospecimen data. It will characterize the relationships of baseline tissue multi-omics features and longitudinal changes in CSF- and blood-derived ctDNA/cfRNA with treatment response, recurrence prediction, and prognosis. The study will also develop diagnostic and risk-stratification models applicable to patients at our institution, across the region, and potentially throughout mainland China, while establishing standardized operating procedures for biospecimen collection and processing. This work is expected to provide high-quality evidence and a sustainable translational research platform for elucidating the biological heterogeneity of PCNSL, validating liquid-biopsy biomarkers, and optimizing precision follow-up strategies.

title: Multi-omics Profiling of Relapsed Extranodal Natural Killer (NK)/T-cell Lymphoma
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] This retrospective observational study characterises the tumour immune microenvironment and clonal architecture of relapsed or refractory extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTCL). Archival tumour tissue and blood samples collected during routine care are profiled by single-cell RNA sequencing, T-cell and B-cell receptor repertoire sequencing, whole-exome sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics. The study examines how immune and stromal cell states, clonal composition and spatial organisation relate to response to programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) blockade and to subsequent relapse.

title: Pre- and On-treatment Multi-omics Profiling of Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] This prospective observational study characterises the tumour immune microenvironment and microbial ecology of locally advanced rectal cancer before and during neoadjuvant therapy. Tumour tissue and peripheral blood are profiled by whole-genome sequencing, single-cell RNA sequencing with paired T-cell and B-cell receptor repertoire sequencing, spatial transcriptomics of formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded sections, multiplex immunofluorescence, and blood-based proteomic, cytokine and bulk T-cell receptor analyses. The study examines how immune and stromal states change during treatment and how they relate to major pathological response.

title: PET/CT-Based Intratumoral Heterogeneity and Multimodal Imaging for Tumor Diagnosis and Prognosis
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: COMPLETED] Background \& Rationale: Intratumoral heterogeneity (ITH) is a recognized hallmark and critical driver of therapeutic resistance, rapid disease progression, and poor survival across solid malignancies, notably advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). While tissue biopsies provide histopathologic confirmation, they are invasive and subject to severe spatial sampling bias. Standard whole-tumor radiomics from single-modality CT often masks localized subregional ecological niches. 18F-FDG PET/CT unites glucose metabolic activity with anatomical resolution, offering an ideal non-invasive tool to map whole-tumor spatial and functional heterogeneity in vivo. Methods \& Design: In this multicenter, bidirectional (retrospective and prospective) observational cohort study, 900 advanced NSCLC patients receiving first-line systemic therapies (chemotherapy, anti-PD-1 immunotherapy, and EGFR-TKIs) were enrolled. Baseline 18F-FDG PET/CT scans obtained within 2 weeks prior to therapy were partitioned into distinct biological habitats using entropy-intensity clustering. IBSI-compliant radiomic features were extracted to develop treatment-specific imaging intratumoral heterogeneity (IITH) signatures. Diagnostic accuracy for staging/metastases and prognostic performance for 6-month progression status, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS) were comprehensively validated across internal, external multicenter, and independent prospective cohorts, with biological explainability benchmarked against digital histopathology (HoVer-Net nuclear morphometrics) and transcriptomics.

title: A Prospective Trial of SFI Plus PD-1 Inhibitors and PBC in Resectable NSCLC (SFI-NSCLC)
text: [Fase: PHASE4; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This prospective, single-center clinical trial will enroll 30 treatment-naïve patients with locally advanced, resectable stage II-IIIA non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) to receive neoadjuvant Shenqi Fuzheng Injection (SFI) in combination with a PD-1 inhibitor and platinum-based chemotherapy. The primary endpoint is the pathological complete response (pCR) rate, while secondary endpoints include the major pathological response (MPR) rate and event-free survival (EFS). Furthermore, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics will be employed to dynamically track alterations in the immune regulatory network within the tumor microenvironment (TME) pre- and post-SFI administration. This approach aims to elucidate how SFI remodels the TME immune landscape and to uncover its potential advantages in improving clinical outcomes. Additionally, we will investigate the synergistic effects of SFI combined with PD-1 blockade and platinum-based chemotherapy, with the ultimate goal of advancing the integration of traditional Chinese medicine into the therapeutic paradigm for resectable NSCLC.

title: Residual Disease MEMory in PSOriasis Skin During EnstiLAR® and Narrow-band Ultraviolet B Therapy: The MEMPSOLAR Study
text: [Fase: PHASE4; Estado: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] Psoriasis is a non-communicable chronic immune-mediated disease. Psoriatic skin is characterized by excessive proliferation of skin cells and infiltration of immune cells. The cause of psoriasis is so far unknown. Established therapeutics include topical, oral-systemic, biologic, narrow-band ultraviolet B (NB-UVB). A persistent antipsoriatic effect by the newest biologic therapies has been demonstrated after treatment discontinuation. However, the remittive hallmark of psoriasis suggests the existence of a molecular scar, a kind of disease memory, in clinically healed skin. It has been suggested that this disease memory can be attributed to the tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cell. The main purpose of the study is to investigate whether (NB-UVB) treatment and concomitant Enstilar® treatment can change the amount of TRMs in the skin as well as change the expression in the microenvironment around these cells in the skin from psoriasis patients. In addition, the investigators will investigate whether the treatment can change the quantity and types of other psoriasis-related cells in the skin. In addition to this, the investigators will also examine the effect of treatment on patient-related parameters.

title: Habitat Analysis of Tumor Thrombus for Vena Cava Wall Invasion in Renal Cell Carcinoma
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Tumor thrombus in the inferior vena cava can invade the vessel wall. Doctors must know the invasion status before surgery. The status changes the surgical plan. Preoperative imaging has limited accuracy for wall invasion. Habitat imaging divides a tumor into subregions. Each subregion is a habitat. The method uses voxel-level image features. This study will test whether habitat imaging can diagnose inferior vena cava wall invasion. The participants have renal cell carcinoma with renal vein or inferior vena cava tumor thrombus. The study will use existing preoperative contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images. The reference standard is the pathology report from surgery. The primary measurement is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of the habitat model for wall invasion. The study will also measure sensitivity, specificity, calibration, and clinical utility. In an exploratory analysis, the study will compare imaging habitats with spatial transcriptomic regions. The study will use available Visium data from two participants. This is a retrospective observational study. The study has no intervention. The study will not change clinical care. The results will show whether habitat imaging can support preoperative planning.

title: Western Sydney Kidney Injury Biopsy Study
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION] The investigators aim to develop a clinically validated, histological acute tubular injury (ATI) scoring system to help improve diagnostic precision and predict clinical outcomes following ATI. To use an unbiased, data-driven approach, correlating pathological features (including digital pathology), key signatures using spatial technologies (transcriptomics or proteinomics) with relevant clinical outcomes. Spatial technologies (including spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteinomics) allow the use of 'precision pathology' to study the critical link between molecular characteristics to histological structure.

title: Neoadjuvant PD-1 Inhibitor and EGFR Inhibitor in Locally Advanced Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma
text: [Fase: PHASE2; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] The NEOPECS trial is a phase II prospective, single-arm, non-randomised interventional trial for patients with borderline resectable locally advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma with a 6-participant safety lead in to ensure safety of the combination in the neoadjuvant setting across 3 sites in Australia.

title: The Impact of Botox on Neuroimmune Interactions in Atopic Dermatitis
text: [Fase: PHASE1; Estado: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] The purpose of this study is to understand cellular and molecular interactions in the skin of participants with mild-to-moderate AD, and how botulinum toxin alters these interactions.

title: The Effect of Oral Semaglutide on Bone Turnover in Patients With T2D: a Randomized Placebo-controlled Clinical Trial
text: [Fase: PHASE2; Estado: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] The hypothesis for this study is that oral Semaglutide, a GLP-1Ra, has a positive effect on the balance between build-up and degradation as well as the strength of the bones in men and women aged 50-85 years with type 2 diabetes and an increased risk of bone fractures. Treatment involves once daily oral GLP-1Ra semaglutide or matching placebo for 52 weeks. The effect will be measured by bone markers in blood samples, bone scans, bone tissue and bone marrow tests (bone marrow aspiration and biopsy), physical activity assessed by a questionnaire, and direct bone strength measured by microindentation at the start and end of the study.

title: Multicenter, Single-Arm, Prospective Phase II Study of Neoadjuvant Cryo-Thermal Ablation Combined With Toripalimab and Chemotherapy for Resectable Stage IB-IIIB Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
text: [Fase: PHASE2; Estado: RECRUITING] Neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy has improved outcomes in patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but a substantial proportion of patients do not achieve a major pathological response. Cryo-Thermal Ablation may induce immunogenic tumor cell death and remodel the tumor immune microenvironment, potentially enhancing the antitumor activity of subsequent chemoimmunotherapy. This multicenter, single-arm, open-label, prospective Phase II study will evaluate the efficacy and safety of CT-guided Cryo-Thermal Ablation followed by toripalimab plus platinum-based doublet chemotherapy as neoadjuvant treatment for patients with resectable stage IB-IIIB NSCLC. For stage IB disease, only patients with cT2aN0M0 disease and a maximum primary tumor diameter of 4.0 cm are eligible. Patients with more advanced disease must be considered resectable by multidisciplinary team assessment according to the study protocol. Approximately 40 participants will receive Cryo-Thermal Ablation followed by 3 planned cycles of toripalimab plus platinum-based doublet chemotherapy and subsequent curative-intent surgical resection. The primary outcome is the pathological complete response (pCR) rate. Secondary outcomes include major pathological response (MPR) rate, objective response rate (ORR), R0 resection rate, event-free survival (EFS), overall survival (OS), treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs), and health-related quality of life. Exploratory translational analyses will investigate treatment-associated local and systemic antitumor immune responses and molecular dynamics using spatial transcriptomics, T-cell receptor sequencing, tumor genomic profiling, circulating tumor DNA analysis, imaging mass cytometry, and exploratory intratumoral metagenomic and metabolomic profiling.

title: D-SOLVE Cohorts (Cohort A and B)
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] Hepatitis D is by far the most severe form of chronic viral hepatitis, frequently leading to liver failure, hepatocellular carcinoma and death. Hepatitis D is caused by coinfection Hepatitis D is caused by co-infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis D virus (HDV). This multicenter cohort should enable a comprehensive and unbiased biomarker screening of well-defined HDV-infected patients, followed by mechanistic studies to determine the functional role of distinct molecules. Patient surveillance strategies and antiviral treatment approaches could be personalized which should reduce clinical and social disease burden, improve quality of life and save direct and indirect costs caused by HDV infection.

title: A Non-interventional, International, Multicentre Clinical Research Study to Build the Largest Collection of Multimodal Data (Including Clinical Data, Imaging Data and Omics Data) in Oncology
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] Cancer is amongst the leading causes of disease-related morbidity and mortality. A major challenge in cancer treatment is the development of biology-informed, personalised treatment strategies. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies have shed further insights into disease biology and treatment pathways, thus identifying new, precision medicine-based therapeutic opportunities. The biological mechanisms leading to cancer development and progression arise from complex and plastic networks of dysregulated cellular programs involving many signalling pathways and effector molecules. Cancer cells alter their surrounding environment via cell-cell interactions with non-tumor cells or by secreting cytokines, chemokines and other factors. This reprogramming of the tumour microenvironment (TME) is critical for cancer progression, invasion, and metastasis. Moreover, there are increasing studies that show that both innate and adaptive immune cell types contribute to tumorigenesis and treatment resistance when present within the TME. Understanding the crosstalk between cancer cells and the surrounding TME will inform on mechanisms of sensitivity and resistance to treatment, including immunotherapy (IO) and targeted therapies. Spatially resolved-Omics is an emerging field that characterises cell types by gene/protein expressions within their spatial context in the tissue organisation. Recent high profile spatial transcriptomics studies have uncovered specific cell identities that define the surrounding TME. The MOSAIC study, a collaborative initiative across industry and top oncology hospitals, proposes to go way beyond current cancer molecular profiling projects by combining the generation and analysis of multiple data modalities (3 essential mandatory modalities: Clinical Data, Hematoxylin and Eosin (H\&E) microscopic image, Spatial transcriptomics; up to 3 high priority data modalities depending on technical feasibility and sample size: bulk Ribonucleic Acid Sequencing (RNAseq), bulk Whole Exome Sequencing (WES), Single-cell transcriptomics; and potentially other optional data modalities and follow-up experiments such as single-cell omics, immunohistochemistry and spatial proteomics or other molecular profiling of proteins and molecules) on a minimum of 2,000 tumour samples across a different cancer indications. This will generate broad molecular and cellular profiling data of the tumour and its microenvironment from cancer patients, integrated with clinical data, at an unprecedented scale and resolution. This study will enroll patients diagnosed with one of the eligible cancer indications and for which a formalin fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) tumor sample from already performed biopsy and/or surgical resection is available within their local pathology archive or their affiliate centers archives. The MOSAIC study expects to have a strong impact for patients in terms of new targeted therapeutic drug discovery, identification of patient subgroups requiring either specific treatment or broader clinical care and identification of novel treatment response and resistance mechanisms.

title: Deployment and Evaluation of Humanoid Robotics in Coalition-Aligned Clinical Care Settings
text: [Fase: PHASE2; Estado: ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION] This clinical trial evaluates the deployment of humanoid robotics in coalition-aligned healthcare settings. The study measures biometric performance, ESG compliance, and operational impact across patient care, sanitation, and intake workflows. Humanoid units are enhanced via biotech integration and compensated through blockchain-based wage tokens. Outcomes will inform coalition governance, wage calibration, and metro-scale deployment strategies.

title: Androgen Deprivation Therapy (Relugolix) for the Improvement of Diagnostic Imaging (PSMA PET/CT Scan) in Patients With High Risk or Very High Risk Prostate Cancer, The EnrichPSMA Trial
text: [Fase: PHASE2; Estado: RECRUITING] This phase II trial studies how well a short course of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) with relugolix works in increasing expression of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) and improving diagnostic imaging with PSMA positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) in patients with high risk or very high risk prostate cancer. PSMA PET/CT has become the standard of care in imaging for high-risk prostate cancer. However, a limitation of PSMA PET/CT is its ability to detect cancer that has spread to the lymph nodes. PSMA is a protein that is usually found on the surface of normal prostate cells but is found in higher amounts on prostate tumor cells. Studies have shown that expression of PSMA is regulated by androgens (male reproductive hormones). Relugolix binds to gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptors in the pituitary gland, which blocks the pituitary gland from making the hormones follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone. This causes the testicles to stop making testosterone. Relugolix may stop the growth of tumor cells that need testosterone to grow. PSMA PET/CT is an imaging procedure that is used to help find prostate tumor cells in the body. For this procedure, a cell-targeting molecule linked to a radioactive substance (flotufolastat F 18 in this trial) is injected into the body and travels through the blood. It attaches to PSMA that is found on the surface of prostate tumor cells. PET/CT scanners detect high concentrations of the radioactive molecule and shows where the prostate tumor cells are in the body. Giving a short course of ADT with relugolix may increase PSMA expression to detect smaller areas of prostate cancer that were not previously detected.

title: Accuracy of 18F-rhPSMA-7.3 PET/ MRI for Prediction of Lymph Node Metastasis in Localized High-Risk Prostate Cancer
