title: Reduced serum carboxymethyllysine is independently associated with Alzheimer's disease
text: INTRODUCTIONAdvanced glycation end products accumulate in Alzheimers disease (AD) brain, but the clinical significance of circulating N{varepsilon}-(carboxymethyl)lysine (CML) remains uncertain. We evaluated serum CML as a complementary peripheral biomarker of AD. METHODSThis observational case-control study enrolled 101 patients with clinically diagnosed AD and 91 healthy controls. Serum CML was quantified in 191 participants. Multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic analyses assessed association and discrimination. A randomly selected subcohort underwent ultrasensitive measurement of amyloid-, tau-, glial-, and neuroaxonal-related biomarkers. RESULTSSerum CML was lower in AD than controls (median 15.26 versus 23.72 ng/mL; P<0.001). In a complete-case model (n=178), each 1-ng/mL increase was associated with lower odds of AD (adjusted odds ratio 0.727, 95% confidence interval 0.656-0.804). CML alone yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.883. Five-fold cross-validation yielded AUCs of 0.727 for a clinical model and 0.911 after adding CML. In the biomarker subcohort, AD showed lower A{beta}42/A{beta}40 and higher p-tau217; exploratory CML plus p-tau217 discrimination reached an AUC of 0.966 (n=60). DISCUSSIONReduced serum CML was independently associated with clinically diagnosed AD and may reflect a systemic glycoxidative dimension complementary to canonical biomarkers. Its biological origins and clinical value require external, longitudinal, and biomarker-defined validation.

title: Scalp EEG seizure warning in children under a pre-specified, locked evaluation: confound audit, structured chance levels and a negative result
text: Reported performance of scalp electroencephalographic (EEG) seizure pre-diction is often inflated by lenient evaluation and by the vigilance-state, clock-time and admission-trend structure of monitoring data. We asked how much short-horizon warning survives a pre-specified, locked evaluation. Continuous video-EEG from 21 monitored children (1315 h) formed the development cohort. A statistical-process-control warning method, evaluated under a written protocol, detected 44% of evaluable seizures at 0.48 false alarms per hour, no better than a random predictor (51%, p = 0.86); its statistic moved three times more with vigilance state than with seizure approach. We re-designed it as a state-conditioned, directional scheme on seven global EEG features, froze it with a hash-recorded configuration and time-stamped pre-specification, and estimated its performance by nested leave-one-patient-out cross-validation: 15 of 45 seizures (33%) at 0.47 false alarms per hour, above analytic (21%, p = 0.034) and permutation chance, but a predictor using only clock time, vigilance state and days since admission reproduced most of this, and the signal was confined to the last 30 min. Applied once to two validation cohorts (a second batch from the same unit and the public CHB-MIT database; 101 evaluable seizures), the frozen scheme detected 19 seizures (19%) at 0.60 false alarms per hour against 26% chance (p = 0.96); no secondary endpoint was met, and with the child as the unit of analysis no cohort was above chance. Scalp-EEG warning should be evaluated under pre-specified rules against structured chance levels; the frozen scheme and framework are offered as a reference.

title: Serum brain-derived tau distinguishes acute neurotrauma diagnoses
text: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) are two common forms of neurotrauma that can present with overlapping clinical features, complicating early diagnosis and management particularly in acute and mixed-trauma settings.1-3 Accurate and rapid biological differentiation remains an unmet need.4 We hypothesized that brain-derived tau (BD-tau), an ultrasensitive blood-based biomarker preferentially selective for tau protein originating from the brain, would distinguish TBI from SCI. In a multi-cohort assessment of 342 patients admitted to the neuro-intensive care unit (285 with TBI, 57 with SCI), and 22 controls, baseline serum BD-tau concentrations were markedly elevated in TBI compared with SCI, discriminating between the two populations with high accuracy (area under the curve [AUC]=0.91, 95%CI 0.87-0.96). In paired serum-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples, serum BD-tau significantly outperformed CSF BD-tau for injury-type discrimination (AUC=0.95, 95%CI 0.89-0.99 vs. 0.80, 95%CI 0.71-0.89). Baseline serum BD-tau also showed superior discrimination of TBI from SCI compared with established blood biomarkers of neurotrauma, including neurofilament light chain, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (AUC=0.82, 95%CI 0.76-0.88; vs. 0.53, 95%CI 0.43-0.63; 0.67, 95%CI 0.58-0.76; 0.71, 95%CI 0.64-0.79; all DeLong p<0.001). Longitudinally, serum BD-tau remained persistently elevated in TBI, but not SCI, for up to 144 hours post-injury, with distinct temporal trajectories between injury types. Together, these findings indicate that serum BD-tau enables rapid and minimally invasive differentiation of TBI from SCI and may support early clinical decision-making, triage, and enrollment into injury-specific therapeutic trials, highlighting the potential of circulating biomarkers to improve precision diagnostics in acute neurotrauma care.

title: Nurse-Led Heart Failure Education and Patient Outcomes: A Mixed-Methods Prospective Registry Study
text: BackgroundPatient understanding of heart failure (HF) self-care varies widely and is inconsistently associated with clinical outcomes. We examined knowledge acquisition and patient experiences related to structured HF education using a patient handbook. Methods and ResultsBetween April and December 2021, 56 patients hospitalized for acute HF (mean age 74 years, 35% women, 46% HFrEF) were enrolled from 176 screened patients at a single center. A 20-item knowledge assessment was administered before and after nurse led HF education and at first outpatient follow-up. Thirty patients met criteria for knowledge improvement ([≥]5-point increase or baseline [≥]15), while 25 did not. Knowledge gaps were most evident in exercise, medication effects, salt restriction, and recognition of exacerbating factors. Patients with knowledge improvement had higher post-education scores (16 vs. 12), sustained knowledge at follow-up, higher serum albumin levels, better inpatient dietary intake. One-year mortality and HF readmission did not differ. A nested qualitative analysis of four readmitted patients identified 94 codes grouped into 9 categories, highlighting personalized symptom recording, persistent self-management challenges despite handbook use, enhanced communication with healthcare professionals, reflection on future care, and a desire for earlier HF education. ConclusionsPatients who achieved higher HF knowledge scores demonstrated better nutritional status but similar one-year clinical outcomes. Qualitative findings underscore ongoing challenges in long-term HF self-care.

title: OVM-200, a recombinant overlapping peptide vaccine, breaks immune tolerance to survivin in patients with advanced solid tumours: a multicentre, open-label, dose-expansion, phase 1 study
text: Survivin (BIRC5) is broadly overexpressed in human cancers but, as a self-antigen, is subject to immune tolerance that limits spontaneous antitumour immunity. OVM-200 is a recombinant overlapping peptide vaccine spanning full-length survivin, with cathepsin S-cleavable linker sequences inserted between adjacent peptides to enhance antigen processing and presentation. OVM-200-100 was a multicentre, open-label phase 1 study conducted at 4 UK sites. The pooled 2,000-g cohort comprised 27 patients with advanced non-small cell lung, ovarian or prostate cancer, including 24 patients from phase 1b and 3 treated at this dose in phase 1a. OVM-200 was administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks for 3 initial vaccinations, with up to 8 additional doses in patients deriving clinical benefit. The primary endpoint was safety and tolerability, secondary endpoints included survivin-specific immunogenicity, and antitumour activity by RECIST v1.1 was exploratory. OVM-200-related adverse events were exclusively grade 1-2, with no treatment-related grade [≥]3 adverse events, dose-limiting toxicities, serious adverse events or deaths. A systematic literature analysis showed low spontaneous anti-survivin seroreactivity in patients with cancer. In our cohort, pretreatment tumours expressed survivin despite low baseline survivin-specific immunity. OVM-200 vaccination subsequently induced robust humoral and cellular responses, with median anti-survivin IgG titres increasing from 20 at baseline to a peak of 81,920 and median interferon-{gamma} ELISpot responses increasing from 16.7 to 504.6 spot-forming units per 10 PBMCs. Patients receiving [≥]4 vaccinations developed higher anti-survivin antibody titres and stronger T cell responses than those receiving fewer doses. Among 24 RECIST-evaluable patients, the best overall response was stable disease (SD) in 6 patients (25%). Patients with SD had significantly higher anti-survivin antibody titres than those with progressive disease (PD) (p=0.0418). OVM-200 was well tolerated and induced robust survivin-specific immunity, providing clinical evidence that it can break immune tolerance to self-antigen survivin and supporting further development. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05104515.

title: Retinopathy is more common, but age-related macular degeneration carries more visual impairment: a cross-sectional study of US adults graded from the same fundus photographs
text: BackgroundRetinopathy and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) are the most common findings on fundus photographs of older adults, yet their frequency, correlates and visual consequences have been estimated in separate samples. We compared them in a national survey that graded both from the same images. MethodsWe analyzed 5593 adults aged [≥]40 years in the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2005-2008 with photographs gradable for both conditions. We estimated survey-weighted prevalence, fitted identically specified logistic models for retinopathy (participants with diabetes) and AMD (full sample), and compared presenting visual impairment (better-eye acuity worse than 20/40) and self-rated vision across four groups: neither condition, retinopathy only, AMD only, and both. ResultsRetinopathy was more prevalent than AMD (9.54% [95% confidence interval (CI) 8.52-10.56] vs 6.52% [5.54-7.50]); AMD overtook it only from age 70 years. In participants with diabetes, retinopathy was associated with HbA1c (odds ratio [OR] 1.54 per percentage point; 1.33-1.78) and male sex (1.54; 1.10-2.17). AMD was associated with age (OR 1.09 per year; 1.07-1.11) and was less common in non-Hispanic Black adults (0.48; 0.33-0.71). Presenting impairment affected 4.91% of participants with neither condition, 7.09% with retinopathy only, 14.57% with AMD only and 26.15% with both. After age adjustment, impairment remained associated with AMD only (OR 2.23; 1.54-3.23) and both conditions (4.09; 2.28-7.37) but not retinopathy only (1.32; 0.91-1.90). Neither retinopathy nor diabetes was associated with AMD. Self-rated vision agreed poorly with measured impairment ({kappa} = 0.15): only 12% of impaired participants rated their vision poor or very poor. ConclusionsRetinopathy is the more frequent retinal finding in US adults aged [≥]40 years, but AMD carries more of the measured visual impairment, independently of age. Grading diabetic screening photographs for AMD, and measuring acuity rather than asking about vision, would reach more people who see poorly.

title: Applications of Fairness Training in Artificial Intelligence to Ophthalmic Disease Diagnosis using External Eye Photographs
text: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and glaucoma are leading causes of preventable blindness, yet whether external eye photographs carry phenotypic information about posterior segment disease remains unclear, and methods to mitigate demographic disparities in such models are largely unexplored. We developed and evaluated deep learning and vision-language models for binary classification of vision-threatening DR (VTDR), advanced AMD, and glaucoma using 40,687 external eye photographs from 9,878 patients at Massachusetts Eye and Ear. Convolutional networks (WResNet, EfficientNet), a vision transformer (ViT), and a finetuned vision-language model (LLaVA) were assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with fairness across sex, race, and ethnicity quantified by the equity-scaled AUC (ES-AUC). Five fairness-training strategies were applied to the best models. LLaVA achieved the highest baseline AUC for VTDR (85{middle dot}4%, comparable to ViT 82{middle dot}6%); advanced AMD was similar across architectures (EfficientNet 86{middle dot}3%; LLaVA 84{middle dot}8%; ViT 84{middle dot}7%), whereas glaucoma was substantially worse (67-74%). Fairness training improved VTDR and AMD AUCs to 86{middle dot}3% and 85{middle dot}9% while partially mitigating demographic disparities. In summary, although AI models that rely on external eye photography to detect posterior segment disease may not yet be suitable for clinical deployment, the fairness methods demonstrated in this proof-of-concept study could be applied to other AI systems to decrease performance disparities and potentially improve model performance.

title: Impact of DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity in Southeast Asia: A modelling study in Thailand
text: Dengue virus (DENV) is endemic across Southeast Asia (SEA), where a large proportion of adults have been infected. Zika virus (ZIKV) has circulated in the region for decades but the extent of transmission remains unclear. Prior infection with one virus can protect against or enhance infection with the other, but the population-level consequences are unknown. We developed an age-structured DENV-ZIKV model with nine cross-reactivity assumptions combining cross-protection and subsequent enhancement, and simulated sustained co-circulation under changing Thai demography. Through cross-reactivity, DENV strongly shaped ZIKV transmission, whereas ZIKV had little effect on DENV transmission. Under cross-protection, ZIKV transmission occurred as infrequent outbreaks without changes in long-term ZIKV burden. When prior DENV infection enhanced both ZIKV infection and symptomatic risk, this burden roughly doubled. Population ageing raised the mean age of DENV and ZIKV cases by over 20 years, more than cross-reactivity did. Simulated ZIKV case ages were closer to those reported in Thailand in 2019-2023 under enhancement of ZIKV infection and symptoms. Over half of individuals aged 15-49 years remained ZIKV-naive under all assumptions, leaving many pregnancies at risk of congenital Zika syndrome. Interpreting ZIKV case counts in SEA requires joint consideration of cross-reactivity, demographic change and case detection.

title: Saturation genome editing of BRCA1 across cell types improves interpretation of variant pathogenicity
text: Abstract Germline pathogenic BRCA1 variants predispose women to breast and ovarian cancer. Despite accumulation of functional evidence, over half of reported single-nucleotide variants in BRCA1 lack a definitive clinical interpretation. Furthermore, the consistency of variant effects across cell types remains largely unexplored. Here we performed saturation genome editing (SGE) of BRCA1 in HAP1 cells to score 4,113 previously unassayed variants. Additionally, we developed an SGE assay in human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs), allowing comparison of effects across cell lines, drug treatments and genetic backgrounds. We identified 538 variants impacting gene function through distinct mechanisms. HAP1 function scores discriminate between known pathogenic and benign variants with near-perfect accuracy. Intriguingly, however, nearly half of HAP1 loss-of-function variants scored neutrally in HMECs. We show that discordantly scored variants are hypomorphic and confer intermediate cancer risk. Overall, this work demonstrates how performing SGE across cell models improves the functional interpretation of rare variants.

title: Effects of calreticulin mutations on HLA class I expression in myeloproliferative neoplasms
text: Essential thrombocythemia (ET) and myelofibrosis (MF) are myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) that can result from heterozygous or homozygous mutations in the calreticulin (CRT) gene (CALR). Mutant CRT binds to the thrombopoietin receptor to induce signaling that drives ET and MF. CRT is also a chaperone for the assembly of the highly polymorphic human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I molecules. The effects of heterozygous versus homozygous MPN CALR mutations on the expression of HLA class I variants are unknown. To assess mutant CRT-induced changes to HLA class I expression, we generated CRISPR-based mutant CALR knock-in cell lines and CALR-knockout cell lines reconstituted with wild-type or MPN mutant CALR and also undertook measurements in MPN patient platelets and monocytes. Collectively, our findings indicate that heterozygous CALR mutations preserve HLA class I surface expression, whereas full loss of wild-type CRT results in marked, allele-dependent reductions in HLA class I expression, which are rescued by wild-type CRT but not MPN mutants. Reduced expression of CRT-dependent HLA class I in cells lacking a functional CRT induces natural killer (NK) cell activation. These studies identify specific HLA class I alleles and homozygous CALR mutations as prerequisites for low HLA class I expression in MPN.

title: Linear scaling reveals low-dimensional structure in observable microbial dynamics
text: Microbial communities often exhibit apparently complex dynamics driven by myriad interactions among community members and with their environments. Yet, practical modeling and control are often based on a limited number of observables, raising fundamental questions: are these observed dynamics low-dimensional? If so, how does the low dimensionality enable predictions with limited information? Here, we report an emergent simplicity that the temporal dynamics of observable microbial populations can be captured by low-dimensional representations. Using variational autoencoders, we define a critical latent dimension ( E c ) that operationally quantifies the smallest latent dimension required for high-fidelity reconstruction of observable microbial dynamics under a specified criterion. Despite the complexity of unobserved background dynamics, we find E c to be drastically lower than the community’s apparent degrees of freedom. E c scales linearly with the number of observables, providing an empirical principle for determining representation complexity. This principle holds across simulations of pairwise interacting communities, consumer–resource dynamics, spatially distributed microbial patches, and plasmid transfer, experiments with engineered and environment-derived communities, and human microbiomes. Our findings establish a scaling law for microbial community dynamics and demonstrate that low-dimensional representations of observable dynamics retain information useful for selected prediction tasks without direct measurement of the complete community.

title: Phototropin-mediated blue light signaling orients the asymmetry of Marchantia polymorpha spores
text: Multicellular organisms produced by sexual reproduction develop from single cells, and the asymmetry of these cells can define the orientation of the earliest developmental axes. The haploid multicellular stage of the plant, Marchantia polymorpha, develops from a single cell—the spore—that divides asymmetrically, producing an apical germ cell that generates the plant body and a smaller basal cell that differentiates as an anchoring germ rhizoid cell. We show that the orientation of this asymmetric cell division is controlled by an external environmental cue—blue light—that is perceived by the photoreceptor phototropin. This process requires the NCH1 (NRL PROTEIN FOR CHLOROPLAST MOVEMENT 1) protein for downstream signaling. Together, these findings define core elements of the mechanism by which a directional environmental signal orients cell division, which, in turn, orients the first axis of symmetry.

title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA
Input-specific deployment of the active zone scaffold RIM tunes synaptic release probability and plasticity
text: The multidomain scaffold RIM (Rab3-interacting molecule) is widely viewed as a broadly required organizer of the presynaptic active zone, clustering voltage-gated Ca 2+ (Ca v 2) channels, priming synaptic vesicles, and supporting neurotransmitter release. Whether this reliance is uniform across synapses with distinct release probabilities, however, has been difficult to resolve at convergent inputs. Here, using neurotoxin-based silencing to isolate transmission at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction, we show that the requirement for RIM is highly input-specific: RIM is essential to empower transmission at a high–release probability phasic synapse, yet is largely dispensable at a neighboring low–release probability tonic synapse. This specificity extends to plasticity: RIM is required for acute homeostatic potentiation at the phasic input, but not for chronic potentiation at the tonic input. Super-resolution imaging reveals that RIM is positioned closer to Ca v 2 channels at phasic synapses and, during acute plasticity, coordinates their nanoscale reorganization to drive the rapid expansion of the readily releasable pool.

title: The single Cryptosporidium rhoptry sequentially drives invasion and host-parasite interface formation
text: The apicomplexan parasite Cryptosporidium is a leading cause of diarrheal disease in young children. Within the intestinal epithelium, Cryptosporidium establishes a unique intracellular niche in the apical brush border of enterocytes. A structurally complex interface between host and parasite acts as a holdfast and enables protein and metabolite transport. How the parasite invades its host cell and builds the interface is poorly understood. Here, we reveal parasite invasion with high temporal and spatial resolution using rigorous molecular markers. We find that sequential discharge of specialized secretory organelles anchors the parasite within the host prior to internalization. The single Cryptosporidium rhoptry persists beyond its initial pre-invasion discharge, acting as a conduit for the secretion of multiple waves of effector proteins. Ultimately, the rhoptry membrane gives rise to the feeder organelle that separates host from parasite cytoplasm. These findings lead us to propose a mechanistic model of Cryptosporidium invasion and intracellular parasitism.

title: Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart
text: Abstract Disruptions to leading-strand synthesis impair and stall replication forks because DNA synthesis by the leading-strand polymerase, Pol ε, is essential for optimal template unwinding by the replicative CMG (CDC45–MCM–GINS) helicase 1,2 . Failure to efficiently restart and/or protect stalled replication forks is a major source of genomic instability 3–6 . Stalled forks can be restarted by a variety of mechanisms, including repriming downstream of the impediment 4 . In human cells, the primase–polymerase PRIMPOL promotes fork progression during replication stress 7–10 , but how its activity is coordinated by the replisome is unresolved. Here, by reconstituting replication fork stalling and restart with purified human proteins, we show that the CMG helicase directs PRIMPOL for efficient replication fork restart. Unexpectedly, the interaction between PRIMPOL and replication protein A 9,11 is not critical for fork restart in this system. We show that PRIMPOL binds directly to CMG, and a cryo-electron microscopy structure illustrates how this targets PRIMPOL specifically for leading-strand priming to minimize the size of post-replicative gaps. Ablating the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction abolishes fork restart in vitro and PRIMPOL-dependent DNA damage tolerance in human cells. Our work establishes PRIMPOL as an integrated component of the human replisome dedicated to leading-strand priming.

title: Understanding the control of perpetual flowering and continuous runnering in strawberry
text: Consumer demand for year-round strawberry fruit has increased the need to extend the cropping season. Perpetual flowering cultivars, which produce fruit continuously throughout the growing season, offer a promising solution. However, these cultivars typically exhibit reduced runner production, due to a genetic trade-off between flowering and runnering, presenting challenges for propagation and breeding efforts. Additionally, limited understanding of the mechanisms controlling these traits in the cultivated strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) has hindered the application of advanced breeding or crop improvement tools. This PhD work aimed to better understand the genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying perpetual flowering and continuous runnering in strawberry, to contribute to the development of perpetual flowering cultivars with extended fruiting periods and improved propagation potential. In this thesis the control of perpetual flowering was explored by functionally studying key f lowering genes TFL1 and FT1 in F. x ananassa seasonal flowering cultivar ‘Malling Centenary’ and perpetual flowering cultivar ‘Calypso’ using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing and phenotyping. FaTFL1 mutant lines exhibited early flowering and reduced runner production under long day conditions, validating its role as a floral repressor and demonstrating the regulatory link between these traits. FaFT1 mutant lines presented alteration in floral and fruit morphology suggesting its role in floral development. Furthermore, the genetic regulation of the trade-off between flowering and runnering was studied through genotyping-by-sequencing based QTL mapping using a woodland strawberry (Fragaria vesca) F₂ mapping population developed from a cross between an ecotype from Spain with continuous runnering habit and an accession from Iceland with a “standard” runnering habit. Two additive QTLs associated with continuous runnering were identified using interval mapping. The most significant QTL was narrowed and validated using cleave amplified polymorphic sequences (CAPS) for genotyping in a second validation population. Candidate genes associated with dormancy and axillary bud outgrowth were identified in both QTLs. Gene expression analysis showed a significant downregulation of two candidate genes in continuous runnering individuals supporting their role in the control of this trait. Finally, the functional role of the two main candidate genes for continuous runnering was explored through CRISPR/Cas9 targeted mutagenesis in F. vesca. Two mutant lines for one of the main candidate genes were obtained, however the editing efficiency was very low and consequently this part of the study was not pursued to completion. The work developed within this thesis provides valuable insight into the mechanisms controlling perpetual flowering and the developmental trade-off between generative and vegetative reproduction that could inform future crop improvement strategies.

title: Balancing Root-Zone Oxygenation and Rhizosphere Stability: The Impact of Aeration and Hypoxia on Hydroponic Plant Growth
text: As the global population and food demand continue to increase, growers must look to innovative and sustainable methods for plant cultivation. Hydroponics is a popular method of sustainable plant cultivation where plant roots are suspended over a liquid nutrient solution. Hydroponics uses less water compared to traditional agriculture because there is no evaporation or solution runoff. It also maximizes land use, requires fewer pesticides and herbicides, and enables year-round cultivation in controlled environments. However, indoor hydroponic systems rely on artificial lighting, which has higher energy costs than traditional farming methods. Optimizing growing conditions is therefore critical to ensure long-term economic and environmental sustainability. Oxygen, which plants require for cellular respiration, is taken up by plant roots and can quickly become limited in hydroponic solutions due to low solubility and rapid uptake. This research ultimately aims to explore which plants can tolerate low oxygen in hydroponic solutions and explores a new method for quantifying low oxygen stress experienced by plants over a growing period. The best practices for supplying oxygen to roots is also examined by manipulating aeration-induced agitation to understand its impact on plant nutrient uptake and growth.

title: TRIB2 supports a high glycolytic phenotype in melanoma cells
text: Background Metabolic adaptation is a crucial driver of melanoma progression and therapy resistance. The pseudokinase Tribbles homolog 2 (TRIB2) is highly expressed in melanoma and is associated with poor outcomes and treatment resistance. However, its specific role in the metabolic profile of melanoma cells remained unexplored. This study aimed to investigate the impact of TRIB2 on cellular metabolism, and its role in metabolic adaptation in melanoma. Materials and methods The study used UACC-62 human melanoma cells with high endogenous TRIB2 expression and isogenic TRIB2-knockout (KO) clones generated via CRISPR-Cas9. Cell proliferation was assessed using trypan blue exclusion assays under treatment with metabolic drugs including 2-deoxyglucose (2-DG), and dichloroacetate (DCA). Metabolic phenotypes were evaluated by measuring glucose consumption, lactate production, and real-time analysis of glycolytic flux (ECAR) and mitochondrial respiration (OCR) using a Seahorse bioanalyzer. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were measured by dihydroethidium (DHE) fluorescence. Gene expression was analyzed by qPCR, and protein levels were determined by western blot. Citrate synthase activity was measured enzymatically. Results TRIB2-KO cells exhibited significantly reduced basal proliferation compared with wild-type (WT) cells. KO cells were also more sensitive to the glycolytic inhibitor 2-DG. Conversely, WT cells were more susceptible to DCA treatment. Metabolic analyses confirmed that TRIB2-KO cells had lower glucose consumption, lactate production, and glycolytic capacity than WT cells. Mitochondrial respiratory function and the protein levels of key respiratory complexes were unchanged. Despite the reduction in glycolytic activity, TRIB2 depletion did not increase mitochondrial respiratory capacity and was associated with elevated basal intracellular superoxide levels. Among the molecular alterations identified, PDK4 was consistently reduced at both the mRNA and protein levels, whereas citrate synthase activity was significantly decreased despite preserved protein abundance, indicating selective alterations in mitochondrial carbon metabolism. Conclusions TRIB2 expression promotes a glycolytic phenotype and contributes to metabolic adaptation in melanoma. Loss of TRIB2 does not induce a metabolic shift towards oxidative phosphorylation but instead results in broader metabolic rewiring characterized by reduced glycolysis together with selective alterations in mitochondrial carbon metabolism. These findings identify the TRIB2–PDK4 axis as a previously unrecognized component of metabolic regulation in melanoma and provide a rationale for further investigating its therapeutic potential.

title: Cellular morphology emerges from polygenic, distributed transcriptional variation
text: Summary Height and disease risk are canonical polygenic traits, but whether an analogous architecture governs cellular phenotypes remains unclear. Here, we show that cellular morphology behaves as a polygenic systems phenotype by integrating cross-modal modeling, perturbation profiling, and human genetic variation. An adversarially aligned autoencoder trained on four perturbation datasets predicted morphology from gene expression and generalized without retraining to matched RNA-seq and Cell Painting profiles from 100 genetically diverse iPSC donors. Seventeen morphological features were strongly predicted, particularly those capturing organelle distribution and cytoskeletal architecture. Predictive signal was broadly distributed across genes, with weak individual gene–morphology correlations. Independent CRISPR perturbations supported model-prioritized genes including TIAM1 , RAB31 , and ABCC5 , while genetic analyses identified variant–gene–morphology associations involving PDHX , SLC11A2 , and MAPKAPK5 . These findings extend polygenic models of complex traits to cellular architecture and provide a framework for interpreting cross-modal prediction in functional genomics. Highlights Cellular morphology is encoded by broadly distributed transcriptional variation Transcriptome-to-morphology relationships generalize from perturbations to human donors CRISPR perturbations validate molecular anchors within distributed transcriptional programs Human genetic variation links regulatory genes to mitochondrial and cellular architecture

title: Global environmental genomics reveals vast uncultivated protist diversity and taxonomic blind spots
text: Protists, defined as eukaryotes distinct from plants, animals and fungi, comprise much of eukaryotic phylogenetic diversity and perform key ecological functions, yet most lineages remain uncultivated and poorly represented in reference databases. Amplicon-based 18S rRNA gene surveys have transformed protist ecology, but primer bias, PCR bias and marker length can limit recovery of divergent lineages. Here, we conduct a cultivation-independent, rDNA operon-centered survey of over 30,000 assembled metagenomes, protist single-cell genomes and 21 long-amplicon datasets spanning marine, freshwater and soil-associated environments. We recover 157,956 long 18S rRNA gene sequences (≥800 bp), which together with reference sequences cluster into 103,338 OTUs at 97% identity and 24,438 OTUs at 85% identity. After excluding non-protist groups and singletons, 81% of the remaining 9543 protist 85%-OTUs consist exclusively of environmental sequences with no described representative. A concatenated 18S-28S rRNA framework reveals strong underrepresentation of Amoebozoa, Discoba, and Rhizaria in current references and identifies 13 candidate deeply divergent lineages with little or no database representation, some of which we link to partial genomes recovered by single-cell genomics. We further characterize their ecosystem distributions and predict associations with bacteria and other eukaryotes. This study provides a global, cultivation-independent resource for targeted sampling and downstream genomic, ecological and experimental characterization. In this study, the authors analyze over 30,000 assembled metagenomes across ecosystems to uncover hidden protist diversity, including major novel uncultivated lineages, and reveal their habitats and connections to other microbes.

title: In situ profiling of plasma cell clonality with image-based single-cell transcriptomics
text: Image-based single-cell transcriptomics can identify diverse cell types in intact tissues. However, in adaptive immunity, V(D)J recombination generates unique immune receptors in cells of the same type, leading to important functional variation that is not yet defined by these methods. Here we introduce B cell receptor multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (BCR-MERFISH), which measures plasma cell clonality based on V gene usage in combination with transcriptome profiling. We demonstrate that BCR-MERFISH accurately identifies V gene usage in cell culture and in mice with restricted or native plasma cell diversity. We then use BCR-MERFISH to elucidate the microbiota-dependent changes in plasma cell abundance, clonal diversity, and public clonotype usage in the mouse gut and the non-uniform distribution of plasma cell clones along the mouse ileum. Given that tissue context is an essential modulator of plasma cell dynamics, we anticipate that BCR-MERFISH may offer new insights into a wide range of immunological questions.

title: Neural integration of acoustic statistics enables mice to detect acoustic targets in noise
text: Sound detection amidst noise presents an important challenge in audition. Many naturally occurring sounds (rain, wind) can be described and predicted only statistically, so-called sound textures. Previous research has demonstrated the human ability to leverage this statistical predictability for sound recognition, but the neural mechanisms remain elusive. We trained mice to detect vocalizations embedded in sound textures with different statistical predictability, while recording and optogenetically modulating the neural activity in the auditory cortex. Mice showed improved performance and neural encoding if they could sample the statistics longer per trial. Textures with more exploitable structure, specifically higher cross-frequency correlations improved behavioral performance as well as neural representation of vocalizations. Activating parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons had an asymmetric effect depending on the acoustic context, improving detection and neural encoding of vocalizations for low correlations, and impoverishing them for high cross-frequency correlations. In summary, mice exploit stimulus statistics to improve sound detection in naturalistic background noise, reflected in behavioral performance and neural activity, relying on PV interneurons for temporal integration.

Host infection selects for sRNA variants that drive bacterial social cheating
text: Single-nucleotide mutations in regulatory small RNAs (sRNAs) represent a largely unexplored route to social cheating during bacterial infection. Here we show that arcZ , encoding a conserved Hfq-dependent sRNA in the plant pathogen Dickeya solani , undergoes recurrent single-nucleotide mutations during potato tuber infection. Five distinct arcZ alleles define a graded series of ArcZ functional impairment in which antifungal and protease activities are progressively reduced while virulence is compromised only in a subset of alleles. All five variants gain a fitness advantage exclusively during coinfection with wild-type arcZ 1 cells. This advantage is strongest when variants are rare and declines as cheater frequency increases, ultimately correlating with reduced total bacterial productivity, the canonical signature of social cheating and a tragedy of the commons. No fitness benefit is detected in vitro . Transcriptomic profiling of five arcZ variants identifies a conserved core of 186 downregulated genes enriched in secreted and diffusible functions. Systematic genetic dissection, supported by quantitative proteomics, establishes BudAB-dependent limitation of tissue acidification as the dominant cooperative public good exploited during infection. Wild-type arcZ 1 cells divert pyruvate flux toward acetoin via the BudAB pathway, maintaining a less acidic tissue environment that sustains disease progression; arcZ variants, which show reduced expression of this pathway, benefit from the less acidic environment maintained by wild-type cells without contributing to it. These results establish pleiotropic regulatory sRNAs as a previously unrecognized class of mutational targets for the emergence of social cheaters during host infection.

title: scMomer: a pretraining framework for inferring robust cellular representations from single-cell transcriptomes
text: Abstract Foundation models offer new opportunities to capture cellular behavior from large-scale single-cell data. However, their development has been greatly constrained due to the limited availability of multi-omics profiles. Consequently, most models are designed for a single modality (e.g. scRNA-seq, or scATAC-seq, etc.), restricting their ability to capture the diversity of heterogeneous biological systems. Here, we introduce scMomer, a modality-aware pretraining framework designed for multi-modal representation learning under missing modality conditions. scMomer adopts a three-stage pretraining strategy that learns unimodal cell representations, models joint representations from multi-omics data, and distills multi-modal knowledge to enable multi-omics-like representations from unimodal input. Its modality-specific architecture and three-stage pretraining strategy enable effective learning under missing modality conditions and help capture cellular heterogeneity. Through extensive experiments, scMomer generates biologically meaningful embeddings and outperforms state-of-the-art unimodal approaches across diverse gene-level and cell-level downstream tasks, including cross-modality translation, gene function prediction, cell annotation, drug response prediction, and perturbation prediction. Overall, these results demonstrate that scMomer serves as a robust, generalizable, and scalable foundation for single-cell multi-modal analysis under missing modality conditions.

title: Swimming motility and type IV pili modulate phagocytosis by shaping physical interactions between Pseudomonas aeruginosa and macrophages
text: During chronic lung infections, Pseudomonas aeruginosa diversifies under selection from antibiotics, metabolic constraints, and host defenses. Macrophages are key sentinels of the innate immune system and play a central role in clearing airway pathogens. Yet, how they process heterogeneous bacterial populations remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how P. aeruginosa evades phagocytosis under conditions that resemble chronic infection. We use an attenuated mutant lacking a functional type III secretion system (T3SS), which reduces macrophage killing, allowing us to isolate determinants of bacterial susceptibility to phagocytosis. Using transposon insertion sequencing (Tn-seq), we identify bacterial fitness factors under phagocytic selection. Our screen reveals that disruption of genes involved in swimming and twitching motility reduces uptake by macrophages. We find that defects in flagellar and type IV pili (T4P) function interfere with the physical interactions between bacteria and macrophages. Live-cell imaging shows that motility-deficient bacteria exhibit reduced surface accumulation and unstable attachment to macrophages, limiting their internalization. Clinical isolates with reduced swimming or twitching motility display similarly impaired uptake. We also test the influence of bacterial motility on macrophage survival by restoring T3SS activity in flagellar and T4P mutants. In the PAO1 background, most motility mutants retained the ability to kill macrophages indicating that cytotoxicity dominates bacteria-macrophage competition in the presence of a functional T3SS. However, the non-flagellated, hyper-piliated Δ fliC Δ pilT mutant showed a surprisingly attenuated killing, which may reflect reduced bacterial encounters with macrophages, impaired engagement of cytotoxic effectors, or both. Together, our results show that swimming motility and type IV pili shape physical interactions between P. aeruginosa and macrophages, thereby influencing phagocytic uptake.

title: Prenatal exposure to maternal stress drives neurodevelopmental disruptions in the fetal hypothalamus
text: The hypothalamus plays a central role in integrating physiological stressors to maintain homeostasis, yet how fetal neurodevelopment in the hypothalamus is shaped by intrauterine maternal stress exposure remains understudied. This is especially true in the context of sex-divergent mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), which are increasingly being linked to perturbation of the intrauterine environment. Herein, we utilize a mouse model of prenatal maternal cold stress exposure to study the impacts on neural stem and progenitor cell (NSPC) developmental programs in the fetal hypothalamus. Pregnant mice were exposed to cold stress from embryonic day 11.5 (E11.5) to E15.5 and fetal hypothalamic NSPCs from both male and female embryos were analyzed. Exposure to maternal stress altered fetal hypothalamic neurodevelopment, increasing TUJ1+ neuron number in males, while enhancing neuronal dendritic arborization in females. To define underlying molecular changes, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing of hypothalamic NSPCs. Interestingly, we identified distinct baseline transcriptional profiles between male and female NSPCs. In females, maternal stress upregulated pathways related to GABAergic differentiation and neuronal projection morphogenesis, with these alterations being maintained across more differentiated neuronal populations. Ligand-receptor analysis further indicated that maternal stress alters cell-cell communication within NSPCs, predominantly in females. Together, these findings demonstrate that prenatal maternal stress alters hypothalamic NSPC developmental programs in both males and females, and suggest that disrupted intercellular signaling may contribute to underlying sex differences in social behaviors previously reported for this model (Rosin et al., 2021). Significance statement Prenatal stress is a known risk factor for NDDs, but how it shapes early brain development in each sex remains understudied. Here, we examined how maternal stress influences NSPCs in the hypothalamus, a brain region critical for regulating the stress response and homeostasis. Using mice as a model system, we found that maternal stress alters how fetal NSPCs develop into neurons. Molecular analyses demonstrate that maternal stress alters female NSPCs transcriptional programs and cell-to-cell communication. This work advances our understanding of how prenatal maternal stress drives sex differences in neurodevelopmental programming and may help to begin to explain sex-biased vulnerabilities to NDDs.

title: Spatially distinct fibroblasts synergize to mainatain intestinal stem cells
text: This repository contains single-cell transcriptomic metadata, and R analysis code for intestinal fibroblast and epithelial populations. It covers five datasets: Smart-seq2 profiling of intestinal fibroblasts. 10X profiling of Mgp+ fibroblasts. 10X profiling of APCmin adenoma epithelial cells and fibroblasts, including normal reference populations. 10X profiling of enriched intestinal stem cell-associated fibroblasts (ISC-Fb). Smart-seq2 profiling of regenerated ISC-Fb alongside reference fibroblasts (the first dataset).

title: Spatially staged SAR features immune microdomains
text: Systemic acquired resistance (SAR) enables uninfected plant tissues to acquire enhanced defensive capacity after local pathogen perception, yet how long-distance immune information is spatially interpreted in distal organs remains poorly understood. Here, we induced effector-triggered immunity (ETI)-associated SAR in Arabidopsis thaliana by local infection with Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000 carrying avrRPM1 and integrated temporal bulk RNA-seq, single-nucleus RNA-seq, Stereo-seq spatial transcriptomics, and multiplex RNA in situ hybridization to resolve systemic immune activation across time, cell identity, and anatomical space. We show that distal systemic immunity is not initiated as a uniform whole-leaf response. Instead, single-nucleus analysis identifies a distinct mesophyll cell substate in distal leaves at 24 hours post local infection, characterized by the coordinated induction of immune receptors, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress/protein-folding machinery, and a jasmonic acid (JA) response signature. Pseudotime trajectory analysis positions this early immune-competent mesophyll state prior to broader SARD1/CBP60g-associated salicylic acid (SA) and N-hydroxypipecolic acid (NHP) defense amplification. Spatially, Stereo-seq and high-resolution multiplex RNA in situ hybridization reveal that this early immune program is selectively confined to multicellular vascular-proximal microdomains surrounding lateral veins. Notably, activation of prominent vascular-proximal markers is detectable in rare perivascular cells as early as 4 hours post-infection. Together, these findings support a spatially staged model of ETI-induced SAR, wherein systemic signals are initially decoded in localized vascular-proximal microdomains along lateral veins before being relayed into broader, tissue-wide SA/NHP defense programs.

title: CRC TMA Dataset to: Bias Identification and Quantification in Image-based Spatial Transcriptomics
text: CosMx 1,000-plex spatial transcriptomics of a colorectal cancer TMA & Post-imaging H&E Single-cell resolution imaging-based spatial transcriptomics of a tissue microarray comprising 120 cores from 13 patients with colorectal cancer and distant organ metastasis. The archive is a SpatialData (v0.2.6) zarr store containing raw, unfiltered counts for 108,483 cells across 1,207 features (1,000 target genes, 197 system control probes, 10 negative probes), together with per-cell segmentation masks, cell boundary polygons, fluorescence images for all 121 fields of view, and per-cell morphology, quality-control and spatial metadata in micrometres.

title: Het opbouwen van ruimtelijke en single-cell transcriptomische atlassen om astrocytenheterogeniteit en -functie in gezondheid en ziekte te ontrafelen
text: Astrocytes comprise one of the major classes of glial cells in the mammalian brain and are essential for central nervous system (CNS) development and function. These cells contribute to diverse processes, including synapse formation, maintenance of synaptic homeostasis through the control of extracellular K+ levels and neurotransmitter clearance, modulation of synaptic transmission, formation and maintenance of the blood-brain barrier, control of cerebral blood flow, and immune responses. Yet,compared with their neuronal counterparts, their diversity and functional specialization remain incompletely understood. Increasing evidence supports the existence of a high degree of astrocyte heterogeneity throughout the CNS, both across and within brain regions, during development, and in injury and disease contexts. Importantly, recent advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics (ST) now enable the exploration of astrocyte heterogeneity with unprecedented depth and resolution. Using state-of-the-art single-cell and ST approaches, the overall aim of this project is to uncover different aspects of astrocyte diversity, from molecular heterogeneity in the healthy mouse brain across development and adulthood to heterogenous astrocyte responses in disease. Recent single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing studies have profiled millions of cells across the mouse brain. However, substantial technical differences between these methods have resulted in the identification of varying numbers of astrocyte populations and the use of distinct nomenclatures, making the alignment of findings across studies challenging. To address this, I established a unified atlas of adult mouse astrocytes by harmonizing multiple single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets into a unified reference framework. This work identified seven major populations and 37 subpopulations that vary in abundance across distinct brain regions and are characterized by specific molecular gene signatures. These findings provide a foundation for the future development of tools to target defined astrocyte populations and manipulate their function. This project further demonstrates how ST can be used to characterize the expression of particularly challenging transcripts, such as clustered protocadherins (cPcdh), which share highly similar sequences. Using a highly sensitive ST approach with subcellular resolution, I generated an atlas of postnatal mouse visual cortical development that enabled the detection of distinct cPcdh transcripts. Particularly, I show that α-cPcdhs are mainly enriched in neurons, whereas γ-cPcdhs are enriched in both neurons and astrocytes, with population-specific enrichment across astrocyte subpopulations. These findings support the idea that different populations of astrocytes may not equally participate in synapse formation and function, with potential implications for neurodevelopmental conditions such as Trisomy 21. Finally, this project extends the study of astrocyte molecular heterogeneity to human disease by generating single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic atlases of the substantia nigra pars compacta from donors with Parkinson's disease (PD) and control donors. Neurodegenerative conditions such as PD have traditionally been considered primary neuronal disorders. However, the contribution of non-neuronal populations in disease pathogenesis and progression remains poorly understood and is increasingly being recognized. Using single-nucleus and ST, I assessed cell-type-specific dysfunction in PD and found that PD is a multicellular disorder. These results support the view that glial cells, including astrocytes, adopt heterogenous molecular states that likely reflect different degrees of vulnerability or resilience in relation to the surrounding diseased environment. Taken together, the work presented in this project provides a multi-scale, spatially resolved view of astrocyte biology, establishing new frameworks to interpret astrocyt

title: SynthStrategy: Extracting and Formalizing Latent Strategic Insights from LLMs in Organic Chemistry
text: Modern computer-assisted synthesis planning (CASP) systems show promise at generating chemically valid reaction steps but struggle to incorporate strategic considerations such as convergent assembly, protecting-group minimization, and optimal ring-forming sequences. We introduce a methodology that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to distill synthetic knowledge into code. Our system analyzes synthesis routes and translates strategic principles into executable Python functions representing diverse strategic and tactical rules, such as strategic functional group interconversions, protecting strategies and ring construction features. We validate the use of LLM-as-a-judge in this domain, demonstrating their efficacy in evaluating synthesis-specific code generation. By formalizing this knowledge as verifiable code rather than simple heuristics, we create testable, interpretable representations of synthetic strategy. We release the complete codebase and the USPTO-ST data set─synthesis routes annotated with strategic tags. This framework unlocks a novel capability for CASP: natural language-based route retrieval, achieving 74.5% Top-3 accuracy on our benchmark. We further validate our library through temporal analysis of historical trends and chemically intuitive route clustering that offers more granular partitioning than common previous methods. This work bridges the tactical-strategic divide in CASP, enabling specification, search, and evaluation of routes by strategic criteria rather than structure alone.

title: Hyperglycemia promotes maladaptive Dectin-1 signaling and impairs skin antifungal host defense
text: ABSTRACT People with chronic hyperglycemia are more susceptible to fungal skin infections, yet the mechanisms behind worse clinical outcomes remain unclear. Using both in vivo and in vitro models, we explored how hyperglycemia affects skin antifungal defenses. Hyperglycemic mice showed increased susceptibility to Candida albicans skin infections, with larger lesions and higher fungal loads at all time points tested. Histology revealed larger abscesses, more extensive myeloid cell infiltration, and poorer control of fungal invasion, all associated with increased chemoattractant production on day 1 post-infection. Glucose reduction with the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist liraglutide reduced lesion size and fungal burden in infected diabetic mice, linking metabolic control to the restoration of innate immune function. Phagocytes and keratinocytes exposed to high glucose exhibited inhibited fungal ingestion. RNA-seq analysis of C. albicans -infected dermal macrophages cultured under high-glucose conditions showed enrichment of genes related to the C-type lectin receptor pathway, including Clec7a (Dectin-1), and also revealed inhibition of downstream signaling pathways required for effective phagocytosis. Pharmacologic blockade or genetic deletion of Dectin-1 restored fungal uptake under high-glucose conditions and improved host defense in vivo . Dectin-1 signaling in hyperglycemia increased prostaglandin E 2 (PGE 2 ) production along with increased abundance of microsomal prostaglandin E synthase-1 (mPGES-1). Inhibition of PGE 2 synthesis rescued deficient phagocytic function. These findings identify maladaptive innate immune sensing as a key mechanism underlying susceptibility to fungal infection in diabetes and reveal how metabolic stress converts antifungal recognition pathways into drivers of inflammatory dysfunction.

title: Equivariant Interatomic Potentials without Tensor Products
text: Abstract Foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials have emerged as powerful tools for atomistic simulations, promising near first-principles accuracy across diverse chemical spaces at a fraction of the cost of quantum-mechanical calculations. However, the most accurate equivariant architectures rely on Clebsch–Gordan tensor products whose computational cost scales steeply with angular resolution, creating a trade-off between model expressiveness and inference speed that ultimately limits practical applications. Here we introduce Geodite, an equivariant message-passing architecture that replaces tensor products while incorporating physical priors to ensure smooth, well-behaved potential energy surfaces. Trained on the Materials Project trajectories dataset of inorganic crystals, Geodite-MP achieves accuracy competitive with leading methods on benchmarks for materials stability prediction, thermal conductivity, phonon-derived properties, and nanosecond-scale molecular dynamics, while running 3–5× faster than models performing similarly. By combining predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, and physicality, Geodite enables faster large-scale atomistic simulations and high-throughput screening that would otherwise be computationally prohibitive.

title: LoRA-BERT: a natural language processing model for robust and accurate prediction of long non-coding RNAs
text: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are key regulators in many biological processes. While they share some sequence features with messenger RNAs (mRNAs), lncRNAs have distinct functions, opening new research opportunities. Recent advances in next-generation sequencing have made it easier to detect lncRNAs, and deep learning methods are increasingly used to classify these transcripts. Although these methods have significantly improved the efficiency of identifying lncRNAs, they often lack robustness, and the prediction accuracy tends to vary significantly depending on the quality of the transcript. To tackle this issue, we introduce LoRA-BERT, a novel lncRNA prediction algorithm built on the bidirectional encoder representation from transformers (BERT). LoRA-BERT is designed to effectively capture information at the nucleotide level that is important for lncRNA classification, leading to more robust and accurate prediction outcomes that are not significantly affected by the quality of the input transcript. Through performance evaluations on comprehensive benchmarks, we demonstrate that LoRA-BERT outperforms existing schemes in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. Especially, unlike other methods, LoRA-BERT retains good predictive capability for partial transcripts, a critical feature that makes it applicable for reliable lncRNA prediction even when the sequencing depth is relatively low. Availability and implementation: The code repository is available at https://github.com/Nick-Jeon/LoRA_BERT .

title: scMomer: a pretraining framework for inferring robust cellular representations from single-cell transcriptomes
text: Abstract Foundation models offer new opportunities to capture cellular behavior from large-scale single-cell data. However, their development has been greatly constrained due to the limited availability of multi-omics profiles. Consequently, most models are designed for a single modality (e.g. scRNA-seq, or scATAC-seq, etc.), restricting their ability to capture the diversity of heterogeneous biological systems. Here, we introduce scMomer, a modality-aware pretraining framework designed for multi-modal representation learning under missing modality conditions. scMomer adopts a three-stage pretraining strategy that learns unimodal cell representations, models joint representations from multi-omics data, and distills multi-modal knowledge to enable multi-omics-like representations from unimodal input. Its modality-specific architecture and three-stage pretraining strategy enable effective learning under missing modality conditions and help capture cellular heterogeneity. Through extensive experiments, scMomer generates biologically meaningful embeddings and outperforms state-of-the-art unimodal approaches across diverse gene-level and cell-level downstream tasks, including cross-modality translation, gene function prediction, cell annotation, drug response prediction, and perturbation prediction. Overall, these results demonstrate that scMomer serves as a robust, generalizable, and scalable foundation for single-cell multi-modal analysis under missing modality conditions.

title: CROWN: Curated Repository of Well-Resolved Noncovalent Interactions
text: Abstract The usefulness of structural data sets for machine-learning models of protein–ligand recognition depends not only on their size, but also on how structural imperfections are handled. Existing resources typically trade structural rigor for scale. Recent data sets such as SPINDR improve large-scale structural data through systematic preprocessing, but restrictive inclusion criteria still discard much of the chemical and biological complexity represented in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Here, we present Curated Repository Of Well-resolved Noncovalent interactions (CROWN), a machine-learning–ready data set built around a repair-first curation philosophy: structural inconsistencies are corrected whenever this can be done without compromising experimental evidence at the binding interface, while filtering is reserved for cases that cannot be repaired conservatively. Starting directly from deposited PDB structures, CROWN resolves alternate conformers and connectivity errors, reconstructs complete interaction environments, repairs missing or nonstandard regions outside the binding pocket, assigns protonation states at physiological pH and applies constrained energy minimization using flat-bottomed restraints to relieve local strain while preserving experimentally supported geometry. This strategy yields 193,374 protein–ligand complexes spanning 81,606 PDB entries and 18,516 UniProt accessions, representing more than a 5-fold increase in both complex count and protein diversity relative to SPINDR while retaining a uniform structural representation. Rather than organizing the data set around sparsely available binding-affinity measurements, CROWN adopts a geometry-centric design in which the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms at the binding interface provides the primary source of information. On CASF-2016, CROWN-trained knowledge-based potentials achieved the highest scoring and ranking performance among five training resources, while matching PDBbind- and HiQBind-trained models in docking and screening and consistently outperforming SPINDR-trained counterparts. Together with multiaxis similarity annotations and a companion web interface, CROWN provides a scalable resource for scoring-function development, pose prediction, binder generation, ligand-conditioned protein design, and other structure-based machine-learning applications.
